Outcome
Livestock breeding programs involving farmers come in many forms, shapes and sizes. They are/have been
variously named Farmer-based breeding programs (FBBPs), Farmer-driven breeding programs (FDBP), Community-associated breeding programs (CABPs), participatory breeding programs/approaches (PBP/A), Community-based breeding programs (CBBPs) etc. The latest terminology has been CBBP, which is a genetic improvement strategy in which communities collaborate and make decisions throughout the program's design and implementation and ultimately take ownership of it. Here, we adopt this term, CBBP, and categorize the others as “its variants”, viz. CBBP and its variants. They have been gaining prominence, especially in rural geographies, as the alternatives to centrally managed and/or top-down breeding programmes for livestock genetic improvement. Under the centrally managed and/or top-down breeding programs, nucleus-breeding units, which are managed by state institutions or joint government and donor-driven projects/programs, distribute superior germplasm through natural service or artificial insemination. However, prohibitive costs and low availability of the services offered under centralized breeding schemes have limited their use by farmers. Furthermore, in their initial design and development, they seldom consider farmers’ preferences, needs and resources when selecting breeds and breeding goal traits. In contrast, CBBPs and its variants relinquish control of key choices, decisions and management of breeding programs to farmers who become the foci. As a technology, CBBPs and its variants provide an avenue to break the cycle of poverty for some of the world’s poorest, many of whom depend on farming for their sustenance. They can be instrumental in attaining five of the 17 UN SDGs viz, SDG2 Zero Hunger, SDG5 Gender Equality, SDG8 Decent Work and Economic Growth, SDG13 Climate Action and SDG15 Life on Land. This study collated information on CBBPs and its variants from grey and published literature to showcase their global distribution and possible local impacts where reported. The study shows that such programs were/are being implemented for cattle, sheep, goats, chickens, pigs, llamas and alpacas by smallholder farmers, predominantly in the Global South and are growing in popularity. Although the impact of most CBBPs and its variants has not been assessed, for the few where such information exists, both biological (production and reproduction) and economic impacts have been realized. Their commercial viability has also been vouched and
demonstrated.
Partners
This was an internally initiated study. No partners were involved in its design and execution.
Why did we do this research?
Anecdotal reports indicate that breeding programs involving farmers are gaining in popularity with farmer-based grassroots organizations and government and non-governmental agencies/institutions. They have been touted as a cost-effective and efficient technology that can help achieve the twin objectives of sustainable improvement and conservation of genetic resources. This study collated information showcasing the extent of the implementation of such programs and evidence of their global prominence. The research involved desktop mining of grey and published literature guided by specific keywords, search items and acronyms viz, Community-associated breeding programs, Community-based breeding programs, Farmer-based breeding programs, farmer-driven breeding programs, participatory breeding programs, CABP, CBBP, FBBP, sheep, goats, cattle, chicken, small ruminants, camel, alpaca, llama, guanaco, vicuna, Africa, Asia (east, west, central, south, southeast), America (south and north), Europe (western, eastern). Following the guidelines set out by the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Review and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA), a literature search was executed upon the following information sources: Scopus, EBSCO, Web of Science, PubMed, PubAg, Google and Semantic Scholars for papers with titles and abstracts containing the keywords, search terms and acronyms. The search was executed between September and November 2024 with no limit set on the publication year. Eligible papers were those that reported any information on CBBPs and/or its variants. Eligibility criteria were carefully discussed and agreed upon by the authors, and they were checked against the papers returned by the search strategy to determine their inclusion. After execution of the search strategy, the returned collection was distilled through a 4 stage, incremental screening process made
up of a duplicate review, title review, abstract review, and full-text review, where the bespoke eligibility criteria previously defined would need to be satisfied before a paper could progress to the next stage. Only those papers that would make it past the final screening stage of the full-text review would then be eligible for inclusion in the study. Due to the diversity of countries, breeds, technologies (CBBPs and its variants), and proxy traits involved in each eligible paper, a meta-analysis was deemed unsuitable, as the heterogeneity of the datasets prevented direct comparisons. A thematic analysis was thus considered a more appropriate approach, as this could compensate for the differences between the eligible papers whilst still addressing the research goal of the study. To facilitate this, a data extraction spreadsheet was created, which recorded the key characteristics of each CBBP and its variants as reported in the eligible publications. This covered the country, production system, livestock species when CBBP was started, breeding goal traits, number of CBBPs, any impacts reported, gender involved, etc. A single author completed the quality assessment and data extraction process for each eligible paper, the results of which were then reviewed and confirmed by the remaining authors, where any conflicts were thoroughly discussed and then corrected.
Where have CBBPs and its variants been implemented?
Figure 1 provides a snapshot of the global distribution of CBBPs and its variants (FBBPs, FDBP, CABPs, PBP/A, etc.)
curated from 31 publications (Literature Global Distribution CBBP) from 24 low- and middle-income countries
(LMICs) primarily in the global south. Table 1 provides a summary of the information on the CBBPs and its variants
extracted from the 31 publications (Outcome stories.xlsx). The CBBPs and its variants included five in Latin America, eight in the Middle East and Asia and 11 in Africa. Two web pages reported the implementation of CBBPs (not its variants) in countries across Africa without supporting publications. These are the Rural Solutions Portal (https://ruralsolutionsportal.org/en/-/39585602-9) of IFAD (International Fund for Agricultural Development) and the e-catalogue (https://e-catalogs.taat-africa.org/gov/technologies/community-based- breeding-program) of TAAT (Technologies for African Agricultural Transformation). The latter shows that the CBBP technology has been adopted in 11 African countries (Senegal, Mali, Burkina Faso, Nigeria, Cameroon, South Sudan, Ethiopia, Kenya, Uganda, Tanzania, and Zimbabwe). The survey shows that CBBPs and/or its variant technologies have been adopted exclusively by smallholder farmers in the global south. This is not surprising; the animal breeding industry in the global north is supported by well-structured breeding programs with good performance recording and progeny testing infrastructure that are managed either by the private sector, breed/breeders’ societies, and/or government agencies. Such infrastructure is conspicuously absent in most countries in the global south, but in the few countries where they are present, they are either poorly managed, understaffed and/or underfunded. The survey also shows that CBBPs and variant technologies are/have been implemented for either indigenous or crossbred livestock species, including cattle, sheep, goats, chickens, pigs, llamas and alpacas. The technologies are, therefore, not species-specific. The highest number of CBBPs and/or its variants are implemented for small ruminants (sheep and goats). These are the livestock species that government agencies normally neglect, the private sector and donor communities, but are popular amongst resource- constrained smallholder farmers due to their versatility and low maintenance. In terms of breeding goal traits, the CBBPs and/or its variants target production traits (body weights/size, growth rates, milk production, wool/fleece weight, wool/fleece quality, etc.) with a few including reproductive traits (twinning rates, litter size, age at first parturition, parturition interval, reproductive efficiency).
Have CBBPs and/or its variants had any impact?
Although some countries lack records from the published articles, the number of established CBBPs and/or its variants range from 1 (Indonesia and Mexico) to 200 (Ethiopia). On the other hand, the number of animals involved ranges from 229 (Liberia) to 131,621 (Ethiopia) and for the participating households, these range between 7 (Mexico) to 7000 (Ethiopia). The leading institutions behind the CBBPs and/or its variants include international organizations (e.g., ICARDA), International NGOs (e.g., Farm Africa), National Agricultural Institutes (e.g., Bonga Agricultural Research Center in Ethiopia, National Agricultural Research Center in Jordan and Central Agricultural Institute in Liberia) as well as farmer-based organizations (e.g., Bonga sheep CBBP (Ethiopia), Burundi Goat Breeders Association (Burundi) and Tuvet Cashmere (Kyrgyzstan)). Taken together, this information suggests that CBBPs have/are not only popular with farmers but have/are also popularized and supported by diverse institutions which have been involved in their establishment.
Except for a few, the impact of most of the CBBPs and/or its variants has not been assessed. Kaumbata et al. (2020) report that in Malawi and Uganda, CBBPs have eliminated negative selection in goats, which occurs when fast- growing animals are gifted to relatives/friends to cement social bonds and are sold off or consumed locally, leaving inferior animals for breeding. These, however, are being retained as parental or replacement breeding
stock. A similar outcome has also been reported in Bangladesh, where CBBPs and/or their variants have not only reduced the scarcity of good quality breeding bucks but also made them available in abundance through community buck stations where they are served on time, resulting in successful and increased conception rates (Solaiman et al. 2020). CBBPs and/or its variants have also resulted in improved average 6-month live weight, increased kid survival rates, and improved twining rates for Malawi and Uganda goats (Kaumbata et al. 2020) and improved the birth weights, growth rates and reproductive performance of Black Bengal goats in Bangladesh (Solaiman et al. 2020). Increases in 6-month weights and litter sizes were also reported for three Ethiopian sheep CBBPs (Haile et al. 2020). A dairy community goat crossbreeding project in Kenya more than doubled the population of improved goats in one of its project areas (Peacock et al 2011) while in Turkey, CBBPs and/or its variant reduced lamb mortality rates by at least 3.47% with CBBP and/or its variant farms recording a mortality rate of 6.56% and non-participating farms experiencing a 10.41% mortality rate for the Akkaraman sheep breed (Güngör et al. 2024). In southern Kyrgyzstan, a 2.6-gram increase in cashmere weight per year was reported for a CBBP flock of a Kyrgyzstan goat landrace (Toigonbaev et al., 2023). The study also reports a proliferation of white coat colour (61.5-84.6%) in the flocks, white coat colour being one of the selection criteria.
Apart from positive impacts on production and reproduction, positive economic effects have been reported for a few CBBPs and/or its variants. The major impact has been the improvement in the socio-economic welfare and well-being of participating farmers. Quoted by Peacock et al. (2011), Olubayo and Kairi (2004), and Karanja- Lumumba et al. (2007) showed that households which kept improved goats in a Kenya community dairy goat project earned an average net annual profit of USD 240 from the sale of weaners, culls and breeding stock, and consumed approximately 1.5kg of milk per day. The daily milk consumption contributed to improved food security, human nutrition and health, and the use of rich goat manure enhanced crop yields. Quoting unpublished sources, Kaumbata et al. (2020) also report improved prices of between EUR 21.60 to EUR 30.10 per adult animal for CBBP goats. The study by Haile et al. (2020) reported a 20% increase in income as well as an increase in household meat consumption from the annual slaughter of three rather than one sheep. An analysis by Kassie et al. (2021) revealed that access to small ruminant health services had increased offtake, return per head of sheep/goat, and gross income per adult equivalent. Furthermore, the participants in CBBP also had higher offtake and gross income per capita than those who were not taking part (Kassie et al. 2021). Güngör et al. (2024) assessed the economic impact of the Community-Based Sheep Breeding Program (CBSBP) on gross profit by comparing CBSBP and non-CBSBP farms. Their analysis shows that each CBSBP farm realised, on average, 6209.13 Turkish Lira (USD 1094.92) more gross profit. A comparison of annual gross profit per animal unit equivalent showed that CSBBP farms earned 4576.75 Turkish Lira (USD 807.07) on average, while non-CBSBP farms earned 3683.04 Turkish Lira (USD 649.47). An additional economic worth of 10% on cashmere production was reported by Toigonbaev et al. (2023) from a Kyrgyzstan goat landrace involved in a community breeding project. As noted by Mueller et al. (2015) and Gutu et al. (2015), CBBPs are not only an effective approach for attaining genetic and economic progress; they also build local capacity and ownership and can be very sustainable given the right level of organisation and support among participating farmers.
Are CBBPs and its variants commercially viable?
Lwiza et al. (2024) demonstrated this from the analysis of the net present value (NPV), which can assess the financial viability of investments. The authors analysed the economic feasibility of investing in communal breeding programs by comparing the financial benefits and costs of a baseline scenario involving purely indigenous breeds to a scenario where indigenous breeds are crossed with exotic breeds for cattle and goats. They show that the discounted and undiscounted net benefits of investing in cattle and/or goat breeding were positive, implying investments in CBBPs and/or its variants and whether involving pure- or crossbreeding is economically feasible. The benefit-cost ratios were greater than one; the net benefits were positive, while the initial investment costs were recovered within 4 years. The authors also conducted a sensitivity analysis to assess how changes in discount rates affect the NPV. It reveals that the net benefits remain positive when there are changes in discount rates. This implies that the stability of CBBPs and/or its variants is not significantly affected by changes in discount rates, indicating lower risk and opportunity costs associated with the investment. Nevertheless, farmer groups need to optimize operational efficiency and put strategies in place to manage risks and uncertainties such as disease outbreaks, thefts and accidents.
Is there potential for CBBPs and/or its variants to have a global impact?
No research has attempted to answer this question. Furthermore, the impacts of CBBPs and/or its variants on the overall economy of a country remain uninvestigated using either empirical or non-empirical methods. However, the
fact that CBBPs and/or its variants are having an impact locally, as seen in the previous section of this synthesis, is evidence that they can result in national and global impacts. Thus, the question would be, “How can CBBPs have a global impact, or rather, how can CBBPs be globalized while operating locally?”. For this to happen cost-effectively, CBBPs and/or its variants must evolve to be the universal “lingua franca” for sustainable animal production in the LMICs riding on the momentum of their popularity. Key CBBP players in LMICs should be at the forefront of forming an umbrella body or consortium viz “CBBP Global Consortium”, which can be the vehicle that drives collaboration, transparency, communication and investment in CBBP research, development and adoption (RD&A) along the lines of ICAR (The International Committee For Animal Recording) and its Working Groups. The consortium would provide an open yet secure network for sharing, learning, and interaction between members and interested stakeholders. It would also strive to stimulate sustainable and efficient animal production that is more than the sum of the individual contributions of local CBBPs and/or its variants. In the current era of large-scale phenotyping combined with genomics, the sharing, learning, and interaction would enable CBBPs and/or its variants to participate in across-countries genomic predictions in the attempt to regionalize and/or globalize the CBBPs. Suppose countries agree to share a subset of their genotypes and phenotypes for commonly recorded traits. In that case, it will allow the integration of genomic information into national and international genetic evaluations and in managing long-term genetic gains. The use of information across populations can increase the accuracy of genomic predictions, especially for local populations/breeds that are genetically diverse and numerically low (Rezende et al., 2020). This is a common characteristic for most populations and breeds in the LMICs. Joint genomic evaluations can be beneficial as they provide an opportunity to increase the size of reference populations, especially for novel or lowly-heritable traits, and consequently improve the accuracy of genomic breeding values without high additional costs to producers (Bonifazi et al. 2020, 2022; Berry et al. 2014). Previous studies using simulated and real data have shown that genomic prediction combining different populations is feasible (Haile-Mariam et al. 2015; Su et al. 2016; Gebreyesus et al. 2019). However, the benefits of combining data depend heavily on the genetic distance between the populations/breeds that are used (Lund et al. 2014) as well as the similarity in trait definition.
Next steps
o Compile this information into a peer-reviewed manuscript that can serve as a reference and showcase the global spread and implementation of the CBBP technology.
o Determine the Impact (economic, socio-cultural, environmental preservation, biodiversity enhancement) of the CBBP technology at a national country level where CBBPs have operated the longest, e.g., Ethiopia.

An innovative genetic improvement strategy for sheep and goat that involves the end users, farmers, in the design and implementation of the scheme Breeding programs that are community-based cover a range of situations. Typically, they target low input systems with farmers within a limited geographical area who have a common interest to work together for the improvement of the genetic resources of their animals. Community-based breeding programs (CBBPs) focus on indigenous stock and consider farmers’ needs, views, decisions and active participation, from inception through to implementation. Most importantly, they provide a participatory and bottom-up approach. CBBP combines farmer training to improve selection methods, consisting of pooling community flocks to create a larger gene pool from which breeding animals can be selected, scientific support to provide farmers with information on different breeding options and data collection to monitor how well individual animals perform. The entire community flock is treated as one. Livestock keepers who choose to participate in the program are organized into sheep/goat breeding associations, many of which later evolve into formal cooperatives. Outcome  
The first community-based breeding programs (CBBPs) were launched in 2009, with limited participation in six model villages focusing on three sheep breeds: Bonga, Menz, and Horro (Haile et al., 2019). The program was primarily facilitated through research centres. However, participation steadily increased. Between 2014 and 2021, there were 73 villages and 7,278 households under the CBBP (Getachew et al., 2024). Based on the successful implementation of the program in previous years and the involvement of ICARDA, along with regional and national research institutions and Universities, the number of participating households and flock size saw significant growth from 2022 to 2024. The number of families involved in the CBBP rose to 7,329 in 2022, 8 980 in 2023, and 10,052 in 2024, with 40,309, 49,390, and 55,269 beneficiaries in 2022,2023, and 2024, respectively. The flock size of small ruminants under CBBP also significantly increased by almost ten thousand (ninety-fold) in each of the subsequent three years. Similarly, the number of villages under CBBP has increased dramatically, reaching 101, 120, and 139 villages in 2022, 2023, and 2024, respectively (Table 1). Considering the distribution of CBBPs across the institution, the number of villages under the research system declined slightly from 2022 to 2023 (82 vs 80) but increased by 12 during 2024 (92). In contrast, villages under the Universities have shown an increasing trend over the three years due to the involvement of additional universities and/or expansion of villages (Table 2).
The scaling approach adopted by the Sustainable Animal Productivity for Livelihoods, Nutrition, and Gender Inclusion (SAPLING) initiative, in partnership with the International Center for Agricultural Research in the Dry Areas (ICARDA), successfully expanded the implementation to 141 production unit villages, benefiting 9,212 households. This effort is closely tied to the community-based breeding programs (CBBPs), which provide improved genetic materials (Getachew et al., 2024). The growth of the CBBPs in terms of the number of villages and households, coupled with the collaboration of various stakeholders, highlights the program's success and widespread acceptance within the community.

The geographical coverage of the distribution of the CBBP has also increased. Currently, the CBBP is being implemented in 139 villages across nearly all regional states of Ethiopia, with the exception of Afar, Gambela and Somalia (Graph 1). Among these, 51(37%) of the CBBP villages are found in the Amhara Regional state, followed by Oromia with 28 villages (20%) and South Ethiopia with 21 villages (15 %). The wider distribution of the CBBPs across the country will ensure the scalability of the program by creating learning sites for stakeholders. It also facilitates the establishment of more production units.

Regarding the species of animals considered for CBBP, most of the villages (79.2 %, 80 %, and 73.4 %) adopted sheep, whereas the remaining villages raised goats during the years 2022, 2023, and 2024, respectively (Graph 2). Seventeen different breeds of sheep and eight breeds of goats have been included in CBBPs (Table 3).
A comprehensive comparative study found that small ruminant CBBP members experienced significant improvements in animal performance, including six-month weight, coat colour, survival rates, and lambing intervals, compared to non-members. These improvements have resulted in a 20% increase in income for participating farmers and a 20-50% improvement in the offtake rates of animals sold compared to non-participant farmers (Jimma et al., 2023; Areb et al., 2022; Haile et al. 2020). This significant increase in income is a clear indication of the tangible benefits of the project, making the farmers' livelihoods more secure and sustainable.

Partners
Different regional, national, and international institutes have been involved in the implementation of community- based breeding programs for small ruminants in Ethiopia. Over the past three years,15 Universities have participated, including Bahir Dar, Gondar, Haramaya, Jimma, Wollo, Wachamo, Wolaiyta Sodo, Woldia, Jinka, Mekdela Amba, Injibara, Debark, Mettu, Debre-Birhan, Debre Markoss, and Assosa. Additionally, 15 research centres have contributed, such as Bonga, Debre-Birhan, Gondar, Sekota, Andassa, Bako, Arbaminch, Hawassa, Adami Tulu, Debre-Markoss, Yabello, Jinka, Worabe, and the Tigray Agricultural Research Institute. The Ethiopian Biodiversity Institute, the Water and Land Research Center, and agriculture extension services at various levels have also played a direct role in the implementation of small ruminant CBBP. Their contributions have been instrumental in the success and expansion of the program.
The SAPLING Initiative has been particularly crucial in scaling up CBBP. It has provided overall leadership, capacity building for researchers, communities, and development agents, and created a data management platform. The initiative has also provided important inputs such as animal identification materials, weighing tools, and data capture equipment. Its role in the expansion of the CBBP cannot be overstated, highlighting its importance in the success of the program.
Why did we do this research?
Ethiopia has a large population of small ruminants, with approximately 42.9 million sheep and 52.5 million goats (CSA, 2021). Small ruminant production is one of the major integral parts of Ethiopian agriculture. They play a significant role in the livelihoods of the smallholder farmers and the pastoralists. They provide multiple tangible benefits, such as a source of cash income, food (meat and milk), skin, and manure, as well as intangible benefits, like insurance against emergencies, and ceremonial and cultural significance (Legese and Fadiga, 2014; Wodajo et al., 2020). However, those benefits are far below the country's potential. Among the major contributing factors to low productivity in small ruminants, the lack of appropriate breed improvement programs is the most
significant. In the past, little attention was given to the small ruminant breed improvement program in the country. There were some efforts by the government and non-governmental institutions to improve the breed by introducing exotic breeds for cross-breeding programs. However, except for some success in sheep crossbreeding programs in a few localities, most of the programs were unsuccessful due to the adaption problem of the exotic breeds and lack of sustainability (Workneh et al., 2003; Gizaw et al., 2013; Oumer and Firew, 2017). Because of this problem, selective breeding for the local breed is getting attention as part of the improvement program for small ruminants (Shapiro et al., 2017).
The recent approaches, such as community-based breeding programs (CBBP), are recommended as an alternative for breed improvement for traditionally low-input systems like Ethiopia. CBBP is the breeding program implemented in specific geographical locations by a group of farmers that focuses on Indigenous breeds, encourages active participation, and addresses the challenges of low-input systems (Sölkner et al., 1998; Wurzinger et al., 2011; Haile et al., 2019).
The CBBPs were piloted with three breeds of sheep and six villages in Ethiopia in 2009 (Haile et al., 2019). Upon the successful implementation of these pilot programs, CBBPs expanded in terms of the breeds of small ruminants, species, villages, and participating households. They have been implemented in 73 CBBP villages and 141 production units throughout the country (Belay et al., 2021; Getachew et al., 2024). CBBPs in Ethiopia have shown substantial improvements in important traits such as growth and survival, along with a 20 % increase in income for participating farmers. Additionally, participating farmers consume meat two to three times more than non-participating farmers, which improves their nutritional quality (Haile et al., 2020; Areb et al., 2022; Jimma et al., 2023).
To maximize the program's benefits, the CBBPs need to be scaled up to reach a wider number of small ruminant keepers. Scaling up the program will ensure the participation of more smallholders, increase animal productivity, and contribute to the economic development of rural smallholders.
Engaging the partner institutions is crucial for the scale-up of CBBPs to address the large and small ruminate keepers and to ensure sustainability. Universities and research centres are particularly appropriate for the coordination and implementation of further scaling of CBBPs. By Considering the multiple roles, these institutions can effectively scale innovations as part of their outreach program in nearby villages, thereby ensuring the synergy of their research, education, and community service. As a result, there has been a consistent increase in participation in universities and research centres running CBBP and benefiting from the experience.
Documenting and analyzing the reach-out success in terms of the number of villages, participating households, flock size, breeds, and species across the country and different institutions will help identify successful strategies and areas needing improvement.
Aim
The main aims of this report were to:
o Collect essential data on the level of outreach programs and practices made by SAPLING, ICARDA, Agricultural research institutes, and/or federal universities in the CBBP program.
o Generate outcome stories that showcase the impact and success of the joint efforts made by the partners.
o Use the lessons learned from achievements through this program to inspire further innovation and collaboration in sustainable livestock breeding programs.
Scope:
The current assessment of the program considers only those universities and research centres that have adopted the CBBP program, covering the period from 2022 to 2024.
Evidence  
The study employed purposive sampling of data on outreach activities using the small ruminant CBBP initiative as described in the scope. All institutions participating in the CBBP program have been invited to provide data on various records of the extensions using sheep and goats. The data was collected using Excel spreadsheet templates with the required checklists. The templates were shared for partners in universities, research centres, and non-governmental organizations to fill and send back after proper onboarding. The templates contain mainly the name of the institution, region, type of institution, number of villages involved in CBBP, budget year, breed, species, number of households per institution, and total flock size. The quantitative data collected through the template were analyzed and summarized in Tables 1-3 and Graphs 1-2 for interpretation.
Next steps
o The partner's involvement in CBBP should be further strengthened to ensure its sustainability and wider dissemination.
o The number of villages and flock size of Goats under CBBP should be increased because the Goats are equally important as sheep for smallholder farmers.
o Appropriate CBBP implementation modality needs further efforts to reach the pastoral communities.

Outcome
Community-based breeding programs (CBBPs) have been suggested as alternatives to the often-failed centralized breeding programs in low-input systems. CBBPs have been designed and implemented with clearly defined guidelines (Haile et al., 2018). However, in practice, it's the communities that adapt and innovate, making changes to improve the program's effectiveness. These modifications- whether in field implementation, organizational structure, benefit sharing, or flock management- are largely driven by the communities themselves, highlighting their crucial role in the success of CBBPs. Some examples of innovative approaches followed by communities in different CBBPs which changed CBBP operations are summarized below.
o Some of the cooperatives have built capital through the sale of breeding sires and culled animals. This capital is being used for different purposes, including uplifting the financial status of the members and others. Therefore, they have devised a system where they advance credit to their members and other cooperatives (https://bit.ly/2PpG4Xr).
o In Bonga (Ethiopia) CBBPs, the cooperative members agreed and are in the process of forming a breeding nucleus for elite ewes. They knew that not all ewes are of the same genetic merit and have started identifying the best ewes based on their own criteria and will only allow breeding rams produced from these elite ewes to be used in the communities. The elite ewes shall be retained by their respective owner farmers and will not move into a central station. They are discussing mechanisms to reward farmers whose ewes are selected. Although the initiative is from the farmers, the research team will support the establishment of the nucleus with performance records derived from the breeding database. Hence, the farmer's selection criteria will be augmented with known performance data. Selection on the dam side has been found to result in genetic gain in CBBPs (Jembere et al., 2019). Therefore, the breeder cooperatives are moving towards more effective selection.
o The cooperative leaders have established subgroups based on neighbourhoods. Any information from both the research team and extension is channelled through the subgroups to all the members, ensuring easy and reliable information flow and action.
o Ram/buck sharing and management has been one of the challenges in CBBPs. However, once bought by the cooperatives, the communities have shown resilience and developed different systems of sharing males and managing potential candidate males. This resilience in the face of challenges is commendable and a testament to the dedication of the communities involved in CBBPs. For example, in Bonga (Ethiopia), following the purchase of potential candidate rams, the cooperative leaders decide who keeps the ram depending on the number required in the mating group, individual experience in managing rams, etc. The farmer manages the communal rams for the period the ram is in service, and thereafter, when the ram is sold, the profit realized from its sale (i.e. the difference between the cost when the young ram was bought and when sold) is shared between the farmers and the cooperative. Similar management of bucks was adopted in Malawi CBBP sites.
o Close follow-up is an important element for a successful CBBP. The research and extension team does this. However, in one of the sites (Bonga, Ethiopia), the cooperative leaders also took the initiative to supervise their members every month and provide feedback to the research centre, enumerators, and their members.
o In the Abergelle (Ethiopia) goat CBBP, each CBBP participant operates a savings bank account. All members unanimously agreed to save ETB 200 (equivalent to US$ 5) for every buck kid sold. This has cultivated a saving culture in the community.
Partners
Community-based breeding programs have been underway in Ethiopia since 2009, with numerous partners playing a key role in their implementation and impact. Key contributors include ICARDA, ILRI, the Ethiopian Ministry of Agriculture, the Ethiopian Institute of Agricultural Research, regional agricultural research institutes, Ethiopian universities, Yazerber Private Limited Company, Boku University, AbacusBio from New Zealand, and local community associations.
Why did we do this research?
Breeding programs that rely on centralized nucleus schemes or the importation of exotic germplasm for crossbreeding have generally been unsuccessful and unsustainable in many African countries. In contrast, community-based breeding programs (CBBPs) are now being proposed as alternatives to improve and conserve local breeds. CBBPs, with their participatory approach and community involvement, have shown to be more successful and sustainable than centralized programs. They provide farmers with the knowledge, skills, and support necessary for long-term improvements, making them well-suited for low-input systems and implemented according to clearly defined guidelines (Haile et al., 2018). However, in practice, communities adapt and innovate, making changes to improve the program's effectiveness. These modifications—whether in field implementation, organizational structure, benefit sharing, or flock management—are largely driven by the communities themselves. Documenting these innovations is crucial for guiding future interventions.
Evidence
When rural communities innovate in livestock management, they benefit from more sustainable, cost-effective, and contextually appropriate practices. These innovations, which are often driven by the communities themselves, help improve livestock health, increase productivity, enhance resilience, and contribute to greater economic stability, all while preserving local knowledge and fostering a sense of empowerment and community. Such changes from the established guidelines are captured in various ways, including a scientific paper (https://hdl.handle.net/20.500.11766/69100) and a blog (https://bit.ly/2PpG4Xr). These resources provide detailed evidence of the impact of community innovations, supporting the need for further research and documentation of these practices.
Next steps
o CBBPs have successfully passed the initial pilot phase and are now being scaled globally, marking a significant milestone. This global scaling is a testament to the impact and potential of CBBPs, and it's important to capture and celebrate the innovations, both local and science-based, that have contributed to this success in the scaling operations moving forward. As stakeholders in this global movement, your contributions are invaluable.
o Innovations by communities should be well synthesized and included in the new version of the guidelines for setting CBBPs.

Data was collected in 2018 from randomly selected 302 households, involving both male and female spouses and household heads. It employed descriptive analysis and inferential statistics. The result revealed that men dominated the sheep breeding cooperatives. When intra-household participation is examined, men are found dominating the access and control over key resources in the breeding cooperatives. Breeding Program is launched Published Date June 11, 2024 Published by ICARDA Communication Team Share CBBP in Mali The launch in Mali in 2023 of the country s first-ever community-based breeding scheme for goats demonstrates that when small-scale livestock keepers collaborate, they can improve the genetic potential of their goats and enhance their livelihoods. By including key public, private, and professional stakeholders in the design of the program, ICARDA and ILRI ensure it is tailored to the Malian context and farmers objectives and capacities. Mali s ruminant army Rooted in a rich agropastoral tradition, Mali s small ruminant farming plays a crucial socio-economic role. With over 21 million heads of sheep and more than 29 million heads of goats, the country boasts the largest herd of small ruminants in the West African Economic and Monetary Union. It ranks second in the Economic Community of West African States. The animals are raised for various purposes, including fattening for sale, exporting live animals, milk production, consumption during social events, and other market outlets. As a result, the sector significantly contributes to Mali s economic growth, rural sector production and employment, and export earnings. The sector relies on a wide diversity of small ruminant breeds and populations selectively bred and raised for specific features and agroecological niches. Among them are Short-Hair Maure, Long-Hair Maure, Touareg, Toronke, Bali-Bali, Djallonk , Macina, etc. Additionally, Mali is home to various goat breeds like Peulh, Gu ra, Boureissa, Djallonk , etc. Yet despite their economic and social importance, small ruminants do not receive the necessary research and political attention for sustainable development towards better livelihoods within the subsector, according to Mamadou D. Coulibaly, a leading breeder and livestock genetic improvement expert based in Mali. In a recent report, Dr. Coulibaly underlines multiple constraints limiting small ruminants' production, such as prevalent diseases, some of which are abortive or zoonotic. Other challenges include feed and feeding difficulties, unsuitable habitats, high mobility of sheep flocks, and the absence (or limited scope) of national programs for the genetic improvement of local sheep and goat breeds. "Most goat keepers aspire to have better access to financial capital, supplementary feeds, and capacity reinforcement," says Dr. Coulibaly. "Unfortunately, these constraints are barriers to the sustainable development and profitability of small ruminant breeding in Mali. Research and development activities must prioritize addressing these issues." Community-Based Breeding Programs - Basic training of the enumerators Community-Based Breeding Program (CBBP) is a cost-effective, decentralized, and a participatory approach to enhancing the genetic performance and productivity of small ruminants in low-income communities. Unlike centralized breeding schemes, CBBP is co-developed and implemented by farmer communities, whose active involvement increases the chances of success. Together with the experts, they define clear breeding objectives, meticulously collect performance and pedigree data, evaluate genetic benefits, and select star bucks within the community flock to raise flock quality. To facilitate the delivery of these improved genetics, three reproductive technologies need to be developed with national partners: sires certification, low-cost and low-infrastructure artificial insemination, and pregnancy diagnosis to reduce reproductive losses. ICARDA s extensive experience in Ethiopia, where CBBPs have been successfully rolled out since 2009, suggests that breeding programs are more efficient when participating farmers simultaneously receive a holistic package of technologies that contribute to improved animal health and feeding practices. The first-ever CBBP in Mali: community consultation and co-design ICARDA and ILRI collaborated with national agricultural research systems, local partners, and farming community representatives to unite all stakeholders. Together, they selected the S gou region in south-central Mali as the location for the country s first goat-based CBBP. A workshop was then convened in September 2023, where the program was introduced to all stakeholders, who defined their breeding objectives and selection traits. After deciding on in which communes the CBBP would be rolled out, the participants then opted for a dual breeding objective, prioritizing milk and meat production. They also identified key selection traits, ranking fertility, milk yield, and growth rate as the top three traits. Furthermore, a provisional institutional arrangement involving various international and national stakeholders was presented to participants. Four villages (Siguidolo Were, Nougoula, Bananido, and N r koro) of the Konobougou commune in Segou were identified for implementation in the program. ICARDA and ILRI have since launched the goat CBBP in Siguidolo Were and Nougoula in December 2023. More than 1,300 goats were identified, and enumerators from the communities, along with national experts, were trained and equipped to collect data. Soon, livestock breeders should be able to reap the benefits of the first-ever CBBP in Mali, marking a promising development for Mali s agropastoral future. Outcome
o Mali’s first Community-Based Breeding Program (CBBP) for goats was launched in 2023.
o Many indigenous breeds are included in the program, namely Djallonké, Bali-Bali, Peulh, and others.
o Until now, two CBBPs were established in two villages, namely Siguidolo Wéré and Noukoula in Ségou cercle. The establishment of a third CBBP in Sikasso cercle is now being discussed.
o These villages were chosen for their easy accessibility in terms of distance and security, the predominance of goats as livestock species, the presence of typical open-minded breeders focused on production and organized in cooperatives, the availability of input and service suppliers (health, feed, extension, etc.), and the low prevalence of transhumant livestock farming.
o In Siguidolo Wéré and Noukoula, a total of 183 households were involved in the CBBP, with a total of 1,237 goats identified. The graphs (Figures 1 and 2) below summarize the details of this output.
o Goat selection traits within Mali’s CBBP include fertility, milk yield, growth rate, longevity, adaptability, and resistance to diseases.

Partners  
The International Center for Agricultural Research in the Dry Areas (ICARDA) and the International Livestock Research Institute (ILRI) are leading the establishment of a CBBP in Mali, together with the national partner Institut d’Économie Rurale (IER) that has the national mandate of the conservation and improvement of livestock breeds in the country. IER has adopted the innovation and is actively contributing to the first steps of its implementation.
The design and implementation processes involved key public, private and professional stakeholders, among which are:

Why did we do this research?
Despite its economic and social importance, the breeding sector of small ruminants does not receive the necessary political attention and has multiple constraints that limit production. These constraints include:
o Absence of national programs for genetic improvement.
o Poor practices in managing genetic resources.
o Uncontrolled crossbreeding, which has led to genetic erosion.
o Prevalent health issues (such as abortive and zoonotic diseases).
o Feed and feeding difficulties.
o Unsuitable habitats and high mobility of sheep flocks.
Evidence
The goat CBBP in Mali is currently in its initial implementation phase, and what has been achieved until now includes:
o Active involvement of national partners and engagement of village leaders and key farmers in discussing the objectives of the CBBP and facilitating the implementation.
o Definition of the breeding objectives, together with farmers’ representatives and national partners: Milk and meat production for local goat breeds in the area, with a focus on improving fertility, milk yield, growth rate, longevity, adaptability and resistance to diseases.
o Two enumerators (one male and one female) were trained and recruited to collect data in Siguidolo Wéré and Noukoula villages in Ségou.
o Data recording is ongoing and involves various indicators, such as births, disposals, and milk production;
o The outputs of the analysis of baseline data collected in December 2023, including flock structure and ranking, were presented to farmers to gather their feedback and get their agreement to move forward to the next steps.
Next steps
o Carry out proper and continuous data recording to ensure consistent follow-up and monitoring and accurate performance assessment.
o Recruit more enumerators per village to cover a higher number of flocks efficiently.
o Follow discussions on flock ranking with key informant farmers in the communities.
o Start rounds of sires’ selection and certification.
o Dissemination of bucks improved genetic material within the CBBPs through artificial insemination.
o Synchronizing females’ estrus using adapted and appropriate protocols before artificial insemination.
o Train farmers on integrated packages to improve herd management.
o Expand the geographical limits of the CBBP and spread the innovation across the country (the implementation of a third CBBP in Sikasso is now being discussed).
o Conduct research activities within Mali’s goat CBBP.

Outcome
Livestock breeding programs involving farmers come in many forms, shapes and sizes. They are/have been
variously named Farmer-based breeding programs (FBBPs), Farmer-driven breeding programs (FDBP), Community-associated breeding programs (CABPs), participatory breeding programs/approaches (PBP/A), Community-based breeding programs (CBBPs) etc. The latest terminology has been CBBP, which is a genetic improvement strategy in which communities collaborate and make decisions throughout the program's design and implementation and ultimately take ownership of it. Here, we adopt this term, CBBP, and categorize the others as “its variants”, viz. CBBP and its variants. They have been gaining prominence, especially in rural geographies, as the alternatives to centrally managed and/or top-down breeding programmes for livestock genetic improvement. Under the centrally managed and/or top-down breeding programs, nucleus-breeding units, which are managed by state institutions or joint government and donor-driven projects/programs, distribute superior germplasm through natural service or artificial insemination. However, prohibitive costs and low availability of the services offered under centralized breeding schemes have limited their use by farmers. Furthermore, in their initial design and development, they seldom consider farmers’ preferences, needs and resources when selecting breeds and breeding goal traits. In contrast, CBBPs and its variants relinquish control of key choices, decisions and management of breeding programs to farmers who become the foci. As a technology, CBBPs and its variants provide an avenue to break the cycle of poverty for some of the world’s poorest, many of whom depend on farming for their sustenance. They can be instrumental in attaining five of the 17 UN SDGs viz, SDG2 Zero Hunger, SDG5 Gender Equality, SDG8 Decent Work and Economic Growth, SDG13 Climate Action and SDG15 Life on Land. This study collated information on CBBPs and its variants from grey and published literature to showcase their global distribution and possible local impacts where reported. The study shows that such programs were/are being implemented for cattle, sheep, goats, chickens, pigs, llamas and alpacas by smallholder farmers, predominantly in the Global South and are growing in popularity. Although the impact of most CBBPs and its variants has not been assessed, for the few where such information exists, both biological (production and reproduction) and economic impacts have been realized. Their commercial viability has also been vouched and
demonstrated.
Partners
This was an internally initiated study. No partners were involved in its design and execution.
Why did we do this research?
Anecdotal reports indicate that breeding programs involving farmers are gaining in popularity with farmer-based grassroots organizations and government and non-governmental agencies/institutions. They have been touted as a cost-effective and efficient technology that can help achieve the twin objectives of sustainable improvement and conservation of genetic resources. This study collated information showcasing the extent of the implementation of such programs and evidence of their global prominence. The research involved desktop mining of grey and published literature guided by specific keywords, search items and acronyms viz, Community-associated breeding programs, Community-based breeding programs, Farmer-based breeding programs, farmer-driven breeding programs, participatory breeding programs, CABP, CBBP, FBBP, sheep, goats, cattle, chicken, small ruminants, camel, alpaca, llama, guanaco, vicuna, Africa, Asia (east, west, central, south, southeast), America (south and north), Europe (western, eastern). Following the guidelines set out by the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Review and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA), a literature search was executed upon the following information sources: Scopus, EBSCO, Web of Science, PubMed, PubAg, Google and Semantic Scholars for papers with titles and abstracts containing the keywords, search terms and acronyms. The search was executed between September and November 2024 with no limit set on the publication year. Eligible papers were those that reported any information on CBBPs and/or its variants. Eligibility criteria were carefully discussed and agreed upon by the authors, and they were checked against the papers returned by the search strategy to determine their inclusion. After execution of the search strategy, the returned collection was distilled through a 4 stage, incremental screening process made
up of a duplicate review, title review, abstract review, and full-text review, where the bespoke eligibility criteria previously defined would need to be satisfied before a paper could progress to the next stage. Only those papers that would make it past the final screening stage of the full-text review would then be eligible for inclusion in the study. Due to the diversity of countries, breeds, technologies (CBBPs and its variants), and proxy traits involved in each eligible paper, a meta-analysis was deemed unsuitable, as the heterogeneity of the datasets prevented direct comparisons. A thematic analysis was thus considered a more appropriate approach, as this could compensate for the differences between the eligible papers whilst still addressing the research goal of the study. To facilitate this, a data extraction spreadsheet was created, which recorded the key characteristics of each CBBP and its variants as reported in the eligible publications. This covered the country, production system, livestock species when CBBP was started, breeding goal traits, number of CBBPs, any impacts reported, gender involved, etc. A single author completed the quality assessment and data extraction process for each eligible paper, the results of which were then reviewed and confirmed by the remaining authors, where any conflicts were thoroughly discussed and then corrected.
Where have CBBPs and its variants been implemented?
Figure 1 provides a snapshot of the global distribution of CBBPs and its variants (FBBPs, FDBP, CABPs, PBP/A, etc.)
curated from 31 publications (Literature Global Distribution CBBP) from 24 low- and middle-income countries
(LMICs) primarily in the global south. Table 1 provides a summary of the information on the CBBPs and its variants
extracted from the 31 publications (Outcome stories.xlsx). The CBBPs and its variants included five in Latin America, eight in the Middle East and Asia and 11 in Africa. Two web pages reported the implementation of CBBPs (not its variants) in countries across Africa without supporting publications. These are the Rural Solutions Portal (https://ruralsolutionsportal.org/en/-/39585602-9) of IFAD (International Fund for Agricultural Development) and the e-catalogue (https://e-catalogs.taat-africa.org/gov/technologies/community-based- breeding-program) of TAAT (Technologies for African Agricultural Transformation). The latter shows that the CBBP technology has been adopted in 11 African countries (Senegal, Mali, Burkina Faso, Nigeria, Cameroon, South Sudan, Ethiopia, Kenya, Uganda, Tanzania, and Zimbabwe). The survey shows that CBBPs and/or its variant technologies have been adopted exclusively by smallholder farmers in the global south. This is not surprising; the animal breeding industry in the global north is supported by well-structured breeding programs with good performance recording and progeny testing infrastructure that are managed either by the private sector, breed/breeders’ societies, and/or government agencies. Such infrastructure is conspicuously absent in most countries in the global south, but in the few countries where they are present, they are either poorly managed, understaffed and/or underfunded. The survey also shows that CBBPs and variant technologies are/have been implemented for either indigenous or crossbred livestock species, including cattle, sheep, goats, chickens, pigs, llamas and alpacas. The technologies are, therefore, not species-specific. The highest number of CBBPs and/or its variants are implemented for small ruminants (sheep and goats). These are the livestock species that government agencies normally neglect, the private sector and donor communities, but are popular amongst resource- constrained smallholder farmers due to their versatility and low maintenance. In terms of breeding goal traits, the CBBPs and/or its variants target production traits (body weights/size, growth rates, milk production, wool/fleece weight, wool/fleece quality, etc.) with a few including reproductive traits (twinning rates, litter size, age at first parturition, parturition interval, reproductive efficiency).
Have CBBPs and/or its variants had any impact?
Although some countries lack records from the published articles, the number of established CBBPs and/or its variants range from 1 (Indonesia and Mexico) to 200 (Ethiopia). On the other hand, the number of animals involved ranges from 229 (Liberia) to 131,621 (Ethiopia) and for the participating households, these range between 7 (Mexico) to 7000 (Ethiopia). The leading institutions behind the CBBPs and/or its variants include international organizations (e.g., ICARDA), International NGOs (e.g., Farm Africa), National Agricultural Institutes (e.g., Bonga Agricultural Research Center in Ethiopia, National Agricultural Research Center in Jordan and Central Agricultural Institute in Liberia) as well as farmer-based organizations (e.g., Bonga sheep CBBP (Ethiopia), Burundi Goat Breeders Association (Burundi) and Tuvet Cashmere (Kyrgyzstan)). Taken together, this information suggests that CBBPs have/are not only popular with farmers but have/are also popularized and supported by diverse institutions which have been involved in their establishment.
Except for a few, the impact of most of the CBBPs and/or its variants has not been assessed. Kaumbata et al. (2020) report that in Malawi and Uganda, CBBPs have eliminated negative selection in goats, which occurs when fast- growing animals are gifted to relatives/friends to cement social bonds and are sold off or consumed locally, leaving inferior animals for breeding. These, however, are being retained as parental or replacement breeding
stock. A similar outcome has also been reported in Bangladesh, where CBBPs and/or their variants have not only reduced the scarcity of good quality breeding bucks but also made them available in abundance through community buck stations where they are served on time, resulting in successful and increased conception rates (Solaiman et al. 2020). CBBPs and/or its variants have also resulted in improved average 6-month live weight, increased kid survival rates, and improved twining rates for Malawi and Uganda goats (Kaumbata et al. 2020) and improved the birth weights, growth rates and reproductive performance of Black Bengal goats in Bangladesh (Solaiman et al. 2020). Increases in 6-month weights and litter sizes were also reported for three Ethiopian sheep CBBPs (Haile et al. 2020). A dairy community goat crossbreeding project in Kenya more than doubled the population of improved goats in one of its project areas (Peacock et al 2011) while in Turkey, CBBPs and/or its variant reduced lamb mortality rates by at least 3.47% with CBBP and/or its variant farms recording a mortality rate of 6.56% and non-participating farms experiencing a 10.41% mortality rate for the Akkaraman sheep breed (Güngör et al. 2024). In southern Kyrgyzstan, a 2.6-gram increase in cashmere weight per year was reported for a CBBP flock of a Kyrgyzstan goat landrace (Toigonbaev et al., 2023). The study also reports a proliferation of white coat colour (61.5-84.6%) in the flocks, white coat colour being one of the selection criteria.
Apart from positive impacts on production and reproduction, positive economic effects have been reported for a few CBBPs and/or its variants. The major impact has been the improvement in the socio-economic welfare and well-being of participating farmers. Quoted by Peacock et al. (2011), Olubayo and Kairi (2004), and Karanja- Lumumba et al. (2007) showed that households which kept improved goats in a Kenya community dairy goat project earned an average net annual profit of USD 240 from the sale of weaners, culls and breeding stock, and consumed approximately 1.5kg of milk per day. The daily milk consumption contributed to improved food security, human nutrition and health, and the use of rich goat manure enhanced crop yields. Quoting unpublished sources, Kaumbata et al. (2020) also report improved prices of between EUR 21.60 to EUR 30.10 per adult animal for CBBP goats. The study by Haile et al. (2020) reported a 20% increase in income as well as an increase in household meat consumption from the annual slaughter of three rather than one sheep. An analysis by Kassie et al. (2021) revealed that access to small ruminant health services had increased offtake, return per head of sheep/goat, and gross income per adult equivalent. Furthermore, the participants in CBBP also had higher offtake and gross income per capita than those who were not taking part (Kassie et al. 2021). Güngör et al. (2024) assessed the economic impact of the Community-Based Sheep Breeding Program (CBSBP) on gross profit by comparing CBSBP and non-CBSBP farms. Their analysis shows that each CBSBP farm realised, on average, 6209.13 Turkish Lira (USD 1094.92) more gross profit. A comparison of annual gross profit per animal unit equivalent showed that CSBBP farms earned 4576.75 Turkish Lira (USD 807.07) on average, while non-CBSBP farms earned 3683.04 Turkish Lira (USD 649.47). An additional economic worth of 10% on cashmere production was reported by Toigonbaev et al. (2023) from a Kyrgyzstan goat landrace involved in a community breeding project. As noted by Mueller et al. (2015) and Gutu et al. (2015), CBBPs are not only an effective approach for attaining genetic and economic progress; they also build local capacity and ownership and can be very sustainable given the right level of organisation and support among participating farmers.
Are CBBPs and its variants commercially viable?
Lwiza et al. (2024) demonstrated this from the analysis of the net present value (NPV), which can assess the financial viability of investments. The authors analysed the economic feasibility of investing in communal breeding programs by comparing the financial benefits and costs of a baseline scenario involving purely indigenous breeds to a scenario where indigenous breeds are crossed with exotic breeds for cattle and goats. They show that the discounted and undiscounted net benefits of investing in cattle and/or goat breeding were positive, implying investments in CBBPs and/or its variants and whether involving pure- or crossbreeding is economically feasible. The benefit-cost ratios were greater than one; the net benefits were positive, while the initial investment costs were recovered within 4 years. The authors also conducted a sensitivity analysis to assess how changes in discount rates affect the NPV. It reveals that the net benefits remain positive when there are changes in discount rates. This implies that the stability of CBBPs and/or its variants is not significantly affected by changes in discount rates, indicating lower risk and opportunity costs associated with the investment. Nevertheless, farmer groups need to optimize operational efficiency and put strategies in place to manage risks and uncertainties such as disease outbreaks, thefts and accidents.
Is there potential for CBBPs and/or its variants to have a global impact?
No research has attempted to answer this question. Furthermore, the impacts of CBBPs and/or its variants on the overall economy of a country remain uninvestigated using either empirical or non-empirical methods. However, the
fact that CBBPs and/or its variants are having an impact locally, as seen in the previous section of this synthesis, is evidence that they can result in national and global impacts. Thus, the question would be, “How can CBBPs have a global impact, or rather, how can CBBPs be globalized while operating locally?”. For this to happen cost-effectively, CBBPs and/or its variants must evolve to be the universal “lingua franca” for sustainable animal production in the LMICs riding on the momentum of their popularity. Key CBBP players in LMICs should be at the forefront of forming an umbrella body or consortium viz “CBBP Global Consortium”, which can be the vehicle that drives collaboration, transparency, communication and investment in CBBP research, development and adoption (RD&A) along the lines of ICAR (The International Committee For Animal Recording) and its Working Groups. The consortium would provide an open yet secure network for sharing, learning, and interaction between members and interested stakeholders. It would also strive to stimulate sustainable and efficient animal production that is more than the sum of the individual contributions of local CBBPs and/or its variants. In the current era of large-scale phenotyping combined with genomics, the sharing, learning, and interaction would enable CBBPs and/or its variants to participate in across-countries genomic predictions in the attempt to regionalize and/or globalize the CBBPs. Suppose countries agree to share a subset of their genotypes and phenotypes for commonly recorded traits. In that case, it will allow the integration of genomic information into national and international genetic evaluations and in managing long-term genetic gains. The use of information across populations can increase the accuracy of genomic predictions, especially for local populations/breeds that are genetically diverse and numerically low (Rezende et al., 2020). This is a common characteristic for most populations and breeds in the LMICs. Joint genomic evaluations can be beneficial as they provide an opportunity to increase the size of reference populations, especially for novel or lowly-heritable traits, and consequently improve the accuracy of genomic breeding values without high additional costs to producers (Bonifazi et al. 2020, 2022; Berry et al. 2014). Previous studies using simulated and real data have shown that genomic prediction combining different populations is feasible (Haile-Mariam et al. 2015; Su et al. 2016; Gebreyesus et al. 2019). However, the benefits of combining data depend heavily on the genetic distance between the populations/breeds that are used (Lund et al. 2014) as well as the similarity in trait definition.
Next steps
o Compile this information into a peer-reviewed manuscript that can serve as a reference and showcase the global spread and implementation of the CBBP technology.
o Determine the Impact (economic, socio-cultural, environmental preservation, biodiversity enhancement) of the CBBP technology at a national country level where CBBPs have operated the longest, e.g., Ethiopia.

Title: High-frequency diet quality data collection and mapping
Description: The innovation is end-to-end integrated system that combines citizen engagement for data curation with modern agile analytics to provide real-time and actionable insights about dietary patterns and food system dynamics. The system is made up of three components: citizen-powered high-frequency data collection, user-centered dashboard analytics, and demand-driven reflexive modeling of intervention options. The innovation stands out by leveraging crowdsourced data collection methods that are both cost-efficient and easily deployable, enabling more frequent and accurate insights compared to traditional in-person methods on diets, markets, and transport infrastructure. It aims to serve as scalable platform to engage, inform, and empower individuals and decision-makers; support data-driven and informed decision-making; and provide robust data to inform policies and interventions, direct capital investments to improve food system resilience, and increase preparedness/planning for potential and direct risk. It is already under development with diet quality, food flows, and transport network being mapped in Rwanda and Kenya.

The following text section comes from a specific evidence file named URL https://www.cgiar.org/news-events/news/novel-crowdsourcing-solution-enables-continuous-diet-quality-monitoring-at-a-national-scale/: "Novel crowdsourcing solution enables continuous diet quality monitoring at a national scale From CGIAR Initiative on Digital Innovation Published on 20.06.23 Impact Area Nutrition, health & food security Share this to : Food systems around the world face a triple burden of malnutrition: undernourishment, micronutrient deficiencies and over-nutrition, with different forms of malnutrition seen in the same country or even in the same person. Many datasets are too small, fragmented or infrequent to capture the dynamic, complex, and fragmented changes in diets, which is necessary to build more responsive food systems focused on better nutrition. Researchers with the CGIAR Digital Innovation Initiative have developed a new solution, capable of generating high frequency diet quality data at a population level. Using a simple survey crowdsourced using mobile phones, this technique has been shown to work in Rwanda, generating a dataset of 87,569 records over 52 weeks at a fraction of the cost of traditional, in-person, collection methods. High-frequency crowdsourced diet quality monitoring has the potential to transform the governance of food systems, providing immediate and deep insights into what different people eat and when, and hopefully point towards the drivers of these changes in [near] real-time, said Rhys Manners, a data scientist leading the work since its beginnings at the International Institute of Tropical Agriculture (IITA), in 2021. Screenshot from the Diet Quality Map (https:///www.dietqualitymap.org) How it works The survey is based on the Diet Quality Questionnaire (DQQ), developed by an international team at The Global Diet Quality Project, applied worldwide by organizations such as Gallup Polling, allowing the Rwandan results to be compared against 50 countries. Using simple yes/no questions, the survey records what kinds of foods respondents have eaten and derives several metrics. The DQQ captures different aspects of nutrition while requiring less than 15 minutes to complete. The Global Diet Quality Project worked with local authorities to adjust the survey to the kinds of foods consumed in Rwanda and for translation to the Kinyarwanda language. To deliver the survey, Digital Innovation worked with VIAMO, a social enterprise that provides mobile phone-based information services to almost a tenth of the Rwandan population. Each week, around 18,000 subscribers were invited to participate in the survey, with balanced responses collected across sex and locational weighting. Around 18% of those contacted responded anonymously, receiving an incentive of 0.30 USD in airtime for their time. This has resulted in the generation of a dataset of weekly data, which can be disaggregated by age, sex, location, and economic status, at a cost less than 1 USD per respondent. Even so, the sample was skewed towards younger, middle-income Rwandans, reflecting mobile phone ownership in the country. More information on the data collection system and its deployment is available here: https://doi.org/10.3389/fsufs.2021.804821 What we can learn The crowdsourced data showed the changes underway in Rwandan society, with urban populations consuming both greater amounts of both healthy and unhealthy foods, so that their overall dietary score was lower. Young people under 24 had the lowest quality diets, a cause for concern given the impact that is known to have on health, well-being and opportunities later in life. Women had more diverse diets, but differed from those in other countries who also tend to consume fewer unhealthy foods than men. Having such high-frequency data available also makes it possible to track the immediate impacts of seasonal change and food system shocks on the kinds of foods eaten by different segments of society. This gives policymakers options to reduce the impact of drought, price fluctuations and conflict on nutrition security, and to measure the success of interventions. Next steps In Rwanda, the team will begin to address one of the key questions always directed at crowdsourcing data quality and reliability. The crowdsourced diet quality questionnaire responses will be compared against the same survey collected in-person, and against the gold standard measure for dietary assessment which requires all food to be weighed before it is eaten. High-frequency data collection will begin again in July 2023, continuing fortnightly for 52 weeks. Over the next two years, we will continue to develop the dataset and more tools to monitor food systems, and support the uptake of these approaches by policymakers and other interested partners, said Manners. The crowdsourced diet quality monitoring system is being adapted to work in Guatemala, using a Human Centered Design approach . Without adaptation, true adoption cannot be achieved, said Daniel Jimenez, Digital Innovation work package lead and data scientist with the Alliance of Bioversity International and CIAT. In Guatemala, we understand the need to tailor our approach to suit the specific digital ecosystem and institutions, which may differ from those in Rwanda. Embracing the principles of Human-Centered Design is paramount to ensuring successful adoption. Equally significant is the collaboration between two esteemed CGIAR centers, IITA and the Alliance, as it allows us to operate more efficiently in the region and leverage the expertise of each center . Digital Innovation is researching how dietary quality data can be used in conjunction with other datasets such as high-frequency weather data to create actionable insights for policymakers. The dietary quality data collection dovetails with another project in partnership with the University of Twente to analyze transport networks and the flow of crops from producers to markets in Rwanda. The study was performed from July-August 2023 in the Musan- ze district of northwest Rwanda (Figure 1). Musanze is a high- land region of Rwanda, characterized by high rainfall and vol- canic rich soils. The region is characterized by agricultural sys- tems dominated by potato, a cash crop; and beans, for home consumption. The inhabitants are largely rural, with agriculture dominating economic activities. Musanze was selected due to the high participation rate in the Manners et al. 2.2. Study Structure
2.3. Sample
This work was structured to generate comparable results from reporting of the DQQ (Herforth et al., 202X) across two mo- dalities of reported collection: i) by enumerator administered (enumerator) and ii) self administered using mobile phones (mobile-phone) - Figure 2. The study followed a framework developed by previous studies comparing data collection methods (e.g. Rogers et al. 2021). Data was collected from a socio-economically homogenous group randomly split into two. Reported responses to the DQQ were compared to a weighed food record (WFR) benchmark. Observations of con- sumption from the WFR allowed for generation of a research- er reported ‘observed DQQ’ benchmark.
Unfortunately, no similar studies are available to direct our understanding of the potential effect size of the mode of data collection that includes using mobile-phones. Therefore, we conservatively assumed a medium effect size (0.35) in the differences between the observed-DQQ benchmark and the two groups (enumerator administered and mobile-phone). With this assumption, the sample size for each group was cal- culated, setting the power at 80% and significance level at 5%, providing a sample size of 130. However, we increased this to 150, as we assumed a 15% non-response rate from the mobile- phone group and to account for participant dropouts (Manners et al., 2022). This sample size is consistent with similar stud- ies (e.g. Matthys et al., 2007; Fallaize et al., 2014; Putz et al., 2019).
Data was generated for the observed and reported DQQs across two days. On day one, both groups (enumerator, mobile -phone) were visited by an enumerator, where their consump- tion was recorded through a WFR (see Data Collection). We also collected more general information from the respondents through the rural household multi-indicator survey - RHoMIS (van Wijk, 2020). RHoMIS modularly collects demographic, economic, and agricultural information.
On the second day, the ‘enumerator’ group was visited by a different enumerator who administered the DQQ, a 24-hr re- call, and collected anthropometric data (height, weight, waist, and hip measurements). In contrast, the ‘mobile-phone’ group received a SMS requesting they administer the DQQ using
Although the sample included both male and female partici- pants, previous WFR- based work has concentrated on female respondents, due to local food preparation conditions. We endeavored to perform the WFR with both male and female respondents, aiming for a 50-50 ratio in responses. Although the two groups will not be stratified representatively across sex, age, or economic groups, we expect to be able to derive inferences on any differences in responses across such groups.
2.4. Respondent Recruitment
We deployed an interactive voice response (IVR) messaging system to contact potential respondents who participated in the
