Introduction
In northern Bangladesh, where agriculture has long been a way of life, women are now emerging as entrepreneurs, transforming not just their livelihoods but the dynamics of their communities. With support from the CGIAR Research Initiative on Mixed Farming Systems, small agricultural machinery like fodder choppers, mini rice husking mills, and oil extractors are changing these women's lives.
Agricultural operations are typically labor-intensive and have historically been male-dominated. While women contribute to agriculture, their roles have often been confined to household tasks. The introduction of small agricultural machinery can empower women to take on more active roles in farming. This shift not only increases their involvement in agricultural operations but also opens up new opportunities for income generation for the family.
This is the story of three women from villages in Nilphamari District in Bangladesh—Ratna Begum, Aruna Rani Roy, and Layla Begum—whose lives have been transformed with the involvement of homestead-based small agricultural machinery.
1
Ratna Begum-a Mini Rice Husking Mill Entrepreneur
Ratna Begum, 27, lived a quiet life in Shahbajpur, Rangpur Sadar, managing her household and caring for her two young children. Her husband, Belal Hossain, worked as a seasonal agricultural laborer and a driver during the off-season, bringing in a modest income of BDT 8,000 per month. Without a steady income of her own, Ratna often struggled to make ends meet.
—
Photo 1: Ratna Begum with her mini rice husking mill.
However, everything changed in 2022 when she joined the MFS initiative. Through the program, Ratna received training and was given a mini rice husking mill. This machine opened a new chapter in her life, transforming her into a budding entrepreneur.
“I used to rely entirely on my husband’s income,” Ratna explains. “Now, with the husking mill, I can mill paddy and wheat for my neighbors and earn BDT 200-300 daily. In addition, I buy paddy from farmers, mill them, and sell the rice in the village.”
Within just a few months, Ratna’s business started generating an additional income of BDT 6,000 to 7,500 per month, a significant contribution to her family’s income. Her goal is to expand her business beyond her village, selling milled rice in the city center. As her name spreads, more and more people are coming to her. Every day, she serves at least 8 to 10 customers with paddy and wheat (flour) milling, with some even coming from nearby villages. The convenience she provides has been a game-changer—villagers no longer have to walk three kilometers to get their rice milled. With her machine, she mills 40 kg of rice in just 20 minutes, and women can visit her at any time of the day.
2
Ratna’s dreams of improved packaging and selling her milled rice, aiming to expand further with additional support. “I want to receive more training in packaging and marketing my agricultural products,” she says with determination.
The earnings from her rice milling business now contribute significantly to her family’s daily expenses, support her children's schooling, and provide her with the independence to plan for future business growth. Ratna Begum’s journey from housewife to entrepreneur is a powerful example of how access to the right tools and training can transform lives, proving that women in rural Bangladesh can not only contribute to their household income but also lead successful businesses in agriculture.

3
Aruna Rani Roy-an Oil Extractor Machine Entrepreneur
At 35, Aruna Rani Roy from Akaskuri, Nilphamari, always dreamed of doing more for her family. With two sons—one preparing for his board exams and the other working toward his graduation—Aruna felt immense pressure to provide better opportunities for them. Yet, before joining the MFS project, she was confined to the role of a housewife, relying on her family’s monthly income of around BDT 12,500, which barely covered their basic needs.

Photo 3: Aruna Rani with her oil extracting machine.
Everything changed in 2022 when Aruna became a member of the MFS initiative. She received not only training but also a” Mustard Oil Extractor” machine, which marked the beginning of her journey as a small business owner. With the machine, she started milling mustard seeds from local farmers into mustard oil at the rate of BDT 600/40 kg mustard grain. Besides oil extraction services, she purchases mustard seeds from the village, extracts and filters the oil, packages it, and sells it in the local market at the rate of BDT 220/liter.
The income from her mustard oil business now supports her family’s daily needs, helps her save for her children’s education, and allows her to contribute to their future without relying on loans.
“I never thought I could run a business,” Aruna reflects. “But now I see how much potential there is in mustard oil extraction.”
Every day, Aruna processes 1.5-2 mounds (local unit, 1 mound around 40 kg) of mustard seeds, earning BDT 400-450 daily. During the mustard harvest season, she works tirelessly, making around 12,000 BDT per month—a life-changing boost for her family. She also stores some mustard to extract oil throughout the year, ensuring a continuous income.
4
Her business not only transformed her financial situation but also allowed her to think bigger for her family’s future. Aruna no longer depends on microcredits from local NGOs, which she once had to take to support her sons, including paying for computer training for her elder son. Now, with the income from her mustard oil business, Aruna can save money and invest directly in her children’s futures.
“I’m saving money for my sons now,” she says proudly. “I dream of my eldest joining the army and serving our country. I want to give them a better future.”
The demand for Aruna’s mustard oil has grown, as mustard cultivation in her areas is increasing, and the use of mustard oil in the daily cooking of the villagers is also increasing. Seeing the potential, Aruna dreams of expanding her business further.
For Aruna, the MFS initiative was the key that unlocked her entrepreneurial potential. It gave her the tools and confidence to transform not only her financial situation but also her family’s future.

Layla Begum-a Chopper Machine Entrepreneur
Layla Begum, 35, lives in Loxmichap, Nilphamari, with her husband, a tea stall worker, and their two children—a son in class 10 and a daughter in class 3. Like many women in her village, Layla tended to her homestead and took care of livestock.

However, she found it difficult to keep her cows healthy and productive with limited resources. She used to buy feed for around 800 BDT per month and chop the rice straw by herself for her cows. For the rice straw chopping she needs to spend around 1 hour per day.
Her situation changed dramatically after joining the MFS initiative, where she received training on improved fodder cultivation and a fodder chopper machine. Now she is cultivating improved fodder in her marginal land. The chopper machine allowed her to chop fodder and rice straw efficiently, making her cows healthier and significantly reducing her expenses and saving her time to spend on other household activities. She does not just use the chopper machine for her own fodder and rice straw chopping but also other neighbors as an entrepreneur.
“The fodder chopper has made a huge difference for me,” says Layla. "Earlier, I did not have any income and completely depended on my husband's income. Now I am earning around BDT 4,000-4,500 per month. With the support of IRRI, the fodder cultivation in our village is increasing, and I expect I can earn more when more farmers cultivate fodder, and they habituate with the chopping of fodder and rice straw.”
With her newfound income, Layla no longer has to worry about small expenses. She spends the money as she wishes, enjoying the financial independence that had once seemed out of reach. Her cows are healthier, thanks to the regular supply of fresh, chopped fodder, and she is saving
6
up to buy more cows. Her plan is to expand her business by selling fodder to neighboring farmers at 15 BDT per kilogram in jute bags.
“I feel proud that I can now support my family with my own money,” Layla shares. “Even though I have more work now, the extra income makes it all worth it.”
The income from selling fodder has eased her family’s financial pressures, allowing her to reinvest in livestock and improve her household’s quality of life while saving for future needs.
Layla’s aspirations extend beyond her current achievements. She plans to acquire additional machines, including a mini rice husking mill, and hopes to receive further training in livestock management to expand her business. Her journey from a homestead caretaker to a confident entrepreneur highlights the transformative impact of mechanization and training in rural Bangladesh.
7
Mechanization as a Pathway to Empowerment
For Ratna, Aruna, and Layla, homestead agricultural mechanization was not just about improving their farming practices—it was about opening doors to independence and entrepreneurship. With the support of the MFS initiative, they were able to break free from the traditional limitations placed on women in rural Bangladesh. Each of these women is now a business owner, earning her income and making decisions that shape their family’s future.
Their stories are a testament to the power of small-scale agricultural mechanization. Beyond the machines, what they truly gained was the confidence to step into roles as leaders in their communities, inspiring other women to take similar steps.
As more women like Ratna, Aruna, and Layla embrace entrepreneurship, the rural landscape of Bangladesh is slowly transforming. Mechanization has proven to be more than just a tool for farming—it is a catalyst for change, fostering women’s empowerment and financial independence, one machine at a time.
These women’s successes are only the beginning. With continued support from initiatives like MFS, more women can access the tools and training needed to thrive as entrepreneurs in agriculture. The future holds great promise for women like Ratna, Aruna, and Layla, whose stories demonstrate that with the right resources, women in rural Bangladesh can drive economic and social progress for their families and communities.

Title: Recicle+ Network: Promoting Circular Entrepreneurship in Colombia
Description:
The NATURE+ Initiative aims to establish circular economy innovation hubs in target countries to create an ecosystem for innovation and entrepreneurship in circular economy. In Colombia, partnering strategically with Servicio Nacional de Aprendizaje (SENA), which operates 118 training centers nationwide, a decision was made to form a collaborative network (Recicle +) instead of creating a new center. This network includes SENA, circular economy businesses, and other key players, forming a supportive ecosystem. With the involvement of universities, research centers, incubators, accelerators, and private sector entities, the network aims to broaden its impact. This diverse collaboration seeks to cultivate a supportive environment, encouraging knowledge exchange, training, coaching, and the promotion of circular economy entrepreneurship._x000D_
In 2024, a number of activities have been organized such as innovation challenges, student hackathons, hands-on workshops have strengthened capacities in students, farmers, and local communities, encouraging sustainable practices.

Summary
Problem: Conventional waste management practices in Colombia are unsustainable and inefficient. Circular economy offers a promising solution by recovering resources from waste for agricultural inputs, reducing emissions, and boosting the local economy.
Solution: The RECICLE+ Network aims to promote circular economy entrepreneurship in rural Colombia by:

Identifying and supporting circular economy initiatives: Collaborating with SENA, a key stakeholder in rural entrepreneurship, to identify promising initiatives and provide training, coaching, and mentorship.
• Bootcamp “Emprendimiento Circular”: This three-day bootcamp provides entrepreneurs with valuable skills in innovation, soft skills, market intelligence, gender inclusivity, and strategic planning.
• Circular Economy Innovation Hub: Establishing a network to strengthen entrepreneurship within the circular economy.
• Foster participatory research involving farmers, SENA instructors, and researchers to find and optimize innovation waste revalorization models for rural Colombia.
Background
Adopting a circular economy approach for rural waste management in Colombia has enormous potential to recover resources for agricultural inputs, cut greenhouse gas emission, and benefit the overall local economy. Small-scale business initiatives, if nurtured, can play a vital role in promoting circularity. Therefore, the CGIAR Initiative Nature Positive Solutions (NATURE+) is exploring the opportunities and approaches to involve entrepreneurs with innovative waste management solutions beyond conventional operators who collect and transport waste to landfills. The overall goal was to identify local waste valorization solutions from the agri-food sector from small and medium enterprises led by youth and women. As a first step, a call was launched in November 2022 for the southwestern region of Colombia, covering the departments of Cauca, Caquetá, Nariño, and Valle del Cauca.
A key stakeholder in promoting rural entrepreneurship in Colombia is SENA, the Servicio Nacional de Aprendizaje, a decentralized public institution dedicated to the provision of free vocational and technical training, fostering employability and entrepreneurial development. SENA runs the rural entrepreneurship program called SENA Emprende Rural (SER), which provides on-site training and advisory services to enhance income generation activities. SENA Emprende Rural operates through two pathways: (i) Nurturing rural entrepreneurship through incubation programs, strengthening training, and advisory sessions, and (ii) Enhancing employability by providing specialized training in rural occupations. Active since 2003 and covering 96% of the nation's municipalities, SER emerged as a major force in identifying circular economy business initiatives in the four selected departments. Collaborating with SENA was identified as crucial for effectively promoting circular economy entrepreneurship in rural Colombia.
Collaboration with SENA
Initial meetings with the SER coordinators in each department allowed the identification of circular economy initiatives for potential inclusion in the call. These coordinators provided valuable references to entrepreneurs and even participated in site visits. SER coordinators were identified as potential multipliers, for example, by training rural producers in applying circular economy principles and spotting business opportunities.

Fact Sheet: SENA – Servicio Nacional de Aprendizaje (2022 Highlights)
Background:
Founded in 1957, SENA provides comprehensive professional training to workers, youth, and adults in industries such as commerce, agriculture, mining, and livestock. SENA is a national public institution affiliated with the Ministry of Labor of Colombia. SENA operates in 1,102 out of 1,104 municipalities in Colombia with 33 Regional Offices and 118 training centers.
Educational Offerings:
SENA offers over 3,000 comprehensive training programs at different levels and modalities to meet the needs of various productive sectors. In 2022, SENA trained 6,994,877 apprentices.
SENA operates 84 mobile classrooms providing supplementary education to rural, vulnerable, or hard-to- reach communities. In 2022, 30,210 apprentices benefited.
Rural strategies:
• CampeSENA: A strategy to recognize and strengthen Colombian farmers, promoting economic growth and providing access to SENA programs.
• SENA Emprende Rural: Promotes income generation, employability, and rural entrepreneurship by developing capacities and supporting rural productive initiatives.
• AgroSENA: Strengthens Rural Extension, training extensionists to modernize agriculture and livestock activities. SENA leads the National School for Rural Extension. In 2022, 6,911 extensionists were trained through complementary courses.
Research and Development:
The research, innovation, and technological development Program – SENNOVA, generates capabilities for applied research and experimental development in SENA Training Centers. It develops science, technology, and innovation projects, transferring innovation, productivity, and competitiveness capacities to businesses.
A network of 18 TecnoParques in 13 departments supports technological projects. In 2022, they assisted 3,053 (individuals and businesses).
Funding:
Fondo Emprender is the largest seed capital source in Colombia for creating productive and job-generating enterprises. It has two lines: "Crear" for grant-financed entrepreneurial initiatives and "Crecer" for repayable financing. In 2022, dispensed about 30 million USD, resulting in the creation of 1,743 enterprises.
Source: SENA (2023): Informe de Gestión 2022
Visiting SENA training centers confirmed significant synergies and potential collaboration opportunities, allowing us to gain firsthand knowledge of their infrastructure and meet their professional teams. Exploring their existing capacity-building programs was instrumental in understanding how they could complement the NATURE+ initiative efforts on promoting circular entrepreneurship in Colombia.

The following three SENA training centers were identified as potential multipliers for circular economy and entrepreneurship:
• The Circular Economy Laboratory in Bogotá focuses on providing consultancy, design, and prototyping services for waste utilization solutions. It is equipped with machinery and tools for plastic recycling.
• The National Technical Assistance Center for Industry (ASTIN) in Cali houses the Plastic School, promoting the development of plastics from fossil and organic materials and the recycling of these products. It features machinery, transformation equipment, and laboratories for analyzing and determining product quality.
• The Agricultural Center in Buga, headquarters of the National School of Rural Extension, boasts the country's most modern agro-industrial pilot complex for food processing. A biogas plant and an agroecological farm are being implemented there.
With its training, research, and entrepreneurship programs, SENA qualified as the most strategically significant national ally for integrating circular economy practices in agriculture, given its nationwide presence. In addition, as the head of the National School of Rural Extension, SENA can spread innovative waste management technologies throughout Colombia's rural areas, supporting the government's bold plan to improve the proficiency of the nation's roughly 4000 extensionists.
Motivated by SENA's capabilities, a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) was signed with the Valle del Cauca regional office to establish long-term technical and institutional cooperation. This includes resource mobilization, joint execution of research and innovation projects, and the design of training programs in areas like Circular Economy, Rural Development, and Agricultural Extension. Within the action plan of the MoU, collaboration activities were prioritized, including establishing a Circular Economy Innovation Hub as a collaborative network to strengthen entrepreneurship in the circular economy in Colombia.
RECICLE+ Network for the Promotion of Circular Economy Entrepreneurship
Considering the overarching goal of NATURE+ to establish a circular economy innovation center in each participating country – envisioned as a hub for knowledge exchange, training, coaching and the promotion of circular economy entrepreneurship – fostering collaboration within the expansive reach of SENA became a strategic decision. With its presence spanning the entire territory of Colombia through 118 training centers, it made more sense to create a collaborative network among these diverse centers rather than establishing a new innovation center at a specific location. This collaborative network involves not only SENA but also incorporates circular economy businesses, forming a supportive ecosystem. By involving additional organizations like universities, research centers, business incubators, accelerators, and private sector businesses, the network's reach is intended to be increased. The goal of this group effort is to foster an atmosphere that encourages the development of circular economy businesses. As a result, the collaborative RECICLE+ Network (Red Recicle+ Colombia) was born, offering as a first action, an entrepreneurial pathway consisting of a three stages support program to strengthen circular entrepreneurs' capacities and business models and promote circular economy practices in rural areas of Colombia.

After identifying circular business cases and analyzing their needs through a mini-survey (first stage), the program will provide a holistic approach to training, coaching, mentoring, and networking for entrepreneurs in rural areas. By equipping entrepreneurs with the skills, knowledge, and resources they need to develop and scale up circular business models (second stage), the program aims to create a dynamic ecosystem of circular economy businesses that drive economic growth, environmental sustainability, and social equity in the agri-food sector. The model will leverage innovative financing mechanisms (third stage), such as impact investment, social enterprise, and public- private partnerships, to create a self-sustaining ecosystem of circular economy ventures.
Bootcamp “Emprendimiento Circular”
The Bootcamp “Emprendimiento Circular” forms the second step of the three-stage Program from RECICLE+ in Colombia. Developed by the Nature+ team, this dynamic three-day event sparked creativity, encouraged teamwork, and equiped participants with valuable skills. Guided by expert speakers from SENA, ICESI University and the Alliance of Bioversity and CIAT, participants engaged with modules spanning innovation, soft skills, market intelligence, gender-inclusive contributions, and strategic planning.

Figure 2: Highlights from the “Emprendimiento Circular” Bootcamp Innovation Session (22nd November 2023)
The event showcased 12 impactful circular economy initiatives, with a notable presence of 13 women entrepreneurs, contributing to a rich entrepreneurial diversity. As a cornerstone of NATURE+, the bootcamp not only provided valuable insights and skills but also laid the groundwork for a collaborative network of circular entrepreneurship in Colombia. By offering competent speakers to lead the modules on market intelligence and soft skills for entrepreneurs, SENA enhanced the educational experience for the Bootcamp participants.
Lessons Learned
1. Focus on strong existing institutions: The strategic choice of collaborating with established institutions like SENA proved to be crucial. Making use of SENA’s strong network and resources, as well as its wide outreach, significantly facilitated the identification and engagement of circular economy business initiatives. The existing infrastructure, expertise and widespread coverage of SENA served as a force multiplier, streamlining the process of connecting with entrepreneurs and coordinating efforts across the country.
2. New collaborations and alliances: A supportive environment emerged by the willingness of entrepreneurs to assist each other. The diversity of the group, ranging from initiatives at ideation phase to consolidated businesses underscores the potential for fostering a self-sustaining network where shared expertise and support drive collective success.

3. Building a unified circular economy community: one significant result of the collaboration was the organic emergence of a sense of belonging among entrepreneurs. At the end of the bootcamp the participant businesses expressed an inclination towards formalizing themselves under an association or comparable body. The potential formation of an association reflects a desire for a structured framework that can further amplify their impact and provide a unified voice for circular economy businesses in Colombia.

Outlook - Ways to integrate SENA's resources and capabilities to achieve a broader impact
To achieve a broader impact, we envision integrating SENA's resources and capabilities through collaborative curriculum and training program development. This involves co-designing educational materials that align with circular economy principles. Furthermore, fostering participatory research processes involving farmers, SENA instructors, apprentices, CGIAR researchers aims at adopting and scaling technological solutions for responsible waste management and valorization in the agri-food sector. Training of trainers in circular economy principles and waste valorization technologies is another key aspect of leveraging SENA's capabilities. Additionally, organizing events for the incubation and acceleration of circular economy enterprises is on the agenda to stimulate innovation and entrepreneurship in this field.

This event was developed within the framework of the CGIAR Positive Solutions for Nature Research Initiative. The FlyInnova 2024 challenge focused on addressing two fundamental problems: the management of organic waste in the agri-food sector and the limited technological innovation in the processes of using this waste. The main objective was to promote innovative solutions developed by students, focused on optimizing the use of organic waste through the use of black soldier fly larvae (Hermetia illucens). A total of 64 students from SENA's CDTI and 6 students from the Universidad Aut noma de Occidente participated in the challenge, which was developed in three phases. The main goal was to design and create an automated production unit for the utilization of organic waste through the use of black soldier fly larvae (Hermetia illucens). First phase of the challenge Students worked in multidisciplinary teams to design and prototype the production units during the three phases of the challenge. The first phase, held on September 24 at the Alliance's Regional Headquarters for the Americas, consisted of a bootcamp where participants had the opportunity to learn in depth about each of the production stages of black soldier fly treatment. In addition, they learned essential concepts about the life cycle of this species and participated in practical exercises designed to facilitate their understanding and application in the development of their projects. Second phase of the challenge In the second phase, participants acquired tools and knowledge about the design thinking methodology and prototyping techniques, which marked the beginning of the digital design of the production unit. Subsequently, the SENA and Universidad Aut noma de Occidente students presented their designs during the event: SENA Biodiversity and Sustainability in the Territoriality, held on October 28 by SENA within the framework of COP16. In this space, the students had the opportunity to show their proposals to the public and receive feedback from the Alliance team. Third phase of the challenge One of the designed prototypes was selected and funding was granted for its development. This process included consulting, construction and testing of the automated production unit, which was to integrate a system that would monitor environmental parameters during the waste treatment process. In addition, it had to have a data processing system to collect quantifiable information and a physical unit that was efficient, sustainable and scalable. The physical unit of the prototype consists of three modules that can be separated. The first module is where the larvae are fed with organic waste and the bioconversion process takes place. The second module incorporates a system for the collection of larvae that are ready for metamorphosis to fly. In addition, this section contains a device with humidity, temperature and gas sensors to monitor these environmental parameters. The third module houses the flies and is where the mating and egg collection process takes place. Finally, on December 11, the participants presented the finalized prototype to an evaluation committee made up of the CDTI's main mentors from SENA and the Alliance. Special guests were Andr s Camargo and Diego Villamil, representatives of Residua Biocircular, a company with offices in Mexico and Colombia, recognized for its experience in the valorization of organic waste through the use of black soldier fly larvae. The evaluation committee indicated that: This is a very interesting prototype, which will allow for research trials related to waste bioconversion processes, facilitating real-time monitoring of some of the most important parameters of the process, such as substrate humidity and temperature, and gas generation during the process. On the other hand, Residua Biocircular invited SENA students to visit their facilities in Bucaramanga, Colombia, creating new learning and collaboration opportunities. This type of initiative strengthens the ties between the public education sector and private companies, facilitating the transfer of knowledge and the development of innovative solutions. The FlyInnova 2024 challenge not only allowed students to design an innovative prototype for the use of organic waste, but also immersed them in a real process of technological innovation. Throughout this experience, students applied their creativity and knowledge to develop concrete solutions, driving technological progress in this sector. In addition, it allowed them to address the problems related to organic waste management in the agri-food sector and the limited technological innovation in the processes of utilization of these wastes with soldier fly larvae. Summary
Problem: Conventional waste management practices in Colombia are unsustainable and inefficient. Circular economy offers a promising solution by recovering resources from waste for agricultural inputs, reducing emissions, and boosting the local economy.
Solution: The RECICLE+ Network aims to promote circular economy entrepreneurship in rural Colombia by:

Identifying and supporting circular economy initiatives: Collaborating with SENA, a key stakeholder in rural entrepreneurship, to identify promising initiatives and provide training, coaching, and mentorship.
• Bootcamp “Emprendimiento Circular”: This three-day bootcamp provides entrepreneurs with valuable skills in innovation, soft skills, market intelligence, gender inclusivity, and strategic planning.
• Circular Economy Innovation Hub: Establishing a network to strengthen entrepreneurship within the circular economy.
• Foster participatory research involving farmers, SENA instructors, and researchers to find and optimize innovation waste revalorization models for rural Colombia.
Background
Adopting a circular economy approach for rural waste management in Colombia has enormous potential to recover resources for agricultural inputs, cut greenhouse gas emission, and benefit the overall local economy. Small-scale business initiatives, if nurtured, can play a vital role in promoting circularity. Therefore, the CGIAR Initiative Nature Positive Solutions (NATURE+) is exploring the opportunities and approaches to involve entrepreneurs with innovative waste management solutions beyond conventional operators who collect and transport waste to landfills. The overall goal was to identify local waste valorization solutions from the agri-food sector from small and medium enterprises led by youth and women. As a first step, a call was launched in November 2022 for the southwestern region of Colombia, covering the departments of Cauca, Caquetá, Nariño, and Valle del Cauca.
A key stakeholder in promoting rural entrepreneurship in Colombia is SENA, the Servicio Nacional de Aprendizaje, a decentralized public institution dedicated to the provision of free vocational and technical training, fostering employability and entrepreneurial development. SENA runs the rural entrepreneurship program called SENA Emprende Rural (SER), which provides on-site training and advisory services to enhance income generation activities. SENA Emprende Rural operates through two pathways: (i) Nurturing rural entrepreneurship through incubation programs, strengthening training, and advisory sessions, and (ii) Enhancing employability by providing specialized training in rural occupations. Active since 2003 and covering 96% of the nation's municipalities, SER emerged as a major force in identifying circular economy business initiatives in the four selected departments. Collaborating with SENA was identified as crucial for effectively promoting circular economy entrepreneurship in rural Colombia.
Collaboration with SENA
Initial meetings with the SER coordinators in each department allowed the identification of circular economy initiatives for potential inclusion in the call. These coordinators provided valuable references to entrepreneurs and even participated in site visits. SER coordinators were identified as potential multipliers, for example, by training rural producers in applying circular economy principles and spotting business opportunities.

Fact Sheet: SENA – Servicio Nacional de Aprendizaje (2022 Highlights)
Background:
Founded in 1957, SENA provides comprehensive professional training to workers, youth, and adults in industries such as commerce, agriculture, mining, and livestock. SENA is a national public institution affiliated with the Ministry of Labor of Colombia. SENA operates in 1,102 out of 1,104 municipalities in Colombia with 33 Regional Offices and 118 training centers.
Educational Offerings:
SENA offers over 3,000 comprehensive training programs at different levels and modalities to meet the needs of various productive sectors. In 2022, SENA trained 6,994,877 apprentices.
SENA operates 84 mobile classrooms providing supplementary education to rural, vulnerable, or hard-to- reach communities. In 2022, 30,210 apprentices benefited.
Rural strategies:
• CampeSENA: A strategy to recognize and strengthen Colombian farmers, promoting economic growth and providing access to SENA programs.
• SENA Emprende Rural: Promotes income generation, employability, and rural entrepreneurship by developing capacities and supporting rural productive initiatives.
• AgroSENA: Strengthens Rural Extension, training extensionists to modernize agriculture and livestock activities. SENA leads the National School for Rural Extension. In 2022, 6,911 extensionists were trained through complementary courses.
Research and Development:
The research, innovation, and technological development Program – SENNOVA, generates capabilities for applied research and experimental development in SENA Training Centers. It develops science, technology, and innovation projects, transferring innovation, productivity, and competitiveness capacities to businesses.
A network of 18 TecnoParques in 13 departments supports technological projects. In 2022, they assisted 3,053 (individuals and businesses).
Funding:
Fondo Emprender is the largest seed capital source in Colombia for creating productive and job-generating enterprises. It has two lines: "Crear" for grant-financed entrepreneurial initiatives and "Crecer" for repayable financing. In 2022, dispensed about 30 million USD, resulting in the creation of 1,743 enterprises.
Source: SENA (2023): Informe de Gestión 2022
Visiting SENA training centers confirmed significant synergies and potential collaboration opportunities, allowing us to gain firsthand knowledge of their infrastructure and meet their professional teams. Exploring their existing capacity-building programs was instrumental in understanding how they could complement the NATURE+ initiative efforts on promoting circular entrepreneurship in Colombia.

The following three SENA training centers were identified as potential multipliers for circular economy and entrepreneurship:
• The Circular Economy Laboratory in Bogotá focuses on providing consultancy, design, and prototyping services for waste utilization solutions. It is equipped with machinery and tools for plastic recycling.
• The National Technical Assistance Center for Industry (ASTIN) in Cali houses the Plastic School, promoting the development of plastics from fossil and organic materials and the recycling of these products. It features machinery, transformation equipment, and laboratories for analyzing and determining product quality.
• The Agricultural Center in Buga, headquarters of the National School of Rural Extension, boasts the country's most modern agro-industrial pilot complex for food processing. A biogas plant and an agroecological farm are being implemented there.
With its training, research, and entrepreneurship programs, SENA qualified as the most strategically significant national ally for integrating circular economy practices in agriculture, given its nationwide presence. In addition, as the head of the National School of Rural Extension, SENA can spread innovative waste management technologies throughout Colombia's rural areas, supporting the government's bold plan to improve the proficiency of the nation's roughly 4000 extensionists.
Motivated by SENA's capabilities, a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) was signed with the Valle del Cauca regional office to establish long-term technical and institutional cooperation. This includes resource mobilization, joint execution of research and innovation projects, and the design of training programs in areas like Circular Economy, Rural Development, and Agricultural Extension. Within the action plan of the MoU, collaboration activities were prioritized, including establishing a Circular Economy Innovation Hub as a collaborative network to strengthen entrepreneurship in the circular economy in Colombia.
RECICLE+ Network for the Promotion of Circular Economy Entrepreneurship
Considering the overarching goal of NATURE+ to establish a circular economy innovation center in each participating country – envisioned as a hub for knowledge exchange, training, coaching and the promotion of circular economy entrepreneurship – fostering collaboration within the expansive reach of SENA became a strategic decision. With its presence spanning the entire territory of Colombia through 118 training centers, it made more sense to create a collaborative network among these diverse centers rather than establishing a new innovation center at a specific location. This collaborative network involves not only SENA but also incorporates circular economy businesses, forming a supportive ecosystem. By involving additional organizations like universities, research centers, business incubators, accelerators, and private sector businesses, the network's reach is intended to be increased. The goal of this group effort is to foster an atmosphere that encourages the development of circular economy businesses. As a result, the collaborative RECICLE+ Network (Red Recicle+ Colombia) was born, offering as a first action, an entrepreneurial pathway consisting of a three stages support program to strengthen circular entrepreneurs' capacities and business models and promote circular economy practices in rural areas of Colombia.

After identifying circular business cases and analyzing their needs through a mini-survey (first stage), the program will provide a holistic approach to training, coaching, mentoring, and networking for entrepreneurs in rural areas. By equipping entrepreneurs with the skills, knowledge, and resources they need to develop and scale up circular business models (second stage), the program aims to create a dynamic ecosystem of circular economy businesses that drive economic growth, environmental sustainability, and social equity in the agri-food sector. The model will leverage innovative financing mechanisms (third stage), such as impact investment, social enterprise, and public- private partnerships, to create a self-sustaining ecosystem of circular economy ventures.
Bootcamp “Emprendimiento Circular”
The Bootcamp “Emprendimiento Circular” forms the second step of the three-stage Program from RECICLE+ in Colombia. Developed by the Nature+ team, this dynamic three-day event sparked creativity, encouraged teamwork, and equiped participants with valuable skills. Guided by expert speakers from SENA, ICESI University and the Alliance of Bioversity and CIAT, participants engaged with modules spanning innovation, soft skills, market intelligence, gender-inclusive contributions, and strategic planning.

The event showcased 12 impactful circular economy initiatives, with a notable presence of 13 women entrepreneurs, contributing to a rich entrepreneurial diversity. As a cornerstone of NATURE+, the bootcamp not only provided valuable insights and skills but also laid the groundwork for a collaborative network of circular entrepreneurship in Colombia. By offering competent speakers to lead the modules on market intelligence and soft skills for entrepreneurs, SENA enhanced the educational experience for the Bootcamp participants.
Lessons Learned
1. Focus on strong existing institutions: The strategic choice of collaborating with established institutions like SENA proved to be crucial. Making use of SENA’s strong network and resources, as well as its wide outreach, significantly facilitated the identification and engagement of circular economy business initiatives. The existing infrastructure, expertise and widespread coverage of SENA served as a force multiplier, streamlining the process of connecting with entrepreneurs and coordinating efforts across the country.
2. New collaborations and alliances: A supportive environment emerged by the willingness of entrepreneurs to assist each other. The diversity of the group, ranging from initiatives at ideation phase to consolidated businesses underscores the potential for fostering a self-sustaining network where shared expertise and support drive collective success.

3. Building a unified circular economy community: one significant result of the collaboration was the organic emergence of a sense of belonging among entrepreneurs. At the end of the bootcamp the participant businesses expressed an inclination towards formalizing themselves under an association or comparable body. The potential formation of an association reflects a desire for a structured framework that can further amplify their impact and provide a unified voice for circular economy businesses in Colombia.

Outlook - Ways to integrate SENA's resources and capabilities to achieve a broader impact
To achieve a broader impact, we envision integrating SENA's resources and capabilities through collaborative curriculum and training program development. This involves co-designing educational materials that align with circular economy principles. Furthermore, fostering participatory research processes involving farmers, SENA instructors, apprentices, CGIAR researchers aims at adopting and scaling technological solutions for responsible waste management and valorization in the agri-food sector. Training of trainers in circular economy principles and waste valorization technologies is another key aspect of leveraging SENA's capabilities. Additionally, organizing events for the incubation and acceleration of circular economy enterprises is on the agenda to stimulate innovation and entrepreneurship in this field.

Title: Penside rapid diagnostics for African swine fever for use by veterinarians and veterinary technicans in Low and Middle Income Countries.
Description: Diagnostic of African swine fever(ASF) includes from clinical diagnostics to identification of the agent to serological tests, according to the World Organisation of Animal Health. Clinical diagnostics is often challenging since ASF shares common clinical signs with other pig diseases in its acute form; and for the chronic forms subtle clinical signs can be overlook. Laboratory diagnostics are more accurate, including the identification of the viral particle or the presence of antibodies against the virus. However, all these laboratory test pose the same problem, they are difficult to implement in the field where infrastructures and human expertise is limited. A new generation of rapid lateral flow assays for the ASF diagnostic have been developed by various companies for both viral particle detection and anti-ASF Virus antibodies detection. We evaluated different LFA with interest for the African market. A report with the findings and a proposed way forward will be provided.

Background
African swine fever (ASF) is a highly fatal disease of pigs. It is a threat to the pig industry as it lowers production and significantly impacts on livelihoods of small-scale producers, while outbreaks continue to be reported in Africa, Europe, Asia, and more recently in the Caribbean. There are no globally available treatment nor commercial vaccines against ASF. The most effective measures to control the disease include early detection using rapid diagnostic test and separation of infected animals from healthy ones, usually by culling/disposing affected pigs.
Diagnostic of ASF includes from clinical diagnostics to the identification of the agent and serological tests, according to the World Organization for Animal health (WOAH). Clinical diagnostics is often challenging since ASF shares common clinical signs with other pig diseases (e.g. classical swine fever) in its acute form; and for the chronic forms subtle clinical signs can be overlook. The lesion identification has the limitation of post-mortem diagnostics and not possible to implement in non-death pigs. Laboratory diagnostics are more accurate, including the identification of the viral particle by means of isolation of the virus from animal samples, hemadsorption tests, fluorescent antibody test; or the detection of the viral genome by polymerase chain reaction (PCR). Serological tests are also useful to detect previous exposure to the virus. They include Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA), indirect fluorescent antibody (IFA) test and immunoblotting. However, even if accurate, all these laboratory tests pose the same problem; they are difficult to implement in the field where infrastructures and human expertise are limited or non-existent, as it is the case in countries where the disease is endemic. The time to get results is also key for the control of ASFV in the field and all the mentioned tests do not provide immediate results.
Objectives
A new generation of rapid lateral flow assays (LFAs) for the ASF diagnostic have been developed by various companies for both viral particle detection and anti-ASFV antibody detection. The LFAs need minimal sample manipulation and the results are obtained in minutes. Here, we report on the evaluation of 5 different lateral flow assays from 3 different companies:
INgezimÒ ASF CROM Ag from Gold Standard Diagnostics, Spain.
INgezimÒ ASF CROM Ag 2.0 from Gold Standard Diagnostics, Spain.
- African swine fever virus antigen ASFV Ag rapid test kit from RingBio, China.
- Celltrix p32 Ag test kit, in collaboration with BioApp, South Korea.
- Celltrix p72 Ag test kit, in collaboration with BioApp, South Korea.
The tests were selected for their feasibility to be used in the field in remote areas in Low Medium Income Countries (LMIC): minimal quantity of sample required, minimal sample manipulation, minimal equipment/infrastructure required, ease of use and ease of results reading.
The objective is to compare the performance of the LFA (SOPs under ANNEX 1) with the gold standard laboratory test recommended by Word Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH) and published by King et al., 2011 (SOP under ANNEX 1) for the detection of ASFV genome using p72/B646L qPCR. The limit of detection of the virus particle was evaluated using 4 different ASFV strains and genotypes: Georgia10 (G-II), Ghana2014 (G-I), Kenya1033 (G-IX) and Ken05/TK1 (G-X). The performance of the LFAs in in vivo assays was evaluated using samples from different time points after infection from animals infected with 4 different ASFV strains and genotypes: Georgia10 (G-II), Ghana2014 (G-I), Kenya1033 (G-IX) and Uganda1965 (G-X).

Specific objectives
1) Evaluate the limit of viral particle detection of the LFAs using four genetically distant ASFV strains.
2) Evaluate the timing of viral particle detection of the LFAs using samples from in vivo acute infections.
3) Evaluate the feasibility of LFAs use in field-like conditions.

The results from the LFAs are compared with the progression of the infection and onset of clinical signs (clinical scoring based on King et al., 2011 and in ANNEX 2).

Conclusions
1) All five LFAs can detect all tested African swine fever virus strains and genotypes.
2) The limit of detection for four out of five of the LFAs between 107 -108 viral particles, regardless of the ASFV strain used.
3) Assays A and B can detect the infection at early time points, from day 4, when animals are starting to show signs of disease.
4) Assays A and B are the most feasible to use in the field: no need of refrigeration, no sample manipulation, no need for infrastructure and easy to read.
5) Assays A and B are the best candidates from the evaluated to be implemented in the field.
Recommendations
After the evaluation of five lateral flow assays (LFAs) in vitro and in field-like conditions we selected two assays as promising for implementation in field conditions. We recommend testing both assays (assays A and B) with samples from infected animals at consecutive time points, days 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 and 7. A pilot study in the field testing both assays is a second recommendation. The third recommendation is to assess both assays with samples from animals with a subacute progression of the disease and with lower levels of viremia in blood.

ANNEX 1. SOPs used in the analysis of samples included in this report
INgezim ASF CROM Ag from Gold Standard Diagnostic, Spain.
1. Bring all the reagents to room temperature prior to use.
2. Remove the device from the aluminium pouch and discard the desiccant.
3. Add 20 µl of the whole blood (with anticoagulant) to the round window and wait for one minute.
4. Add 3-4 drops, drop by drop and waiting for the total absorption between drops, of the running buffer on the same round window.
5. Wait 10 minutes to read the results.

Background
African swine fever virus (ASFV) is a large, complex DNA arbovirus (Hakizimana et al., 2020) in the family Asfarviridae (Mebus, 1988), responsible for African swine fever (ASF), which causes severe outbreaks in both domestic and wild pig populations. It is a highly fatal pathogen, with mortality rates reaching 100% in pig herds (Sánchez-Cordón et al., 2018). The disease originally endemic in Africa and Sardinia, has now spread globally posing a threat to the pig industry worldwide (Olesen et al., 2017). Recent epidemics in Russia have caused economic losses of around 1 billion USD, with cases now seen in Eastern Europe, Asia, and the Americas (FAO, 2016; Khomenko et al., 2013). The lack of a globally available safe and effective vaccine against ASFV has driven extensive research into the genetic makeup, protein function, and host-pathogen interactions (García-Belmonte et al., 2019). A major part of this effort involves using DNA plasmids, which are crucial tools in molecular biology for cloning, gene expression, protein production, and functional assays (Stevenson et al., 2021).
Plasmids are small, circular, double-stranded DNA molecules that function independently of chromosomal DNA in various host organisms (Russell and Sambrook, 2001). Since their discovery and integration into recombinant DNA technology, plasmids have become indispensable in research and development labs focused on genetic engineering, recombinant protein design, vaccine
1
development, and the study of gene function and regulation (Russell and Sambrook, 2001). Clinically, plasmids are foundational in developing vaccines and viral vector-based gene therapies (Nagy & Arce, 2020). Researchers can precisely control the number and location of gene expression or translation by manipulating elements such as promoter and terminator sequences, coding regions, selectable markers, and origins of replication (De Wet et al., 1985).
Given their critical role, maintaining a well-organized plasmid collection is crucial for ensuring error-free and reproducible results (Shin et al., 2019). During processes such as cloning, passaging through hosts, or sequence optimization, slight alterations in plasmid sequences can occur (Russell and Sambrook, 2001). Additionally, plasmid quality may degrade over time due to improper storage or contamination (Shin et al., 2019). As plasmid libraries grow, organizing and tracking plasmid properties, location, and usage history becomes increasingly complex (Shin et al., 2019). Many labs implement robust record-keeping and storage practices to address these challenges, using unique identifiers, routine quality control checks, and digital plasmid databases, such as Excel trackers or specialized Laboratory Information Management Systems (LIMS) (Kouprina and Larionov, 2008). These systems require meticulous care and attention; errors in the plasmid backbone, antibiotic resistance markers, selection markers, or bacterial strains used for transformation can result in confusion, mistakes, and wasted resources (Sambrook et al., 2001).
The de novo synthesis (from the beginning) of the genes and further cloning under the control of the CMV promoter will ensure the accuracy of the gene sequences (García-Belmonte et al., 2019). GeneMill, a synthetic biology facility at the University of Liverpool, is a leading expert in DNA design and cloning strategies (Johnson et al., 2016). In the past, constructing a library like this one faced significant drawbacks due to the difficulty of amplifying all 161 ORFs and cloning them into individual plasmids (Kollnberger et al., 2002; Lacasta et al., 2014). In most cases, the alternative was the construction of random libraries (Kollnberger et al., 2002; Lacasta et al., 2014); however, these have intrinsic limitations. The automated DNA assembly technology in GeneMill allowed the fast and efficient cloning of all the studied ASFV ORFs in individual vectors, enabling the study of individual genes of interest (Johnson et al., 2016).
We describe the development of an ASFV plasmid library and the accompanying database, designed to support research efforts in ASF vaccine development, gene function analysis, and protein characterization. The ASFV DNA library will be a valuable antigen-screening resource (Lacasta et al., 2014).
Objectives
This project aimed to create a comprehensive database of plasmid vectors containing all coding genes from the ASFV isolate “Kenya 1033” (Genotype-IX). This database will be accessible to all ILRI researchers, facilitating and accelerating
2
vaccine research and development efforts against African swine fever. By consolidating the antigenic coding sequences of this isolate into a unified resource, the project aims to streamline studies on viral gene functions, immune responses, and the development of effective vaccines.
Methodologies and key results
Plasmid synthesis
The plasmid vectors containing the ASFV genes of the isolate “Kenya 1033” genes were de novo synthesized by GeneMill at Liverpool University UK (Johnson et al., 2016).
Plasmid design and key features
The ASFV plasmid library consists of a collection of plasmids, each containing specific ASFV open reading frames (ORFs). These plasmids are designed for various applications, such as the expression of viral proteins, mutational analysis, and the creation of recombinant viruses. Each plasmid in the library includes the following key elements:
a) Origin of replication that ensures the plasmid can replicate within prokaryotic systems.
b) Promoters that enable controlled expression of ASFV ORFs in mammalian cells, such as the CMV promoter, or selection markers like ampicillin resistance (cat promoter) and puromycin resistance (SV40 promoter).
c) Selectable markers which enable the selection of transformed cells and in this case Ampicillin for selection in prokaryotic systems and Puromycin in eucaryotic systems.
d) Restriction enzyme sites which provide flexibility for cloning and manipulation of the ASFV gene sequences.
e) Tags such as the His-tag (N-terminal) and FLAG-tag (C-terminal) have been included to make it easy to purify expressed proteins.
Plasmid maps
The plasmid sequences were used to develop plasmid maps on SnapGene® (from Dotmatics; available at snapgene.com), and the images (Figure 1) were uploaded to the ILVAC LIMS database (Powered by LabCollector).

Use of restriction enzymes in the ASFV plasmid
library
Restriction enzymes play a crucial role in plasmid manipulation and cloning (Russell and Sambrook, 2001). The ASFV plasmid library includes information on the restriction enzyme sites in each plasmid, allowing for easy cloning of additional gene fragments or modifications. These restriction enzymes allow for the insertion, deletion, or replacement of gene sequences, facilitating the creation of plasmids with different ASFV genes or mutations for various experimental purposes.
The study used BamHI and NotI (double digestion) to release inserted ASFV genes and verify the presence of the inserted ASFV genes (Figure 4).

Potential applications of the ASFV plasmid library
Vaccine development
One of the most important uses of the ASFV plasmid library is in developing recombinant vaccines. By expressing various ASFV proteins in vitro or in vivo, researchers can study the immune responses generated and identify potential vaccine candidates. The plasmids can also be used to create viral vectors or subunit vaccines, which rely on the expression of key ASFV proteins to induce protective immunity in pigs.
Gene function analysis
The ASFV plasmid library can be used to express individual viral proteins in cell culture systems to study their function. This allows researchers to investigate how ASFV proteins interact with host cell machinery, evade the immune response, or contribute to viral replication and pathogenicity. Additionally, plasmids can be used to generate mutations or deletions in ASFV genes, providing insights into the roles of specific genes in the virus life cycle.
Gene editing and mutagenesis studies
The plasmid library facilitates the insertion, deletion, or replacement of gene sequences to study the effects of specific mutations on virus-host interactions and virulence.
Diagnostic assay development
ASFV proteins expressed using the plasmids can be used to develop or improve diagnostic assays, such as enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays (ELISA) or polymerase chain reaction (PCR)-based tests. These assays are critical for detecting ASFV infections early and preventing the spread of the disease.

Maintaining and updating the ASFV plasmid
library
Ensuring the accuracy and usability of the ASFV plasmid library requires careful management. The MS Excel and ILVAC LIMS plasmid database shall be updated regularly to reflect the addition of new plasmids, sequence verifications, and any changes in plasmid properties. Quality control measures, including periodic plasmid sequencing and restriction enzyme digestion checks, are implemented to prevent errors and ensure the integrity of the plasmid library.
Conclusions
The ASFV plasmid library and accompanying database represent a valuable resource for the research community, facilitating studies on ASFV biology, vaccine development, potential therapeutics and diagnostics. By organizing key plasmid information in a searchable, accessible format and including detailed information on restriction enzyme sites, the library supports efficient, high-quality research. As the library expands, it will continue to play a central role in advancing our understanding of ASFV and developing effective control strategies for this devastating disease.
The development of this plasmid library also offers a critical resource for accelerating not only African swine fever (ASF) vaccine research and molecular investigations but also paves the way for broader applications across various microorganisms, enhancing the scope of pathogen research and vaccine development.

Background
African swine fever (ASF) is a highly fatal disease of pigs. It is a threat to the pig industry as it lowers production and significantly impacts on livelihoods of small-scale producers, while outbreaks continue to be reported in Africa, Europe, Asia, and more recently in the Caribbean. There are no globally available treatment nor commercial vaccines against ASF. The most effective measures to control the disease include early detection using rapid diagnostic test and separation of infected animals from healthy ones, usually by culling/disposing affected pigs.
Diagnostics of ASF range from clinical diagnostics to the identification of the agent and serological tests, according to the World Organisation for Animal Health. Clinical diagnostics are often challenging since ASF shares common clinical signs with other pig diseases (e.g. classical swine fever) in its acute form; and for the chronic forms subtle clinical signs can be overlooked. The lesion identification has the limitation of post-mortem diagnostics and not possible to implement in non-death pigs.
Laboratory diagnostics are more accurate, including the identification of the viral particle by means of isolation of the virus from animal samples, hemadsorption tests, fluorescent antibody test; or the detection of the viral genome by polymerase chain reaction.
Serological tests are also useful to detect previous exposure to the virus. They include enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA), indirect fluorescent antibody test and immunoblotting.
However, even if accurate, all these laboratory tests pose the same problem; they are difficult to implement in the field where infrastructures and human expertise are limited or non-existent, as it is the case in countries where the disease is endemic. The time to get results is also key for the control of African swine fever virus (ASFV) in the field and all the mentioned tests do not provide immediate results.
Objectives
A new generation of rapid lateral flow assays (LFAs) for the ASF diagnostic have been developed by various companies for both viral particle detection and anti-ASFV antibody detection. The LFAs need minimal sample manipulation and the results are obtained in minutes. Here, we report on the evaluation of 2 different lateral flow assays from 2 different companies:
- Herdscreen ASFV test from Global DX.
INgezim PPA CROM Anticuerpo from Gold Standard Diagnostics.
The tests were selected for their feasibility to be used in the field in remote areas in Low Medium Income Countries (LMICs): minimal quantity of sample required, minimal sample manipulation, minimal equipment/infrastructure required, ease of use and ease of results reading.
The objective was to compare the performance of the two LFA (SOPs under ANNEX 1) with the gold standard laboratory test used by the majority of the research community, INgezim PPA COMPAC (11.PPA.K.3/5) competitive ELISA (SOP under ANNEX 1) detecting antibodies against the p72 ASFV protein.
The LFAs were evaluated using positive and negative domestic pig (Sus scrofa domesticus) serum samples from in vivo experiments performed at the International Livestock Research Institute (ILRI) and warthog (Phacochoerus africanus) samples from outbreak areas in Kenya to evaluate sensitivity and specificity of the assays. Positive domestic pig samples

were used at serial dilutions to evaluate the limit of detection of the assays compared to the gold standard test.
Specific objectives
Objective 1: Evaluate the sensitivity and specificity of the LFAs using domestic and wild pig serum samples.
Objective 2: Evaluate the limit of detection of the LFAs using positive domestic pig serum samples.
Objective 3: Evaluate the feasibility of LFAs use in field-like conditions.

Conclusions
1) Both tests are very similar in sample manipulation and ease of use.
2) Both assays have a specificity of 100%, no false positive samples.
3) Assay 1 has better sensitivity than Assay 2 (100% versus 78.9%).

Recommendations

Background
African swine fever (ASF) is a highly fatal disease of pigs. It is a threat to the pig industry as it lowers production and significantly impacts on livelihoods of small-scale producers, while outbreaks continue to be reported in Africa, Europe, Asia, and more recently in the Caribbean. There are no globally available treatment nor commercial vaccines against ASF. The most effective measures to control the disease include early detection using rapid diagnostic test and separation of infected animals from healthy ones, usually by culling/disposing affected pigs.
Diagnostic of ASF includes from clinical diagnostics to the identification of the agent and serological tests, according to the World Organization for Animal health (WOAH). Clinical diagnostics is often challenging since ASF shares common clinical signs with other pig diseases (e.g. classical swine fever) in its acute form; and for the chronic forms subtle clinical signs can be overlook. The lesion identification has the limitation of post-mortem diagnostics and not possible to implement in non-death pigs. Laboratory diagnostics are more accurate, including the identification of the viral particle by means of isolation of the virus from animal samples, hemadsorption tests, fluorescent antibody test; or the detection of the viral genome by polymerase chain reaction (PCR). Serological tests are also useful to detect previous exposure to the virus. They include Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA), indirect fluorescent antibody (IFA) test and immunoblotting. However, even if accurate, all these laboratory tests pose the same problem; they are difficult to implement in the field where infrastructures and human expertise are limited or non-existent, as it is the case in countries where the disease is endemic. The time to get results is also key for the control of ASFV in the field and all the mentioned tests do not provide immediate results.
Objectives
A new generation of rapid lateral flow assays (LFAs) for the ASF diagnostic have been developed by various companies for both viral particle detection and anti-ASFV antibody detection. The LFAs need minimal sample manipulation and the results are obtained in minutes. Here, we report on the evaluation of 5 different lateral flow assays from 3 different companies:
INgezimÒ ASF CROM Ag from Gold Standard Diagnostics, Spain.
INgezimÒ ASF CROM Ag 2.0 from Gold Standard Diagnostics, Spain.
- African swine fever virus antigen ASFV Ag rapid test kit from RingBio, China.
- Celltrix p32 Ag test kit, in collaboration with BioApp, South Korea.
- Celltrix p72 Ag test kit, in collaboration with BioApp, South Korea.
The tests were selected for their feasibility to be used in the field in remote areas in Low Medium Income Countries (LMIC): minimal quantity of sample required, minimal sample manipulation, minimal equipment/infrastructure required, ease of use and ease of results reading.
The objective is to compare the performance of the LFA (SOPs under ANNEX 1) with the gold standard laboratory test recommended by Word Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH) and published by King et al., 2011 (SOP under ANNEX 1) for the detection of ASFV genome using p72/B646L qPCR. The limit of detection of the virus particle was evaluated using 4 different ASFV strains and genotypes: Georgia10 (G-II), Ghana2014 (G-I), Kenya1033 (G-IX) and Ken05/TK1 (G-X). The performance of the LFAs in in vivo assays was evaluated using samples from different time points after infection from animals infected with 4 different ASFV strains and genotypes: Georgia10 (G-II), Ghana2014 (G-I), Kenya1033 (G-IX) and Uganda1965 (G-X).

Specific objectives
1) Evaluate the limit of viral particle detection of the LFAs using four genetically distant ASFV strains.
2) Evaluate the timing of viral particle detection of the LFAs using samples from in vivo acute infections.
3) Evaluate the feasibility of LFAs use in field-like conditions.

Conclusions
1) All five LFAs can detect all tested African swine fever virus strains and genotypes.
2) The limit of detection for four out of five of the LFAs between 107 -108 viral particles, regardless of the ASFV strain used.
3) Assays A and B can detect the infection at early time points, from day 4, when animals are starting to show signs of disease.
4) Assays A and B are the most feasible to use in the field: no need of refrigeration, no sample manipulation, no need for infrastructure and easy to read.
5) Assays A and B are the best candidates from the evaluated to be implemented in the field.
Recommendations
After the evaluation of five lateral flow assays (LFAs) in vitro and in field-like conditions we selected two assays as promising for implementation in field conditions. We recommend testing both assays (assays A and B) with samples from infected animals at consecutive time points, days 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 and 7. A pilot study in the field testing both assays is a second recommendation. The third recommendation is to assess both assays with samples from animals with a subacute progression of the disease and with lower levels of viremia in blood.

This report presents the development of an ASFV plasmid library and a corresponding database to support research efforts in ASF vaccine development, gene function analysis, and protein characterization. The library contains plasmids encoding 161 ASFV open reading frames (ORFs) cloned under the control of a CMV promoter. The plasmid collection facilitates antigen screening and functional assays with restriction enzyme sites within the plasmids that can be leveraged for cloning and expression studies, ensuring the versatility and reproducibility of the ASFV research. The development of this plasmid library is a crucial resource for accelerating ASF vaccine research and advancing molecular studies. It also establishes a foundation for its application to other microorganisms, enhancing its utility in broader infectious disease research.
Background
African swine fever virus (ASFV) is a large, complex DNA arbovirus (Hakizimana et al., 2020) in the family Asfarviridae (Mebus, 1988), responsible for African swine fever (ASF), which causes severe outbreaks in both domestic and wild pig populations. It is a highly fatal pathogen, with mortality rates reaching 100% in pig herds (Sánchez-Cordón et al., 2018). The disease originally endemic in Africa and Sardinia, has now spread globally posing a threat to the pig industry worldwide (Olesen et al., 2017). Recent epidemics in Russia have caused economic losses of around 1 billion USD, with cases now seen in Eastern Europe, Asia, and the Americas (FAO, 2016; Khomenko et al., 2013). The lack of a globally available safe and effective vaccine against ASFV has driven extensive research into the genetic makeup, protein function, and host-pathogen interactions (García-Belmonte et al., 2019). A major part of this effort involves using DNA plasmids, which are crucial tools in molecular biology for cloning, gene expression, protein production, and functional assays (Stevenson et al., 2021).
Plasmids are small, circular, double-stranded DNA molecules that function independently of chromosomal DNA in various host organisms (Russell and Sambrook, 2001). Since their discovery and integration into recombinant DNA technology, plasmids have become indispensable in research and development labs focused on genetic engineering, recombinant protein design, vaccine

development, and the study of gene function and regulation (Russell and Sambrook, 2001). Clinically, plasmids are foundational in developing vaccines and viral vector-based gene therapies (Nagy & Arce, 2020). Researchers can precisely control the number and location of gene expression or translation by manipulating elements such as promoter and terminator sequences, coding regions, selectable markers, and origins of replication (De Wet et al., 1985).
Given their critical role, maintaining a well-organized plasmid collection is crucial for ensuring error-free and reproducible results (Shin et al., 2019). During processes such as cloning, passaging through hosts, or sequence optimization, slight alterations in plasmid sequences can occur (Russell and Sambrook, 2001). Additionally, plasmid quality may degrade over time due to improper storage or contamination (Shin et al., 2019). As plasmid libraries grow, organizing and tracking plasmid properties, location, and usage history becomes increasingly complex (Shin et al., 2019). Many labs implement robust record-keeping and storage practices to address these challenges, using unique identifiers, routine quality control checks, and digital plasmid databases, such as Excel trackers or specialized Laboratory Information Management Systems (LIMS) (Kouprina and Larionov, 2008). These systems require meticulous care and attention; errors in the plasmid backbone, antibiotic resistance markers, selection markers, or bacterial strains used for transformation can result in confusion, mistakes, and wasted resources (Sambrook et al., 2001).
The de novo synthesis (from the beginning) of the genes and further cloning under the control of the CMV promoter will ensure the accuracy of the gene sequences (García-Belmonte et al., 2019). GeneMill, a synthetic biology facility at the University of Liverpool, is a leading expert in DNA design and cloning strategies (Johnson et al., 2016). In the past, constructing a library like this one faced significant drawbacks due to the difficulty of amplifying all 161 ORFs and cloning them into individual plasmids (Kollnberger et al., 2002; Lacasta et al., 2014). In most cases, the alternative was the construction of random libraries (Kollnberger et al., 2002; Lacasta et al., 2014); however, these have intrinsic limitations. The automated DNA assembly technology in GeneMill allowed the fast and efficient cloning of all the studied ASFV ORFs in individual vectors, enabling the study of individual genes of interest (Johnson et al., 2016).
We describe the development of an ASFV plasmid library and the accompanying database, designed to support research efforts in ASF vaccine development, gene function analysis, and protein characterization. The ASFV DNA library will be a valuable antigen-screening resource (Lacasta et al., 2014).
Objectives
This project aimed to create a comprehensive database of plasmid vectors containing all coding genes from the ASFV isolate “Kenya 1033” (Genotype-IX). This database will be accessible to all ILRI researchers, facilitating and accelerating
2
vaccine research and development efforts against African swine fever. By consolidating the antigenic coding sequences of this isolate into a unified resource, the project aims to streamline studies on viral gene functions, immune responses, and the development of effective vaccines.
Methodologies and key results
Plasmid synthesis
The plasmid vectors containing the ASFV genes of the isolate “Kenya 1033” genes were de novo synthesized by GeneMill at Liverpool University UK (Johnson et al., 2016).
Plasmid design and key features
The ASFV plasmid library consists of a collection of plasmids, each containing specific ASFV open reading frames (ORFs). These plasmids are designed for various applications, such as the expression of viral proteins, mutational analysis, and the creation of recombinant viruses. Each plasmid in the library includes the following key elements:
a) Origin of replication that ensures the plasmid can replicate within prokaryotic systems.
b) Promoters that enable controlled expression of ASFV ORFs in mammalian cells, such as the CMV promoter, or selection markers like ampicillin resistance (cat promoter) and puromycin resistance (SV40 promoter).
c) Selectable markers which enable the selection of transformed cells and in this case Ampicillin for selection in prokaryotic systems and Puromycin in eucaryotic systems.
d) Restriction enzyme sites which provide flexibility for cloning and manipulation of the ASFV gene sequences.
e) Tags such as the His-tag (N-terminal) and FLAG-tag (C-terminal) have been included to make it easy to purify expressed proteins.
Plasmid maps
The plasmid sequences were used to develop plasmid maps on SnapGene® (from Dotmatics; available at snapgene.com), and the images (Figure 1) were uploaded to the ILVAC LIMS database (Powered by LabCollector).

Organization of the plasmid library in MS Excel and ILVAC LIMS database
The library is managed through an organized Microsoft Excel database (Figure 2 and https://hdl.handle.net/20.500.11766.1/FK2/6NKCMQ ) and ILVAC LIMS database (Figure 3), which is structured to include the following columns:
a) Plasmid ID: A unique identifier for each plasmid.
b) ASFV ORF Name: The name of the ASFV ORF or gene fragment cloned into the plasmid.
c) Insert Size: The length of the ASFV gene insert (in base pairs).
d) Promoter: The promoter used for gene expression.
e) Selectable Marker: The antibiotic resistance marker is included in the plasmid.
f) Restriction Enzyme Sites: A list of restriction sites available for cloning or linearization.
g) Sequence: Whether the plasmid sequence has been confirmed by sequencing.
h) Application: The intended use of the plasmid (e.g., protein expression, mutagenesis).
i) Storage Location: Details on the physical location of the plasmid and bacteria glycerol stocks prepared in the lab freezer or storage facility.

Use of restriction enzymes in the ASFV plasmid
library
Restriction enzymes play a crucial role in plasmid manipulation and cloning (Russell and Sambrook, 2001). The ASFV plasmid library includes information on the restriction enzyme sites in each plasmid, allowing for easy cloning of additional gene fragments or modifications. These restriction enzymes allow for the insertion, deletion, or replacement of gene sequences, facilitating the creation of plasmids with different ASFV genes or mutations for various experimental purposes.
The study used BamHI and NotI (double digestion) to release inserted ASFV genes and verify the presence of the inserted ASFV genes (Figure 4).
