Background
The highlands of North Shoa in Amhara region are dominated by cereals (wheat, barley and tef) followed by food legumes. The productivity of cereals and food legumes is low due to biotic and abiotic factors as well as insufficient input supplies like certified seed, inoculants, and other inputs. Because of diseases and insect pests, acidity and water logging problems, farmers are reducing areas of food legumes and growing more cereals leading to low crop diversity leading to reduced soil fertility, incomes, and food diversity. Several cereal and food legume varieties are released by many centres but did not reach farmers due to limited demonstration to create awareness and demand and shortage of quality early generation seed. The poor access to quality seed contributes to low crop productivity.
Objectives
Identifying farmer preferred cereal and legume varieties.
2. Production of early generation seed of food and legume varieties; and
3. Creating awareness and demand of new varieties to growers.
Methodologies
Participatory variety selection of food legumes and food oat:
PVS trials of desi chickpea, faba bean, field pea and food oat were conducted on farmers’ fields and Farmer Training Centres (FTCs) in Moretina Jiru,Siyadebir- wayu, Menz-Lalo and Basona Worana districts in North Shoa. The plot size for each variety of food legumes and food oat was 25 m2. All recommended agronomic practices were applied to the trials.
Chickpea and lentil: The PVS trials were planted in 2022 and evaluations were made in 2023 for both crops. Six desi chickpea varieties (Eshete, Dimtu, Natoli, Mastewal, Girar, Dalota) released by different centres were evaluated as mother-baby trial in three farmer fields and one FTC in Moretina-Jiru district. Eight released lentil varieties (Beredu, Furi, Derash, Alem Tena, Jiru, Alemay and Debine) with local check were planted at one FTC and three farmers’ fields in Moretina Jiru, Siyadebirna Wayu and Menz Lalo districts in 2022/23 cropping season.
Faba bean and field pea: Six released faba bean varieties (Shewa, Gora, Dagim, Walki, Chalew and Hachalu) were planted at one FTC and one farmer field in Woiramba kebele, Moretina Jiru district and one farmer field each at Aba- mote and Mush kebeles in Basona-Worana district. Three released field pea varieties (Jeldu, Bilalo and Etatu) with local checks were planted at two farmers’ fields in Aba Mote and Mush kebeles in Basona-Worana district.
Food oat: As an alternative crop to acid affected soils in the highlands, four released food oat varieties (Tena, Enat, Hulegeb and Sorataf) were planted in two farmers’ fields in Aba Mote and Mush kebeles in Basona-Worana district.
Early generation seed production: Breeder seed of bread wheat, barley and faba bean were planted in 2023/2024 cropping season under rainfed condition in research stations and farmers’ fields in North Shoa zone.
Demonstration of cereal and food legume varieties and
liquid foliar fertilizer: A bread wheat variety Emegwa released in 2022 for North Shoa and similar highlands for its high yield was demonstrated in Moretina Jiru (Kusaye and Woiramba kebeles) and Menz Lalo (Tole and 05 kebeles) districts on 100m2 plots on 10 farmer’s fields and two farmer training centers. Moreover, four bread wheat varieties (Boru, Hachalu, Dursa and Galan) selected from 2022 PVS were demonstrated in Basona-Worana (four farmers) and Moretina Jiru (four farmers) districts.
Two farmers preferred food barley varieties (Hagere and HB1307) were demonstrated in one female farmer at Mush kebele in Basona-Worana district. Nationally registered liquid foliar fertilizer (WUXAL foliar liquid fertilizer) containing macro and micronutrients was demonstrated on bread wheat on three farmers’ fields and faba bean on four farmer fields in North Shoa.
Results
Participatory variety selections
Chickpea: The most important criteria of variety selection were grain yield followed by adaptation, frost, and disease resistance. A total of 32 (10 female) farmers and three experts evaluated the varieties using traits identified by farmers (Fig 1). Based on male and female farmer ranking, cvs. Mastewal and Natoli were selected for further seed production and scaling in 2023/2024 cropping season.

Figure 0.1 Participatory variety Selection of Desi Chickpea, North Shoa, Ethiopia
Lentil: Farmers preferred cv. Jiru in the three districts based on key criteria for diseases and agronomic traits (Fig. 2) as compared to the most popular cvs. Alemaya and Derash (Table 1). Although local lentil varieties are preferred by farmers, during rust epidemics farmers can lose all their crops. For the past five years, viruses like Pea seed born mosaic virus (PsBMV) have been devastating lentil crops in North Shoa due to vector activities and infected seeds. High virus epidemics was observed in SiyaDebir-Wayu and Moretina-Jiru districts and varieties showed different levels of reactions to virus infection (Table 2).

Early generation seed production of cereals and food legumes
To increase availability and access to certiﬁed seed, production of early generation seed (breeder, pre-basic and basic seeds) of farmer preferred varieties of bread wheat (Emegwa, Tsehay and Dendaa), food barley (cvs. HB1307 and Hagere), malt barley (cv. Holker) and faba bean (cvs. Shewa, Walki and Hacahlu) was carried out on 6.3 ha in two districts of North Shoa. A total of 2.13 t of nine varieties of bread wheat, malt barley, food barley and faba bean was produced for next year pre-basic seed production.

Conclusion
The activities were jointly implemented with ARARI, Debre Berhan Agricultural Research Centre to increase the availability of male and female preferred varieties for community seed growers. The cereal and faba bean varieties were selected by farmers through PVS by different projects in North Shoa. Through the support of SI-MFS, production of breeder seed by research center can contribute to drive scaling in the coming season and beyond. The faba bean varieties are targeted to waterlogged black soils in North Shoa.

Activities will be implemented in six focus countries globally representing diverse mixed farming systems as follows: Ghana (cereal–root crop mixed), Ethiopia (highland mixed), Malawi: (maize mixed), Bangladesh (rice mixed), Nepal (highland mixed), and Lao People's Democratic Republic (upland intensive mixed/ highland extensive mixed).

Background
The highlands of North Shoa in Amhara region are dominated by cereals (wheat, barley and tef) followed by food legumes. The productivity of cereals and food legumes is low due to biotic and abiotic factors as well as insufficient input supplies like certified seed, inoculants, and other inputs. Because of diseases and insect pests, acidity and water logging problems, farmers are reducing areas of food legumes and growing more cereals leading to low crop diversity leading to reduced soil fertility, incomes, and food diversity. Several cereal and food legume varieties are released by many centres but did not reach farmers due to limited demonstration to create awareness and demand and shortage of quality early generation seed. The poor access to quality seed contributes to low crop productivity.
Objectives
Identifying farmer preferred cereal and legume varieties.
2. Production of early generation seed of food and legume varieties; and
3. Creating awareness and demand of new varieties to growers.
Methodologies
Participatory variety selection of food legumes and food oat:
PVS trials of desi chickpea, faba bean, field pea and food oat were conducted on farmers’ fields and Farmer Training Centres (FTCs) in Moretina Jiru,Siyadebir- wayu, Menz-Lalo and Basona Worana districts in North Shoa. The plot size for each variety of food legumes and food oat was 25 m2. All recommended agronomic practices were applied to the trials.
Chickpea and lentil: The PVS trials were planted in 2022 and evaluations were made in 2023 for both crops. Six desi chickpea varieties (Eshete, Dimtu, Natoli, Mastewal, Girar, Dalota) released by different centres were evaluated as mother-baby trial in three farmer fields and one FTC in Moretina-Jiru district. Eight released lentil varieties (Beredu, Furi, Derash, Alem Tena, Jiru, Alemay and Debine) with local check were planted at one FTC and three farmers’ fields in Moretina Jiru, Siyadebirna Wayu and Menz Lalo districts in 2022/23 cropping season.
Faba bean and field pea: Six released faba bean varieties (Shewa, Gora, Dagim, Walki, Chalew and Hachalu) were planted at one FTC and one farmer field in Woiramba kebele, Moretina Jiru district and one farmer field each at Aba- mote and Mush kebeles in Basona-Worana district. Three released field pea varieties (Jeldu, Bilalo and Etatu) with local checks were planted at two farmers’ fields in Aba Mote and Mush kebeles in Basona-Worana district.
Food oat: As an alternative crop to acid affected soils in the highlands, four released food oat varieties (Tena, Enat, Hulegeb and Sorataf) were planted in two farmers’ fields in Aba Mote and Mush kebeles in Basona-Worana district.
Early generation seed production: Breeder seed of bread wheat, barley and faba bean were planted in 2023/2024 cropping season under rainfed condition in research stations and farmers’ fields in North Shoa zone.
Demonstration of cereal and food legume varieties and
liquid foliar fertilizer: A bread wheat variety Emegwa released in 2022 for North Shoa and similar highlands for its high yield was demonstrated in Moretina Jiru (Kusaye and Woiramba kebeles) and Menz Lalo (Tole and 05 kebeles) districts on 100m2 plots on 10 farmer’s fields and two farmer training centers. Moreover, four bread wheat varieties (Boru, Hachalu, Dursa and Galan) selected from 2022 PVS were demonstrated in Basona-Worana (four farmers) and Moretina Jiru (four farmers) districts.
Two farmers preferred food barley varieties (Hagere and HB1307) were demonstrated in one female farmer at Mush kebele in Basona-Worana district. Nationally registered liquid foliar fertilizer (WUXAL foliar liquid fertilizer) containing macro and micronutrients was demonstrated on bread wheat on three farmers’ fields and faba bean on four farmer fields in North Shoa.
Results
Participatory variety selections
Chickpea: The most important criteria of variety selection were grain yield followed by adaptation, frost, and disease resistance. A total of 32 (10 female) farmers and three experts evaluated the varieties using traits identified by farmers (Fig 1). Based on male and female farmer ranking, cvs. Mastewal and Natoli were selected for further seed production and scaling in 2023/2024 cropping season.

Lentil: Farmers preferred cv. Jiru in the three districts based on key criteria for diseases and agronomic traits (Fig. 2) as compared to the most popular cvs. Alemaya and Derash (Table 1). High virus epidemics was observed in SiyaDebir-Wayu and Moretina-Jiru districts and varieties showed different levels of reactions to virus infection (Table 2).

The Sustainable Intensification of Mixed Farming Systems Initiative aims to provide equitable, transformative pathways for improved livelihoods of actors in mixed farming systems through sustainable intensification within target agroecologies and socio-economic settings.
Through action research and development partnerships, the Initiative will improve smallholder farmers' resilience to weather-induced shocks, provide a more stable income and significant benefits in welfare, and enhance social justice and inclusion for 13 million people by 2030.
Activities will be implemented in six focus countries globally representing diverse mixed farming systems as follows: Ghana (cereal–root crop mixed), Ethiopia (highland mixed), Malawi: (maize mixed), Bangladesh (rice mixed), Nepal (highland mixed), and Lao People's Democratic Republic (upland intensive mixed/ highland extensive mixed).

Background
The highlands of North Shoa in Amhara region are dominated by cereals (wheat, barley and tef) followed by food legumes. The productivity of cereals and food legumes is low due to biotic and abiotic factors as well as insufficient input supplies like certified seed, inoculants, and other inputs. Because of diseases and insect pests, acidity and water logging problems, farmers are reducing areas of food legumes and growing more cereals leading to low crop diversity leading to reduced soil fertility, incomes, and food diversity. Several cereal and food legume varieties are released by many centres but did not reach farmers due to limited demonstration to create awareness and demand and shortage of quality early generation seed. The poor access to quality seed contributes to low crop productivity.
Objectives
Identifying farmer preferred cereal and legume varieties.
2. Production of early generation seed of food and legume varieties; and
3. Creating awareness and demand of new varieties to growers.
Methodologies
Participatory variety selection of food legumes and food oat:
PVS trials of desi chickpea, faba bean, field pea and food oat were conducted on farmers’ fields and Farmer Training Centres (FTCs) in Moretina Jiru,Siyadebir- wayu, Menz-Lalo and Basona Worana districts in North Shoa. The plot size for each variety of food legumes and food oat was 25 m2. All recommended agronomic practices were applied to the trials.
Chickpea and lentil: The PVS trials were planted in 2022 and evaluations were made in 2023 for both crops. Six desi chickpea varieties (Eshete, Dimtu, Natoli, Mastewal, Girar, Dalota) released by different centres were evaluated as mother-baby trial in three farmer fields and one FTC in Moretina-Jiru district. Eight released lentil varieties (Beredu, Furi, Derash, Alem Tena, Jiru, Alemay and Debine) with local check were planted at one FTC and three farmers’ fields in Moretina Jiru, Siyadebirna Wayu and Menz Lalo districts in 2022/23 cropping season.
Faba bean and field pea: Six released faba bean varieties (Shewa, Gora, Dagim, Walki, Chalew and Hachalu) were planted at one FTC and one farmer field in Woiramba kebele, Moretina Jiru district and one farmer field each at Aba- mote and Mush kebeles in Basona-Worana district. Three released field pea varieties (Jeldu, Bilalo and Etatu) with local checks were planted at two farmers’ fields in Aba Mote and Mush kebeles in Basona-Worana district.
Food oat: As an alternative crop to acid affected soils in the highlands, four released food oat varieties (Tena, Enat, Hulegeb and Sorataf) were planted in two farmers’ fields in Aba Mote and Mush kebeles in Basona-Worana district.
Early generation seed production: Breeder seed of bread wheat, barley and faba bean were planted in 2023/2024 cropping season under rainfed condition in research stations and farmers’ fields in North Shoa zone.
Demonstration of cereal and food legume varieties and
liquid foliar fertilizer: A bread wheat variety Emegwa released in 2022 for North Shoa and similar highlands for its high yield was demonstrated in Moretina Jiru (Kusaye and Woiramba kebeles) and Menz Lalo (Tole and 05 kebeles) districts on 100m2 plots on 10 farmer’s fields and two farmer training centers. Moreover, four bread wheat varieties (Boru, Hachalu, Dursa and Galan) selected from 2022 PVS were demonstrated in Basona-Worana (four farmers) and Moretina Jiru (four farmers) districts.
Two farmers preferred food barley varieties (Hagere and HB1307) were demonstrated in one female farmer at Mush kebele in Basona-Worana district. Nationally registered liquid foliar fertilizer (WUXAL foliar liquid fertilizer) containing macro and micronutrients was demonstrated on bread wheat on three farmers’ fields and faba bean on four farmer fields in North Shoa.
Results
Participatory variety selections
Chickpea: The most important criteria of variety selection were grain yield followed by adaptation, frost, and disease resistance. A total of 32 (10 female) farmers and three experts evaluated the varieties using traits identified by farmers (Fig 1). Based on male and female farmer ranking, cvs. Mastewal and Natoli were selected for further seed production and scaling in 2023/2024 cropping season.

Figure 0.1 Participatory variety Selection of Desi Chickpea, North Shoa, Ethiopia
Lentil: Farmers preferred cv. Jiru in the three districts based on key criteria for diseases and agronomic traits (Fig. 2) as compared to the most popular cvs. Alemaya and Derash (Table 1). Although local lentil varieties are preferred by farmers, during rust epidemics farmers can lose all their crops. For the past five years, viruses like Pea seed born mosaic virus (PsBMV) have been devastating lentil crops in North Shoa due to vector activities and infected seeds. High virus epidemics was observed in SiyaDebir-Wayu and Moretina-Jiru districts and varieties showed different levels of reactions to virus infection (Table 2).

Early generation seed production of cereals and food legumes
To increase availability and access to certiﬁed seed, production of early generation seed (breeder, pre-basic and basic seeds) of farmer preferred varieties of bread wheat (Emegwa, Tsehay and Dendaa), food barley (cvs. HB1307 and Hagere), malt barley (cv. A total of 2.13 t of nine varieties of bread wheat, malt barley, food barley and faba bean was produced for next year pre-basic seed production.

Conclusion
The activities were jointly implemented with ARARI, Debre Berhan Agricultural Research Centre to increase the availability of male and female preferred varieties for community seed growers. The cereal and faba bean varieties were selected by farmers through PVS by different projects in North Shoa. Through the support of SI-MFS, production of breeder seed by research center can contribute to drive scaling in the coming season and beyond. The faba bean varieties are targeted to waterlogged black soils in North Shoa.

Title: Area-based Yield Index Insurance for rice based on satellite data
Description: An area-based yield (ARBY) index insurance for rice based on satellite data is being developed and tested in the Philippines. ARBY provides coverage based on historical average yield of a specific geographic area, rather than individual farmers’ yields, to determine payouts in the event of crop losses. The current and historical yields are based on the Philippine Rice Information System (PRISM, https://prism.philrice.gov.ph/), an innovative satellite-based rice mapping and monitoring system. Operational since 2018, PRISM uses time series Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR), a smart detection system, and crop growth simulation modeling to map rice areas and provide timely yield forecasts and end-of-season rice yields. It is more efficient than the traditional indemnity-based crop insurance which involves manual visits and verifications for each claim. By leveraging modern technologies, better crop insurance products and services can be offered to farmers to help improve their resilience to climatic risks.

The partnership will kick-start its initiatives by simulating the ARBY products in three significant rice-producing provinces in the country: Isabela, Camarines Sur, and Capiz. This pioneering phase aims to engage an initial batch of 3,000 rice farmers in simulating application of the proposed new insurance product. Title: Improving the the Agro-Climatic Bulletin (ACB) provided to farmers using human-centered design methods in the Vietnam Mekong Delta
Description: The use of the Human-Centered Design (HCD) approach improved the Agro-Climatic Bulletin (ACB), providing better quality, and consistency of advisories, and accessibility to farmers. This process focused on farmers for their practical use, and the Technical Working Groups from the district and provincial government for their development and dissemination of the ACB. The improvements include (1) an enhanced ACB template, in which practice cards are based on historical data, with expert inputs replacing manual recommendations; (2) a user-friendly design featuring icons, pictures, and a more engaging design and color scheme; and (3) supplementary training materials with new videos and guides integrated as QR codes within the ACB practice cards. By using separate practice cards, advisories can be tracked over time and across different locations, providing opportunities for further analysis, and improvement, and as a step towards ACB digitalisation.

Human-Centered Design in Action:    Bridging Gaps in Climate Information Services  INFO NOTE 1   Usability Testing and Assessment of   the Agro-Climatic Bulletin in Vietnam 
Lam Van Luong, Diana Giraldo Mendez, James Giles, Huong Mai Nguyen, Tam Thi Le, Kees Swaans
Key Messages
Introduction
� Human-Centered Design is a problem- solving approach that prioritizes users, their needs, and their context by involving them throughout the design process, and it is increasingly used to create effective climate information services.
� Usability testing, as part of the Human- Centered Design process, helps understand how farmers interact with climate information services and identify valuable and intuitive insights that other methods might overlook.
The Agro-Climatic Bulletin (ACB) is a climate information service initiated by the Alliance of Bioversity International and CIAT and the Department of Crop Production in the Mekong River Delta of Vietnam. Based on the “Local Technical Agroclimatic Committees” (LTAC) approach (Giraldo-Mendez et al., 2021), the ACB is developed through a co-design process with input from provincial Technical Working Groups (TWGs), including agricultural and extension experts, as well as hydrometeorological staff.
� Usability testing and assessment of the Agro- Climatic Bulletins show that the bulletin can be easily accessed and navigated as it is shared in an image-based format on a messaging platform familiar to farmers.
� Key recommendations to enhance usability of the Agro-Climatic Bulletins include: improve accessibility, simplify navigation, enhance design with visuals, increase frequency of updates, use simpler language, provide more localized content, and prioritise key information.
� As Human-Centered Design is iterative, the cycle does not end with implementing recommendations for improvement; it continues with testing, feedback, and refinement to ensure the ACBs align with user needs.
The ACB provides district-localized advisories based on seasonal, monthly and 10-day climate and weather forecasts (Swaans et al., 2023). As of June 2024, the ACB has reached over 270,000 farmers across 70 districts and 547 communes through multiple channels, including loudspeakers, posters, and the Zalo messaging app (CIAT, 2024). In 2023, the ACB approach was recognized by Vietnam’s Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Development as a “technical advance” and subsequently scaled to all 13 provinces of the Mekong River Delta of Vietnam.
Human-Centred Design (HCD) is a creative and iterative problem-solving approach that prioritizes the needs, experiences, and contexts of users throughout the design process of a product or service (CIAT, 2023; IDEO, 2015). To enhance the ACB’s content and delivery, the HCD approach has been applied in the framework of the CGIAR initiative Asian Mega-Deltas to reduce risks in key
1
value chains in the Mekong River Delta in Vietnam since 2023 (Giraldo et al., 2024). The application of this approach involves direct engagement with farmers as end users, using tools such as user personas, journey mapping, and usability testing to refine and improve the ACB.
This info note is part of a series, highlighting key results and lessons learned from applying the HCD to the ACBs. Each info note focuses on a specific tool of the process:
• Info Note 1: Presents findings from usability testing, revealing how farmers interacted with the bulletins and highlighting areas for improvement.
• Info Note 2: Develops user personas, providing a deeper understanding of the diverse farmer profiles and their unique needs.
• Info Note 3: Delves into user journey mapping, showing how farmers engage with the ACBs at different touchpoints and uncovering opportunities for enhancing service delivery.
Human-Centered Design and Usability
Usability refers to the ease with which users can interact with a system, product, or service to achieve their goals effectively, efficiently, and satisfactorily (Nielsen, 1994). It is defined by five quality elements: learnability, efficiency, memorability, errors and satisfaction (Nielsen, 1994). In other words, a service with high usability is easy to learn, allows users to complete tasks efficiently, is easy to remember after a break, minimizes errors or makes them easy to fix, and provides the users with a satisfying overall experience. In the agriculture sector, usability is an important factor which impacts farmers’ effective use and adoption of digital tools (Budiastuti et al., 2023; Sebald et al., 2024).
Human-centered design (HCD) is defined as an iterative process with five phases, namely Scope (identifying research challenges), Explore (gathering user insights), Create (designing prototypes), Validate (testing prototypes with users and stakeholders), and Scale (iterating designs through continuous evaluation during scaling) (Figure 1). Specifically, usability testing is used in the Validation phase of the HCD process, in which a prototype of a product or service is tested with real users to identify any usability issues before final implementation. This helps ensure solutions align with user needs and real-world contexts (Harte et al., 2017; ISO, 2019).

Usability testing and assessment
The HCD study of ACBs in Vietnam was conducted during the rice winter-spring season of 2023-2024 in the Mekong River Delta. We targeted farmers receiving 10-day ACBs throughout the season via Zalo (Whatsapp-like message app) group chats managed by local government officials. The bulletin took the form of a set of images with each image providing district-localized weather forecasts for the next 10 days and advisories based on these (Figure 2).

To assess the usability of the ACBs, we used two approaches: an expert assessment and a usability test with the actual farmer users. This dual approach ensures that the product is not only designed to be functional, accessible, and useful for the users based on their responses, but also complies with common practices for user-friendly interface design
Researchers from the Alliance of Bioversity International and CIAT in Vietnam, who were trained in HCD, conducted the expert usability evaluation of the ACBs. The purpose of this assessment was to evaluate the ACBs against key usability principles proposed by Jakob Nielsen (Harley, 2018; Nielsen, 2024) to identify design issues and improve user- friendliness.

The usability test was conducted with 25 rice farmers (12 men, 13 women) in Soc Trang and Hau Giang provinces in the Mekong River Delta of Vietnam from February to May 2024. The two provinces were selected to represent different ecological zones: Soc Trang, a coastal area, faces greater climate-related challenges such as drought and saltwater intrusion, while Hau Giang, located inland in the freshwater zone, is less affected (Figure 3). The participants, all current ACB users, were purposefully selected to ensure diversity in age and gender.

The usability test aims to evaluate the user experience of accessing and interacting with the ACB on the Zalo messaging app. More specifically, it consisted of three parts (Luong et al., 2024), as follows:
• First, farmers were instructed to access the ACB on their phones while verbalizing their thought processes, enabling researchers to assess how easily they could locate and open the bulletin.
• Secondly, farmers were tasked with finding specific types of information within the bulletin to evaluate how easy the navigation was.
• Finally, individual interviews were conducted to collect detailed feedback from farmers about their experiences with the ACB, including accessibility, design and readability, content comprehension and usefulness.
The usability test was conducted by Vietnamese interviewers (Figure 4), who played complementary roles to ensure the collection of both qualitative and observational data. One interviewer took the lead in giving instructions, guiding the users through tasks, and engaging in direct interaction. The second interviewer focused on observing the user’s behaviour, paying close attention to verbal feedback, non-verbal cues, and how users interacted with the ACBs during the session. After each testing session, the interviewers debriefed, comparing notes, sharing observations, and collaboratively identifying key usability issues. Additionally, a non-Vietnamese HCD expert was involved in designing the tests and analyzing the findings. This helps counterbalance potential cultural biases and ensure a more comprehensive interpretation of the results. two

Findings from usability testing
Interviews with farmers and observation of their interactions with the ACBs on their phones revealed the following usability and user experience-related issues:
Accessibility: Most farmers could quickly find the ACBs in group chats on the Zalo messaging app, as the platform was familiar to them. However, 8 out of 25 farmers reported difficulty locating the group chat where the ACBs were shared. Farmers often forgot the location of the bulletin, with a 37-year- old female farmer saying, “I don’t remember… I just saw it this morning”, and a 36-year-old male farmer stating, “It just disappeared automatically; I don’t know why I don’t see it anymore”. Observations revealed that farmers received the bulletin through diverse sources — some directly from extension officials via Zalo, others from a Zalo group chat of their cooperative, and/or in other group chats for sharing local information (e.g., salinity updates). This overlap between communication channels likely contributed to the confusion. Moreover, as Zalo is used for various communication purposes, the bulletin often gets lost among other messages. The 10-day sharing interval during rice cropping seasons aggravates the issue, as more frequent messages overshadow the bulletin updates.
• Visual design and Presentation: Farmers preferred more visual aids, such as photos or diagrams, to simplify key messages. For example, one 36-year-old male farmer said, “If salinity levels are high, just draw a diagram showing high or low levels instead of writing so much text.”
• Colour and Emphasis: Participants suggested using bold text or colours to draw attention to critical information like weather alerts. As a 56-year-old female farmer explained, “Create emphasis by making key points bold or highlighted to draw attention. If everything is written the same, people often don’t pay attention.”
Frequency of updating: 9 out of 25 farmers expressed a need for more frequent updates, favouring weekly or even daily intervals to enhance relevance and accuracy. As one 28-year-old male farmer explained, “Ten days is too long; weekly updates would be better”. Shorter intervals were considered more actionable and precise, especially
Navigation: The ACB, presented as a set of 4 - 15 images, made it easy for farmers to locate the content they needed. While some read the bulletin sequentially from start to finish, others skipped directly to images featuring pests and diseases or the image with detailed weather forecasts for each day. Most farmers reported paying most attention to pest and disease information. Observations revealed that farmers often skimmed through the bulletin quickly rather than reading it in detail, prioritizing information they deemed immediately useful.

Discussion
HCD is an iterative process that emphasizes gradual improvement through cycles of testing, feedback, and refinement rather than aiming for a perfect solution upfront. Usability testing helps identify areas for improvement, and based on these findings, feasible solutions are prioritized considering available resources and potential impact. Selected solutions are implemented and tested in real-world conditions to gather feedback and evaluate their effectiveness. If necessary, further adjustments are made, followed by retesting. This continuous loop of testing, improving, and refining ensures the product evolves to become more user- friendly and effective.
Usability issues are often addressed by HCD experts. However, for the ACBs as well as other climate information services using the LTAC approach, the TWGs including of governmental officials and other local stakeholders play a crucial role in the service design. Hence, addressing usability of a climate information service like the ACBs requires not only HCD expertise, but also a broader view at the development process of the services. In the short term, usability enhancements and changes should be discussed and implemented collaboratively with them. In the long term, automation may provide the potential to address certain usability issues, reduce human subjectivity, and minimize errors in designing, but it will always require a participatory approach and local involvement to ensure human centered and localized services.
Since the HCD study, many of the recommendations have been implemented in a pilot involving an improved version of the 10-day ACB in three target provinces during the summer-autumn rice season of 2024. Main change was to no longer post the full ACB on Zalo groups, but to use ‘risk, impact and practice cards’ instead. This allows for short and concise information on risks, impacts and advisories based on newly designed templates for each, using standardized colours. It also allows for more consistency in bulletins and the sharing of extra information and videos (e-training materials) on certain practices through links; in addition, the ACB was branded with a new logo for both the group chat and the ACBs to enhance visual recognition of the service. Integrating further lessons in consultation with the Department of Crop Production and TWGs, the Alliance plans to scale the improved 10-day ACB across all provinces of the Mekong River Delta, Vietnam, in 2025.
Conclusion
The findings from the usability test of the Agro- Climatic Bulletins (ACBs) offer key insights for other climate information services using the LTAC approach, particularly those in bulletin format. While usability testing is often used for systems like apps or websites, this study shows that it can be effectively applied to straightforward systems like digital bulletins. Applying HCD, the usability test conducted in this study revealed intuitive insights into farmers’ interactions with the ACBs — insights that would be hard to capture otherwise. These findings emphasize the importance of making climate information services accessible, useful, and easy to use for their intended users.

Improving the the Agro-Climatic Bulletin (ACB) provided to farmers using human-centered design methods in the Vietnam Mekong Delta The use of the Human-Centered Design (HCD) approach improved the Agro-Climatic Bulletin (ACB), providing better quality, and consistency of advisories, and accessibility to farmers. This process focused on farmers for their practical use, and the Technical Working Groups from the district and provincial government for their development and dissemination of the ACB. The improvements include (1) an enhanced ACB template, in which practice cards are based on historical data, with expert inputs replacing manual recommendations; (2) a user-friendly design featuring icons, pictures, and a more engaging design and color scheme; and (3) supplementary training materials with new videos and guides integrated as QR codes within the ACB practice cards. By using separate practice cards, advisories can be tracked over time and across different locations, providing opportunities for further analysis, and improvement, and as a step towards ACB digitalisation. Human-Centered Design in Action:    Bridging Gaps in Climate Information Services  INFO NOTE 1   Usability Testing and Assessment of   the Agro-Climatic Bulletin in Vietnam 
Lam Van Luong, Diana Giraldo Mendez, James Giles, Huong Mai Nguyen, Tam Thi Le, Kees Swaans
Key Messages
Introduction
� Human-Centered Design is a problem- solving approach that prioritizes users, their needs, and their context by involving them throughout the design process, and it is increasingly used to create effective climate information services.
� Usability testing, as part of the Human- Centered Design process, helps understand how farmers interact with climate information services and identify valuable and intuitive insights that other methods might overlook.
The Agro-Climatic Bulletin (ACB) is a climate information service initiated by the Alliance of Bioversity International and CIAT and the Department of Crop Production in the Mekong River Delta of Vietnam. Based on the “Local Technical Agroclimatic Committees” (LTAC) approach (Giraldo-Mendez et al., 2021), the ACB is developed through a co-design process with input from provincial Technical Working Groups (TWGs), including agricultural and extension experts, as well as hydrometeorological staff.
� Usability testing and assessment of the Agro- Climatic Bulletins show that the bulletin can be easily accessed and navigated as it is shared in an image-based format on a messaging platform familiar to farmers.
� Key recommendations to enhance usability of the Agro-Climatic Bulletins include: improve accessibility, simplify navigation, enhance design with visuals, increase frequency of updates, use simpler language, provide more localized content, and prioritise key information.
� As Human-Centered Design is iterative, the cycle does not end with implementing recommendations for improvement; it continues with testing, feedback, and refinement to ensure the ACBs align with user needs.
The ACB provides district-localized advisories based on seasonal, monthly and 10-day climate and weather forecasts (Swaans et al., 2023). As of June 2024, the ACB has reached over 270,000 farmers across 70 districts and 547 communes through multiple channels, including loudspeakers, posters, and the Zalo messaging app (CIAT, 2024). In 2023, the ACB approach was recognized by Vietnam’s Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Development as a “technical advance” and subsequently scaled to all 13 provinces of the Mekong River Delta of Vietnam.
Human-Centred Design (HCD) is a creative and iterative problem-solving approach that prioritizes the needs, experiences, and contexts of users throughout the design process of a product or service (CIAT, 2023; IDEO, 2015). To enhance the ACB’s content and delivery, the HCD approach has been applied in the framework of the CGIAR initiative Asian Mega-Deltas to reduce risks in key
1
value chains in the Mekong River Delta in Vietnam since 2023 (Giraldo et al., 2024). The application of this approach involves direct engagement with farmers as end users, using tools such as user personas, journey mapping, and usability testing to refine and improve the ACB.
This info note is part of a series, highlighting key results and lessons learned from applying the HCD to the ACBs. Each info note focuses on a specific tool of the process:
• Info Note 1: Presents findings from usability testing, revealing how farmers interacted with the bulletins and highlighting areas for improvement.
• Info Note 2: Develops user personas, providing a deeper understanding of the diverse farmer profiles and their unique needs.
• Info Note 3: Delves into user journey mapping, showing how farmers engage with the ACBs at different touchpoints and uncovering opportunities for enhancing service delivery.
Human-Centered Design and Usability
Usability refers to the ease with which users can interact with a system, product, or service to achieve their goals effectively, efficiently, and satisfactorily (Nielsen, 1994). It is defined by five quality elements: learnability, efficiency, memorability, errors and satisfaction (Nielsen, 1994). In other words, a service with high usability is easy to learn, allows users to complete tasks efficiently, is easy to remember after a break, minimizes errors or makes them easy to fix, and provides the users with a satisfying overall experience. In the agriculture sector, usability is an important factor which impacts farmers’ effective use and adoption of digital tools (Budiastuti et al., 2023; Sebald et al., 2024).
Human-centered design (HCD) is defined as an iterative process with five phases, namely Scope (identifying research challenges), Explore (gathering user insights), Create (designing prototypes), Validate (testing prototypes with users and stakeholders), and Scale (iterating designs through continuous evaluation during scaling) (Figure 1). Specifically, usability testing is used in the Validation phase of the HCD process, in which a prototype of a product or service is tested with real users to identify any usability issues before final implementation. This helps ensure solutions align with user needs and real-world contexts (Harte et al., 2017; ISO, 2019).

Usability testing and assessment
The HCD study of ACBs in Vietnam was conducted during the rice winter-spring season of 2023-2024 in the Mekong River Delta. We targeted farmers receiving 10-day ACBs throughout the season via Zalo (Whatsapp-like message app) group chats managed by local government officials. The bulletin took the form of a set of images with each image providing district-localized weather forecasts for the next 10 days and advisories based on these (Figure 2).
Hau Giang  Soc Trang 
To assess the usability of the ACBs, we used two approaches: an expert assessment and a usability test with the actual farmer users. This dual approach ensures that the product is not only designed to be functional, accessible, and useful for the users based on their responses, but also complies with common practices for user-friendly interface design
Researchers from the Alliance of Bioversity International and CIAT in Vietnam, who were trained in HCD, conducted the expert usability evaluation of the ACBs. The purpose of this assessment was to evaluate the ACBs against key usability principles proposed by Jakob Nielsen (Harley, 2018; Nielsen, 2024) to identify design issues and improve user- friendliness.
Figure 3. Map of the Mekong River Delta in Vietnam, highlighting the study provinces.
The usability test was conducted with 25 rice farmers (12 men, 13 women) in Soc Trang and Hau Giang provinces in the Mekong River Delta of Vietnam from February to May 2024. The two provinces were selected to represent different ecological zones: Soc Trang, a coastal area, faces greater climate-related challenges such as drought and saltwater intrusion, while Hau Giang, located inland in the freshwater zone, is less affected (Figure 3). The participants, all current ACB users, were purposefully selected to ensure diversity in age and gender.

The usability test aims to evaluate the user experience of accessing and interacting with the ACB on the Zalo messaging app. More specifically, it consisted of three parts (Luong et al., 2024), as follows:
• First, farmers were instructed to access the ACB on their phones while verbalizing their thought processes, enabling researchers to assess how easily they could locate and open the bulletin.
• Secondly, farmers were tasked with finding specific types of information within the bulletin to evaluate how easy the navigation was.
• Finally, individual interviews were conducted to collect detailed feedback from farmers about their experiences with the ACB, including accessibility, design and readability, content comprehension and usefulness.
The usability test was conducted by Vietnamese interviewers (Figure 4), who played complementary roles to ensure the collection of both qualitative and observational data. One interviewer took the lead in giving instructions, guiding the users through tasks, and engaging in direct interaction. The second interviewer focused on observing the user’s behaviour, paying close attention to verbal feedback, non-verbal cues, and how users interacted with the ACBs during the session. After each testing session, the interviewers debriefed, comparing notes, sharing observations, and collaboratively identifying key usability issues. Additionally, a non-Vietnamese HCD expert was involved in designing the tests and analyzing the findings. This helps counterbalance potential cultural biases and ensure a more comprehensive interpretation of the results. two

Findings from usability testing
Interviews with farmers and observation of their interactions with the ACBs on their phones revealed the following usability and user experience-related issues:
Accessibility: Most farmers could quickly find the ACBs in group chats on the Zalo messaging app, as the platform was familiar to them. However, 8 out of 25 farmers reported difficulty locating the group chat where the ACBs were shared. Farmers often forgot the location of the bulletin, with a 37-year- old female farmer saying, “I don’t remember… I just saw it this morning”, and a 36-year-old male farmer stating, “It just disappeared automatically; I don’t know why I don’t see it anymore”. Observations revealed that farmers received the bulletin through diverse sources — some directly from extension officials via Zalo, others from a Zalo group chat of their cooperative, and/or in other group chats for sharing local information (e.g., salinity updates). This overlap between communication channels likely contributed to the confusion. Moreover, as Zalo is used for various communication purposes, the bulletin often gets lost among other messages. The 10-day sharing interval during rice cropping seasons aggravates the issue, as more frequent messages overshadow the bulletin updates.
• Visual design and Presentation: Farmers preferred more visual aids, such as photos or diagrams, to simplify key messages. For example, one 36-year-old male farmer said, “If salinity levels are high, just draw a diagram showing high or low levels instead of writing so much text.”
• Colour and Emphasis: Participants suggested using bold text or colours to draw attention to critical information like weather alerts. As a 56-year-old female farmer explained, “Create emphasis by making key points bold or highlighted to draw attention. If everything is written the same, people often don’t pay attention.”
Frequency of updating: 9 out of 25 farmers expressed a need for more frequent updates, favouring weekly or even daily intervals to enhance relevance and accuracy. As one 28-year-old male farmer explained, “Ten days is too long; weekly updates would be better”. Shorter intervals were considered more actionable and precise, especially
Navigation: The ACB, presented as a set of 4 - 15 images, made it easy for farmers to locate the content they needed. While some read the bulletin sequentially from start to finish, others skipped directly to images featuring pests and diseases or the image with detailed weather forecasts for each day. Most farmers reported paying most attention to pest and disease information. Observations revealed that farmers often skimmed through the bulletin quickly rather than reading it in detail, prioritizing information they deemed immediately useful.

Discussion
HCD is an iterative process that emphasizes gradual improvement through cycles of testing, feedback, and refinement rather than aiming for a perfect solution upfront. Usability testing helps identify areas for improvement, and based on these findings, feasible solutions are prioritized considering available resources and potential impact. Selected solutions are implemented and tested in real-world conditions to gather feedback and evaluate their effectiveness. If necessary, further adjustments are made, followed by retesting. This continuous loop of testing, improving, and refining ensures the product evolves to become more user- friendly and effective.
Usability issues are often addressed by HCD experts. However, for the ACBs as well as other climate information services using the LTAC approach, the TWGs including of governmental officials and other local stakeholders play a crucial role in the service design. Hence, addressing usability of a climate information service like the ACBs requires not only HCD expertise, but also a broader view at the development process of the services. In the short term, usability enhancements and changes should be discussed and implemented collaboratively with them. In the long term, automation may provide the potential to address certain usability issues, reduce human subjectivity, and minimize errors in designing, but it will always require a participatory approach and local involvement to ensure human centered and localized services.
Since the HCD study, many of the recommendations have been implemented in a pilot involving an improved version of the 10-day ACB in three target provinces during the summer-autumn rice season of 2024. Main change was to no longer post the full ACB on Zalo groups, but to use ‘risk, impact and practice cards’ instead. This allows for short and concise information on risks, impacts and advisories based on newly designed templates for each, using standardized colours. It also allows for more consistency in bulletins and the sharing of extra information and videos (e-training materials) on certain practices through links; in addition, the ACB was branded with a new logo for both the group chat and the ACBs to enhance visual recognition of the service. Integrating further lessons in consultation with the Department of Crop Production and TWGs, the Alliance plans to scale the improved 10-day ACB across all provinces of the Mekong River Delta, Vietnam, in 2025.
Conclusion
The findings from the usability test of the Agro- Climatic Bulletins (ACBs) offer key insights for other climate information services using the LTAC approach, particularly those in bulletin format. While usability testing is often used for systems like apps or websites, this study shows that it can be effectively applied to straightforward systems like digital bulletins. Applying HCD, the usability test conducted in this study revealed intuitive insights into farmers’ interactions with the ACBs — insights that would be hard to capture otherwise. These findings emphasize the importance of making climate information services accessible, useful, and easy to use for their intended users.

Title: AquaIndex: a framework of indicators for sustainable aquatic foods.
Description: Reliable qualitative and quantitative data on aquatic food systems are essential for ensuring sustainable food production and development. AquaIndex is a structured framework of indicators designed to assess the sustainability of aquatic food systems, covering environmental, social, and economic dimensions.AquaIndex provides a standardized approach for evaluating sustainability outcomes, enabling stakeholders—including researchers, policymakers, industry actors, and development agencies—to measure, compare, and track progress over time. The framework will help synthesize and benchmark the sustainability performance of aquatic food systems at local, national, and international levels. AquaIndex supports evidence-based decision-making to improve aquaculture governance, policy interventions, and investment strategies. It will help guide sustainable practices, ensuring that aquatic food systems contribute to food security, climate resilience, and economic stability while minimizing environmental impact.

Executive Summary
The WorldFish AquaIndex Kick-off Workshop served as a milestone event, bringing together a diverse group of stakeholders to lay the foundation for the development of a transformative tool designed to assess the sustainability of aquatic food systems. This AquaIndex is envisioned as a comprehensive and modular framework integrating economic, social, environmental, and governance indicators, addressing the multidimensional challenges faced by aquatic food systems globally. By leveraging innovative technologies, expert insights, and collaborative stakeholder engagement, the AquaIndex aims to provide actionable data and strategies that can guide policymakers, industry leaders, and local communities toward sustainable practices.
During the workshop, participants critically examined the limitations of existing sustainability frameworks, most of which were found to emphasize environmental criteria while often neglecting social and economic dimensions crucial for holistic sustainability. Furthermore, the challenges of adapting these frameworks to small-scale and artisanal fisheries underscored the need for a new, inclusive tool that considers the unique contexts and constraints of diverse aquatic food systems.
A key highlight of the workshop was the introduction of environmental DNA (eDNA) as a cutting-edge technique for biodiversity monitoring. Presented as a non- invasive and cost-effective tool, eDNA offers high-resolution insights into aquatic ecosystems, enabling the frequent assessment of biodiversity and ecosystem health. This technique, combined with traditional methods and advanced data analytics, is expected to play a central role in the AquaIndex’s data collection and validation processes.
The workshop also focused on governance, emphasizing the critical role of decision-making structures, institutional frameworks, and stakeholder inclusivity in achieving sustainability goals. Governance indicators were identified as essential components of the AquaIndex, addressing gaps in policy alignment, resource allocation, and equitable participation. Similarly, social and economic indicators, such as gender representation, livelihood sustainability, and market price data, were recognized as vital for ensuring that the benefits of sustainable practices are distributed equitably among stakeholders.
The collaborative discussions culminated in the identification of pilot regions for initial testing of the AquaIndex, with Bangladesh, India, and Japan highlighted as potential sites due to their diverse aquatic ecosystems and governance structures. The formation of a global consortium was proposed to oversee the development,

implementation, and scaling of the AquaIndex, ensuring that it remains adaptable to various contexts while maintaining scientific rigor and data integrity.
Key outcomes of the workshop included a commitment to produce a detailed white paper and a peer-reviewed journal article to document the AquaIndex’s conceptual framework and development process. Additionally, participants agreed on the importance of aligning the index with global sustainability frameworks, such as the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and the Global Biodiversity Framework (GBF), to maximize its policy relevance and impact.
In conclusion, the workshop set the stage for a transformative initiative aimed at redefining sustainability in aquatic food systems. By addressing critical gaps in existing frameworks, integrating innovative technologies, and fostering global collaboration, the AquaIndex has the potential to drive systemic change in how aquatic resources are managed and conserved. This initiative promises to contribute significantly to the achievement of global sustainability targets while ensuring equitable and inclusive development for all stakeholders involved in the aquatic food systems sector.

1. Background and Introduction
The WorldFish AquaIndex Kick-off Workshop marked a pivotal moment in the global effort to transform aquatic food systems into more sustainable and equitable enterprises. Aquatic food systems, encompassing activities from fisheries and aquaculture to supply chain management and consumption, play a crucial role in global food security, livelihoods, and ecological health. However, these systems face complex challenges, including overexploitation, environmental degradation, inequitable benefit distribution, and governance inefficiencies. The need for an integrated, science-driven approach to address these challenges is more pressing than ever.
Existing sustainability frameworks, such as the Ocean Health Index (OHI) and certification schemes such as the Marine Stewardship Council (MSC), Aquaculture Stewardship Council (ASC), and Global Sustainable Seafood Initiative (GSSI), have made significant contributions to advancing responsible practices. Yet, their limitations – such as a narrow focus on environmental criteria, underrepresentation of socio-economic dimensions, and difficulty in application to small-scale and artisanal fisheries – highlight gaps that must be addressed for a truly holistic approach. These gaps necessitate the development of a new, comprehensive sustainability assessment tool: the AquaIndex.
The AquaIndex initiative, spearheaded by WorldFish in collaboration with the Institute for Global Environmental Strategies (IGES), aims to bridge these gaps by integrating environmental, economic, social, and governance dimensions in the area of aquatic food systems. The index will provide actionable insights to policymakers, industry leaders, researchers, and local communities, enabling them to make informed decisions that balance conservation goals with the socio-economic needs of stakeholders.
The kick-off workshop brought together a multidisciplinary group of experts, including researchers, government officers, private sector representatives, and NGOs, to lay the groundwork for this ambitious initiative. The event aimed to pool collective expertise, critically evaluate existing frameworks, and explore innovative solutions, including advanced technologies such as environmental DNA (eDNA). By doing so, the workshop set the stage for the AquaIndex to become a globally recognized tool for advancing the sustainability of aquatic food systems.

2. Workshop Objectives and Themes
2.1. Objectives of the Workshop
The primary objectives of the workshop are as follows:
2.1.1. Identify Gaps and Limitations in Existing Frameworks
The workshop aimed to critically assess existing sustainability frameworks and identify their shortcomings in addressing the needs of diverse aquatic food systems. Identifying the gaps would also highlight areas where the AquaIndex can provide added value, particularly in integrating socio-economic and governance aspects.
2.1.2. Establish a Conceptual Framework for the AquaIndex
The workshop also looked at developing a modular and inclusive framework adaptable to different regions, ecosystems, and stakeholder needs. Additionally, it explored key indicator categories spanning environmental, economic, social, and governance dimensions.
2.1.3. Leverage Innovative Technologies for Sustainability Monitoring
The workshop also aimed to explore the potential of cutting-edge tools such as eDNA for biodiversity and ecosystem health monitoring. Additionally, it was essential to discuss the challenges in scaling these technologies and their applicability across diverse contexts.
2.1.4. Align the AquaIndex with Global Goals
One of the key objectives is to ensure that the AquaIndex contributes to international sustainability frameworks, including the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and the Global Biodiversity Framework (GBF). This would be essential in positioning the AquaIndex as a tool that drives policy alignment and actionable outcomes.
2.1.5. Foster Stakeholder Collaboration
A new index would only be successful if it engaged a broad spectrum of stakeholders, including researchers, policymakers, private sector representatives, and local communities. Hence, one of the key objectives of the workshop was to build
6
partnerships and lay the foundation for a global consortium to oversee AquaIndex development and implementation.
2.2. Themes of the Workshop
To achieve these objectives, the workshop was structured around the following key themes:
2.2.1. Holistic Integration of Sustainability Dimensions
Participants emphasized the need for an index that integrates environmental, social, economic, and governance dimensions. Unlike existing frameworks that often prioritize environmental criteria, the AquaIndex aims to capture the full spectrum of sustainability indicators, including equitable benefit distribution, gender representation, and livelihood security.
Moreover, the workshop acknowledged the significant challenges in data collection, standardization, and accessibility, particularly in low-resource settings. Participants emphasized the need for robust and trustworthy data systems that can support the AquaIndex while being sensitive to issues of data ownership and equity.
Participants also discussed how the AquaIndex could contribute to achieving global targets, such as the 30 by 30 biodiversity protection goal and SDG indicators on life below water (SDG 14) and sustainable production and consumption (SDG 12). The importance of aligning with frameworks like the Global Biodiversity Framework (GBF) was also emphasized. Importance of contributions to the Taskforce for Nature- related Financial Disclosures (TNFD) were also considered.
2.2.2. Advanced Technologies for Monitoring and Data Collection
The introduction of environmental DNA (eDNA) was a major focus, showcasing its potential as a non-invasive, cost-effective tool for biodiversity monitoring. Discussions covered the technique's ability to provide high-resolution data, its scalability for frequent monitoring, and the challenges associated with standardizing its application across diverse regions.
The workshop proposed conducting pilot studies in diverse regions, including Bangladesh, India, and Japan. These locations were chosen for their varying ecological and governance contexts, providing an opportunity to refine the index and ensure its adaptability across different scales and systems.
7
2.2.3. Governance and Institutional Arrangements
Participants highlighted the importance of decision-making structures, institutional capacity, and policy alignment in ensuring the effective implementation of sustainability initiatives. Strong governance was identified as a cornerstone for the successful and sustainable deployment of a new index.
A collaboration between various stakeholders to create a global consortium to oversee the AquaIndex development and implementation was discussed, and potential partners were identified.
3. Workshop Proceedings
The WorldFish AquaIndex Kick-off Workshop was designed as a platform for knowledge exchange and collaborative problem-solving to establish the foundation for a globally relevant sustainability index for aquatic food systems. Over the course of the workshop, participants engaged in presentations, group discussions, and brainstorming sessions, each contributing to the refinement of the AquaIndex concept, identify the appropriate sustainability indicators, and devise the practical next steps for index development.
3.1. Opening Session and Welcome Remarks
The workshop began with introductory remarks by Dr. Osamu Saito, principal policy researcher at the Institute for Global Environmental Strategies (IGES), who emphasized the significance of integrating science, policy, and practice to address the multifaceted challenges of aquatic food systems. Dr. Saito highlighted IGES's role in global environmental governance, drawing attention to its collaborations with the Intergovernmental Science-Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services (IPBES) and the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD).
Dr. Cristiano Rossignoli, research leader of Monitoring, Evaluation and Learning (MEL) and Impact Assessment at WorldFish, provided an overview of WorldFish’s history and mission. He also introduced the wider One CGIAR network that WorldFish is a part of. He introduced the organization’s strategic focus on sustainability and transformational research in aquatic food systems. By framing aquatic foods as inclusive of finfish, shellfish, aquatic plants, and more, Dr. Rossignoli underscored the complexity and interconnectedness of these systems. He stressed
8
the necessity of developing tools like the AquaIndex to achieve equitable and sustainable outcomes.
3.2. Presentations on Key Topics
3.2.1. The AquaIndex Concept
Dr. Rodolfo Dam Lam, WorldFish scientist and a core team member, presented the vision for the AquaIndex. Dr. Dam Lam also introduced the datasets already with WorldFish and how they could help in the selection of the indicators for the index and their sustainability.
He also proposed a framework that was modular, enabling it to adapt to diverse contexts, from large commercial fisheries to small-scale, and proposed a roadmap and timeline for index development.
3.2.2. Sustainability Indicators
Dr. Rohit Ramachandran from IGES presented about the sustainability indicators for aquatic food systems and proposed that they should be organized into five main categories, rather than the three categories usually associated with sustainability. The five categories should be:
1. Environmental: These indicators are crucial for assessing the ecological viability of aquatic ecosystems and their capacity to sustain production over the long term. For example, species diversity, ecosystem health, and climate change.
2. Economic: These indicators will focus on the financial sustainability and economic resilience of aquatic food systems. For example, employment, market dynamics, and cost to consumer.
3. Social: These indicators will ensure that social dimensions such as community well-being and equitable access are not overlooked. For example, gender equity, stakeholder participation, and cultural practices.
4. Governance: These indicators will emphasize the importance of robust governance structures in achieving sustainability goals. For example, institutional capacity, decision-making processes, and funding.
5. Sector Specific: These indicators will address metrics unique to fisheries and aquaculture. For example, type of fisheries/aquaculture operation, type of fishing gear, and bycatch management.
By organizing indicators into these five categories, the AquaIndex aims to provide a holistic and modular framework that supports the entire aquatic food
9
system value chain, from production to consumption. This approach fosters transparency, inclusivity, and adaptability, ensuring that the diverse needs of stakeholders are effectively addressed and that sustainability goals are met comprehensively.
3.2.3. Limitations of Current Indexes
Dr. Ramachandran also presented a comprehensive review of existing sustainability frameworks, including the Global Fishing Index and the Ocean Health Index (OHI), as well as sustainability certification schemes such as the Marine Stewardship Council (MSC), Aquaculture Stewardship Council (ASC), and Global Sustainable Seafood Initiative (GSSI). While these frameworks have made significant strides in promoting responsible fisheries and aquaculture practices, several key limitations were identified, underscoring the need for a more comprehensive and adaptable approach.
One major limitation lies in their narrow focus. Most existing frameworks prioritize environmental indicators, often overlooking critical socio-economic dimensions that are essential for holistic sustainability. For example, while they may address biodiversity and ecosystem health, they fail to adequately consider the livelihoods of small-scale fishers, labour rights, or equitable access to resources.
Data challenges also present a significant obstacle. Many of these frameworks rely on data that are inconsistent or incomplete, particularly when it comes to small-scale fisheries and aquaculture systems. This lack of robust data infrastructure makes it difficult to accurately assess the sustainability of these sectors, leaving them underrepresented in global assessments.
Another critical issue is the lack of inclusivity. Small-scale and artisanal fisheries, which provide livelihoods for millions of people worldwide, are often excluded or inadequately represented in these frameworks. This exclusion not only undermines the credibility of the assessments but also marginalizes some of the most vulnerable stakeholders in aquatic food systems.
Additionally, the policy implications of these frameworks remain unclear. Their real-world impact on influencing policy outcomes and their contributions to global sustainability goals, such as the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), have not been sufficiently documented or evaluated. This lack of demonstrated policy relevance limits their ability to drive meaningful systemic change.
This review set the stage for discussions on how the AquaIndex could address these gaps. By integrating environmental, social, economic, and governance dimensions, the AquaIndex aims to provide a more holistic and adaptable tool for
10
assessing and enhancing the sustainability of aquatic food systems. This approach seeks to ensure that all stakeholders, from small-scale fishers to global policymakers, are considered and empowered in the journey toward sustainable practices.
3.2.4. Introduction to eDNA Technology
Prof. Michio Kondoh from Tohoku University provided an insightful introduction to the transformative role of environmental DNA (eDNA) in biodiversity monitoring. This innovative technology uses non-invasive sampling of environmental materials such as water, soil, or sediment to identify the species present within an ecosystem. By analysing genetic material shed by organisms into their surroundings, eDNA offers an efficient and precise way to monitor biodiversity and ecosystem health.
One of the major strengths of eDNA is its ability to provide high-resolution data. It allows for the accurate identification of species and a comprehensive understanding of ecosystem conditions, making it a powerful tool for sustainability assessments. Additionally, eDNA is cost-effective, offering scalable monitoring capabilities with significantly lower operational costs compared to traditional field survey methods. Its non-invasive nature minimizes disruption to habitats and ecosystems, further enhancing its utility in conservation and management practices.
Prof. Kondoh elaborated on the eDNA application process, from initial sampling to the analysis of results, and presented case studies from Japan where eDNA has been successfully employed. In these examples, eDNA was used to assess the impacts of aquaculture on marine biodiversity, demonstrating its practical relevance and effectiveness. He also highlighted the indirect benefits of eDNA technology, such as fostering collaboration with local communities and creating partnerships with shipping companies to support sampling initiatives.
Participants engaged actively during the session, raising questions about the scalability of eDNA across regions with varying levels of technical capacity and data literacy. Prof. Kondoh addressed these concerns, emphasizing the need for tailored implementation strategies to ensure that the technology is accessible and effective in diverse contexts. His presentation underscored the transformative potential of eDNA as a cornerstone of the AquaIndex’s sustainability framework.
3.3. Group Discussions
The group discussions during the workshop focused on four major indicator categories – environmental, social, economic, and governance – as well as additional feedback on fostering stakeholder collaboration. Online tool Google Forms was used
11
to elicit the participants views to aid the group discussion session. In addition to these topics participants also expresses their views on related cross-cutting themes. Below is a synthesis of key points raised by participants:
3.3.1. Environmental Indicators
Participants emphasized the importance of ecological sustainability and robust biodiversity monitoring as critical components of the AquaIndex. Marine Protected Areas (MPAs) were a key focus of discussion, with participants debating their effectiveness. They suggested the need for more specific information to evaluate MPAs, such as their size, duration, and degree of protection. Additionally, questions were raised about how to assess the management effectiveness of these protected areas, which is vital for ensuring their intended conservation outcomes.
In terms of monitoring metrics, participants proposed that assessments should go beyond capturing the current status of ecological health. They highlighted the importance of incorporating trends and variability over time to provide a more dynamic understanding of ecosystem changes. Metrics such as habitat quality and water quality were identified as essential indicators for evaluating the health and sustainability of aquatic ecosystems.
A balanced approach to dependency and impact indicators was also advocated. Participants emphasized the need to account for both the dependencies of human communities on ecosystems and the impacts of human activities on these natural systems. This dual perspective ensures that sustainability efforts address both ecological resilience and the needs of dependent populations.
Innovative indicators were suggested to enhance the scope and precision of biodiversity assessments. Proposed additions included monitoring species population composition, understanding the relevance of biodiversity to specific stakeholders, and measuring ecological productivity. These indicators aim to provide deeper insights into the functioning and value of ecosystems, aligning conservation efforts with socio-economic priorities.
3.3.2. Economic Indicators
Participants discussed the need for robust economic indicators to capture the financial sustainability of aquatic food systems. They highlighted the importance of metrics such as profitability, benefit-cost ratios, and job creation across the value chain as key priorities. These indicators are crucial for assessing not only the financial viability of aquatic food systems but also the broader economic benefits they generate, including employment opportunities within local communities.
12
Another area of focus was the supply chain assessment. While evaluating supply chains is critical to understanding the overall economic sustainability of the sector, participants acknowledged the complexity of this task. They suggested that the AquaIndex should refine its approach by focusing on specific elements, such as resource efficiency and market access, which can provide more actionable insights for improving supply chain performance.
The discussion also touched on consumer behaviour, particularly in relation to the price sensitivity of consumers when it comes to sustainable products. A concern was raised about how higher prices for sustainably sourced goods could impact consumer purchasing decisions and, in turn, influence long-term resource use. This brings to light the need for economic indicators that not only evaluate current financial metrics but also consider broader market dynamics and consumer trends that could shape the future of aquatic food systems.
3.3.3. Social Indicators
Social sustainability emerged as a prominent theme during the discussions, with a strong emphasis on human well-being and community resilience within aquatic food systems. Participants stressed the need for broader human rights and inclusion indicators, moving beyond basic labour conditions. They proposed incorporating factors such as gender equality, the prevention of child labour, and land and sea use rights for local communities. These indicators are essential to ensure that aquatic food systems promote not only economic sustainability but also
social justice and equity.
In addition, the discussions highlighted the importance of adapting indicators to cultural and regional contexts. Recognizing that different regions and fishing practices have unique socio-economic conditions, participants emphasized the need to tailor the AquaIndex’s social indicators to reflect these variations. This adaptability ensures that the AquaIndex remains relevant and effective across diverse settings, considering the specific challenges and opportunities that different
communities face.
Dietary and nutrition security was another key focus, with food security and dietary diversity being identified as vital aspects of social sustainability. Aquatic food systems must not only provide sufficient quantities of food but also ensure that this food meets nutritional needs, contributing to healthier and more resilient communities.
Finally, the well-being of fishers and local communities was deemed central to the AquaIndex’s social indicators. This includes access to essential services like healthcare, education, and opportunities for participation in decision-making roles.
13
Ensuring that fishers and their communities have these opportunities is essential for building long-term sustainability and resilience within the sector.
3.3.4. Governance Indicators
Governance was seen as a foundational pillar influencing the success of all other categories in ensuring sustainable aquatic food systems. Several participants emphasized the importance of community-driven approaches, advocating for bottom-up management systems where local communities play a central role in governance. This approach not only empowers communities but also ensures that governance structures reflect the needs and priorities of those directly affected by aquatic food systems.
