(ii) Leaf Area Index temporal dynamics for selected fields for calibrating crop growth
Leaf Area Index measurements were taken starting 20 days after transplanting, every 12 days corresponding to the days of Sentinel-1 image acquisition, until flowering, for capturing and calibrating crop growth temporal dynamics. A total of 8 fields were selected and sampled (Figure 2b). Fields are selected in such a way that they represent the diversity of the location being monitored, consisting of ecosystems and/or productivity classes. A total of 5/6 sets (dates) of LAI data were collected during the crop growing season between October 10 and November 3. The LAI measurements were done with the PocketLAI app, an android based application developed by Cassandra Lab at the University of Milan, Italy. PocketLAI estimates LAI based on the gap fraction which is the fraction of sky that can be seen from below the canopy. The protocol used to measure across a single field is shown in Figure 3. Across fields and during the season/period monitored, field recorded LAI values varied from 1.0 to 3.1 (Figure 4). Significant LAI variability is observed between fields, with some fields showing little LAI increase across crop stages and over time. This might be due to handling the PocketLAI app and/or some issues like crops damaged by animals or damaged by weeding operations.

2. 3. Methods
A combination of Sentinel-1A and Landsat 8-9 imagery was used to detect, and map cultivated rice areas and the start of the season. The following methods and technologies were implemented to map the rice area using the MAPScape-Rice tool.
Satellite data acquisition and data processing
The processing of SAR and Optical data is done using MAPscape-RICE, an image processing software developed by sarmap specifically for rice information extraction. The downloaded SAR data (Sentinel-1 Ground range intensity data, VV and VH polarization) and optical data (Sentinel-2 and Landsat 8/9) are processed using dedicated and automated processing chains. The SAR processing chain performs, in a fully automated way, a series of steps to convert the multi-temporal SAR GRD data into terrain geocoded backscatter σ° values: (i) strip mosaicking, (ii) co-registration, (ii) time-series speckle filtering, (iv) terrain geocoding, radiometric calibration and normalization, (v) anisotropic nonlinear diffusion (ANLD) filtering, (vi) removal of atmospheric attenuation and (vii) temporal smoothing. Rice classification
Nelson et al. (2004) proposed the MAPscape-RICE knowledge-based rice detection algorithm, and is used in this study (Figure 5). Before the main rule-based rice classification can take place, we need to generate a rice and non-rice mask showing potential rice growing regions. This helps us focus on areas where rice is likely to be grown and exclude areas where there is very likely no rice. Much effort is made on generating a rice baseline map (rice and non-rice mask) and analyzing different temporal features from both SAR and optical time series data. The Bouake region has a challenging crop ecosystem where the land cover is heterogeneous, and the rice fields are small and scattered, mostly less than 1 hectare in size. Also, cloud cover is very common across the country most of the time, which makes it difficult to use optical data for rice classification. Additionally, the poor road network, especially during rainy days when roads become impracticable, and security concerns make it hard to access the fields for ground data collection. Ground data quality is crucial for accurate mapping of rice in a complex ecosystem like the Bouake region.

Using processed time series SAR and optical data, we generated an initial version of a rice baseline map (Figure 6). This was achieved by using multi-temporal features from SAR (e.g., min and span ratio) and NDVI features (e.g., min at season start, max at midseason, increment) from Landsat- 8/Sentinel-2. The selection of temporal descriptors was based on agronomic practices, local knowledge, and crop calendar (Nelson et al., 2014). These descriptors were combined with the Sentinel-2 based global LULC map (layer) provided by the European Space Agency (ESA) (Zanaga et al., 2022) and used to classify rice and non rice using unsupervised methods and expert rice mapping knowledge. A higher likelihood of the presence of rice (or weight, through the classification tolerance parameters) was given in the cropland class identified in the LULC ESA map than in the grassland and shrubland classes. Visual inspection did identify crops in the latter two classes. This allowed the exclusion of rice crops in classes such as forest, settlement, etc., but still allowed for the possibility of crops in the shrubland and grassland classes.
The resulting classified initial rice baseline map was then mapped and compared to the cropland, shrubland, and grassland classes identified in the LULC ESA map (Figure 6). The green- colored areas represent the primary rice-growing areas, as captured in the ESA LULC map under the

Though the primary rice and non-rice masks captured potential rice growing regions with the help of SAR and optical temporal features, visual inspection of the product and comparison with Google Earth data showed still there are commission and omission errors across the study region. Particularly, wetland vegetation near water bodies was classified as potential rice-growing areas due to its similar temporal signature patterns. In addition, agriculture fields which are probably growing rice but are small in size, and/or covered with shrubs and/or trees may be omitted from the rice baseline map. The moderate radiometric and spatial resolution of Sentinel-1 and Landsat data (20-30m) are not enough to capture those small and tree-covered rice growing fields in the rice baseline map. Therefore, there is a need to improve this map, as it is a critical input for the main rice classification. To achieve this, the geospatial intelligence team is intending to incorporate additional datasets like SAOCOM and PlanetScope. These datasets offer longer wavelength (L-band) and spatial (5m) resolution, respectively, enabling the team to generate features that can delineate rice and crop fields from other land covers more effectively. DEM information can also serve as discriminant variables for inland valleys and higher lands. This is still in progress and is expected to be completed in the following months of 2024. The updated rice baseline and rice ecosystem, followed by the final rice map, will be produced in 2024 and shared with stakeholders and the project team.
Yield estimation
In terms of yield processing, rice mapping and yield estimation are interconnected, as the products of the rice mapping process, particularly the SOS map and LAI, are used in generating the input for the crop yield model (CYM). The CYM inputs are a crucial component within the Rice-Yield Estimation System (Rice-YES), in generating the yield estimates. Rice-YES captures the spatial variability of rice yield based on the inference of rice crop growth indicator in the form of Leaf Area Index (LAI) derived from SAR temporal signature during the early expansion stage of rice crop. The algorithm correlating SAR signature to LAI is embedded in MAPscape-RICE software. Rice-YES software serves as an interface that integrates the SAR-derived spatial information (LAI and SOS date) and the ORYZA crop growth model. ORYZA is a weather-driven and process-based rice crop growth model that captures complex and dynamic interactions among weather, soil, varietals, and agronomic management practices affecting rice yield (see Setiyono et al., 2019).
Figure 7 illustrates the operational diagram of the yield estimation processing. The assimilation of SAR-derived LAI products begins after the rice crop reaches the early expansion stage (roughly 40 days after SoS for a 120-days cropping duration of rice). During this early part of the rice-growing cycle, leaf expansion parameters in ORYZA can be effectively calibrated against real ground conditions inferred from satellite observations. LAI values derived from SAR are used to recalibrate the early leaf growth parameters in ORYZA, in particular the relative leaf growth rate (RGRL) variable. The RGRL variable was an ideal target for calibration given the known sensitivity of biomass accumulation and yield output of ORYZA to changes in this coefficient (Tan et al. 2016).

⚫ Varietal characteristics (maturity duration and other growth parameters such as leaf death rate, fraction of stem reserves, and maximum grain weight): See experimental data in next section.
⚫ Soil data (soil physical and hydrological properties): soil samples were taken from the AfricaRice research experimental station field, Bouake analyzed in the lab (texture, organic

Field experiment
Calibration of the dominant varieties for a particular geographical region is required for optimal performance of the crop growth model used for yield estimation, ORYZA. The variety/crop file used in ORYZA contains the phenological and growth characteristics of the variety being used for yield estimation in a given geographical area. These data were not available for the varieties generally planted in the Bouake region. Consequently, field experiments were established and implemented at the AfricaRice experimental station at Bouake to acquire such phenological data and analyze the rice yield performance of dominant rice varieties in the irrigated rice ecosystems.
The experiment also allowed us to check and validate the response of different fertilizer rates to the yield of two dominant rice varieties, WITA9 and JT11, under irrigated ecosystems. A randomized complete block design (RCBD) with fertilizer (four levels) as the main plot and variety (two rice varieties ; WITA9 (V1) and JT11 (V2)) as a subplot, with three replications, included four levels of fertilizer (F) treatments with different doses of N fertilizer with P and K fixed. The four fertilizer levels were as follows:
● F0 – No NPK (0-0-0)
● F1 – Low N (49.96 Kg N/ha)
● F2 – Medium NPK (99 Kg/ha)
● F3 – High NPK (149 Kg N/ha)
The specific date of sowing, panicle initiation, flowering, and maturity, along with the biomass information from the field experiment, are to be used as a starting point to calibrate local varieties in the Bouake irrigated ecosystem. ABSTRACT
Côte d'Ivoire has significant potential for rice production, yet the country
remains heavily reliant on imports due to low yields and limited adoption of improved technologies. Climate change further exacerbates these challenges, affecting rice productivity and food security. The Remote Sensing-based Information and Insurance for Crops in Emerging Economies (RIICE) decision support system was introduced to provide reliable, real-time data on rice cultivation, yield forecasts, and climate-related risks. This report details activities conducted by AfricaRice in 2024 related to the adaptation and implementation of the RIICE tool in Côte d'Ivoire through field experiments, georeferencing of rice fields, and the collection of leaf area index (LAI) data as well as feedback from stakeholders to ensure the tool is co-designed, responds to the local needs and that challenges related to infrastructure requirements and capacity building are addressed in the road for institutionalization. The findings highlight the potential of RIICE to enhance rice sector planning, improve resilience among smallholder farmers, and support policy decisions for achieving rice self-sufficiency.
Keywords. RIICE, insurance, monitoring, area, yield, climate change impacts.
1. INTRODUCTION
Despite the large rice production potential, Côte d'Ivoire remains highly dependent on imports due to the under-exploitation of available resources. Less than 50% of rice consumption is met by local production, leading to an import of 1.4 million tonnes of milled rice for USD 0.6 billion in 2021 (FAOSTAT, 2023). The low rice production relative to demand in the country is attributed to the low yield of rice (2.8 t/ha on average) compared to the world average (4.8 t/ha). Several factors, including limited adoption of high-yielding varieties, poor water management, limited access to climate information services and finance, declining soil fertility, biotic constraints (weeds, birds, rodents, insects, and diseases), and high post-harvest losses (Dossou-Yovo et al., 2021, 2023) explain the low rice yield in the country. These constraints faced by smallholder farmers are exacerbated by climate change that leads to higher temperatures and changes in rainfall patterns with more frequent dry spells, floods, and pests and diseases. During the 2016- 2017 season, rice yields decreased by 27% due to the rainfall deficit. By 2070, a
TAFS-WCA REPORT DECEMBER 2024 4
decrease in yields by up to 29% was predicted due to climate change (van Oort and Zwart, 2018). Coupled with rapid population growth and increased food requirements, reduced yields due to climate change will have a direct effect on food insecurity and the contribution of the rice sector to economic growth.
Climate change vulnerabilities and their impacts on rice communities in Côte
d'Ivoire are also gendered (Zossou et al., 2016). Women are more vulnerable than men to climate change due to several factors, including lack of literacy and mobility, which limits women's access to climate information and agricultural practices, increased workload as a result of men out-migration in search of off-farm income opportunities, and insecure land tenure and social norms that disadvantage women. Given the huge investment in rice imports, the government of Côte d'Ivoire sets the ambitious goal of achieving rice self-sufficiency by 2030. However, achieving this goal will necessitate an adequate investment in the rice sector based on the identification of suitable regions for rice cultivation, the deployment of appropriate technologies, and the monitoring of rice production. Consultations with stakeholders and government institutions revealed that the questions of where, when, and how much rice is produced, which are critical for planning investment in the rice sector, remained unaddressed.
2. ABOUT THE RIICE DECISION SU PPORT SYSTEM
Reliable and seasonally updated information on the effective rice cultivated area,
forecasted, and harvested yield are essential requirements for governments to support decision-making related to food security, management of natural resources, agricultural productivity, and insurance. The Remote Sensing based Information for Insurance and Crops in Emerging Economies (RIICE) is a decision support system that provides the government with reliable rice production data at harvest time and yield losses due to flood and drought to support planning in rice development and reduce the vulnerability of smallholder rice farmers by contributing to setting up affordable insurance schemes. RIICE relies on the integration of Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) derived products such as the rice area (where), the beginning of the rice crop season (when), the Leaf Area Index (LAI) and a crop growth simulation model to provide spatially explicit forecast and estimate yield at harvest time (how much will rice yield be). Given the spatial and temporal information provided by remote sensing data, RIICE is scalable to any extent with the use of local rice
TAFS-WCA REPORT DECEMBER 2024 5
agronomic knowledge incorporated in rice ecosystem model and it makes it possible to attain detailed spatial yield information at 1 – 2 ha. RIICE offers an effective alternative to conventional terrestrial methods that are time-consuming, expensive, and which result in area and yield statistics that are often questioned. Today, RIICE has been calibrated for the three major rice growing environments in Mali. In Asia, rice is operationally used in the Philippines, Cambodia, Vietnam, and three Indian states – Odisha, Andhra Pradesh, and Tamil Nadu.
3. RIICE ADAPTAT ION IN COTE D’IVOIRE
Three major activities were conducted for the RIICE adaptation in Côte d’Ivoire:
i)
i) A field experiment at a station to calibrate the ORYZA2000 crop growth model for irrigated rice simulation.
ii) Georeferencing of rice fields to calibrate and validate a remote sensing- based approach for assessing rice field occurrence.
iii) Leaf area index data collection to calibrate the remote sensing-based approach for monitoring rice growth on farmers' fields.
iv) Organization of a workshop with stakeholders on the status of implementation of the 2024 pilot project and outlook
3.1. FIELDS EXPERIMENT ON STATION
Two field experiments were carried out from August 19, 2024 to December 04, 2024 in an irrigated lowland and from August 21, 2024 to December 06, 2024 at the AfricaRice station in M'bé (7 ° 53' 58'' N, 5 ° 3' 33'' W) located in the Gêkê department (Bouaké) and on numerous other plots in the surrounding area. The climate is tropical, with two dry seasons from November to March and July to August, and two rainy seasons from April to June and September to October.
The experiments were conducted over an area of 800 square meters, divided into 24 sub-plots of 25 square meters each, representing three treatments in irrigated and rainfed lowlands. The experimental design used was a completely randomized block (split-plot).
The main plots were delimited by 0.5-metre bunds and 0.5-metre drainage channels, separating the main plots and their replicates. In addition, each sub-plot was separated by approximately 0.4 m to distinguish the two rice varieties (Fig. 1).

A pre-emergence herbicide was applied one day after transplanting, followed by manual weeding at 30 and 60 days. Additionally, regular cleaning of the areas surrounding the field experiment was rigorously carried out to prevent weed and pest infestations.
The water management practiced was continuous flooding (CF) for the irrigated lowland, where the land was kept constantly flooded. Before planting, soil data were collected by dividing the plot into four quadrants, and in each quadrant, we took samples at different depths (0-20 cm, 20-40 cm, 40-60 cm, and 60-80 cm). The following tools were utilized for the calibration and validation of the RIICE tool: a GARMIN GPS for recording the position and photographs of plots of interest, a tablet with a KoboCollect questionnaire for documenting various observations and specific field information, and a water-resistant Armor X5 Pro phone equipped with a Pocket LAI for measuring the average leaf area index (LAI) of rice plants.
The calibration, validation, and LAI studies in a farming environment involved selecting the site of interest according to the protocol. During a single pass for calibration (from the sowing period until maturity) and validation (from sowing until post-harvest), GPS points and field observations were recorded. For LAI, multiple regular visits were required every 12 days, starting 30-40 days after sowing for directly sown rice and 20 days after transplanting for transplanted rice, continuing until flowering. We selected rice fields that were at least one kilometre apart, easily accessible, and located 30 to 40 meters from roads and vegetation. In the validation fields, a single GPS point was collected at the centre of the plot, and the rest of the data collected was identical to that of the calibration fields (Fig. 7).

Abstract
Rice plays a vital role in the agricultural landscape of Ivory Coast in West Africa, serving as a keystone of the country's agricultural sector and food security, especially in the Bouake region, which significantly contributes to the country's rice production. With ongoing efforts in modernization, irrigation, and technological advancements, rice cultivation in the Bouake region continues to thrive, supporting local livelihoods and contributing to the nation's food security. To achieve sufficient rice productivity and promote sustainable agricultural practices, the Ivory Coast government has been actively taking many interventions, while monitoring rice areas and production estimates is crucial for designing/targeting interventions and for taking sound policy decisions. Transforming Agri-Food Systems in West and Central Africa (TAFS-WCA) is an CGIAR integrated regional initiative that aims to improve nutrition and food security within the context of climate change in West and Central Africa through nutritious, climate-adapted and market-driven food systems. As part of this initiative, Work Package 2 (Digital Agriculture) is implementing the Remote Sensing-based Information and Insurance for Crops in Emerging Economies (RIICE) tool (www.riice.org) , which is piloted in the Bouake region of Ivory Coast. This tool supports the government's endeavors to achieve rice self-sufficiency, and the pilot will aim to propose the implementation of this technology for monitoring rice production at national scale. This report presents the preliminary activities and initial outputs of the wet season 2023 over the Bouake region using RIICE technology, in collaboration with sarmap, Switzerland, AfricaRice, the Alliance of Bioversity International, CIAT, and local partners.

1. Introduction
Rice holds strategic importance for ensuring food security in West Africa. Its consumption has rapidly increased over time due to population growth, urbanization, and rising purchasing power (Fofana et al., 2014). In Ivory Coast, rice is grown across the country, mostly by smallholders. It is cultivated in both rainfed lowland (33%) and upland (64%) (source: Global Yield Gap Atlas) with 3- 5% under irrigated conditions . There is a significant disparity between locally produced rice and consumer demand in Côte d’Ivoire, as in most West African countries, with imported rice comprising approximately 50% of the country's rice consumption (United States Department of Agriculture Foreign Agricultural Service, 2016). According to the FAO/GIEWS report (2022), the national rice production for the year 2022 was 1,704,000 metric tons, with an estimated increase of 8.6% in rice production projected for the year 2023.
Remote sensing-based rice monitoring holds a high potential to enhance Ivory Coast's efforts towards sustainable rice production and self-sufficiency by improving rice production monitoring and management practices, supporting land use planning and policy making, etc. Numerous studies have reported the use of SAR rice mapping in various regions of the world, including Vietnam (Chen et al. 2016, Nguyen et al. 2016, Lasko et al. 2017), China (Mansaray et al. 2017), Myanmar (Torbick et al. 2017), France (Bazzi et al. 2019), Taiwan (Son et al., 2021), and the Philippines (Mabalay et al. 2022). Fiorillo et al. (2020) demonstrated the utilization of dense time series data from free optical and microwave sources to identify paddy rice areas in the Sédhiou region through object-based Random Forest classification. In 2014, IRRI, AfricaRice, and Sarmap conducted tests using radar COSMO- SkyMed to map rice areas in uplands and lowlands, and the Fanaye rice hub in the Senegal River Valley. Results indicated that radar time-series data could effectively map and monitor African rice systems with high accuracy, even in small field sizes (Zwart et al., 2014).
This study’s methodology applies on geospatial technology developed since 2011 by Remote Sensing-based Information and Insurance for Crops in emerging Economies (RIICE, http://www.riice.org/) to produce validated rice products, such as rice area (where?), start of season (when?), and yield (how much?). The service was developed and implemented by IRRI and sarmap, institutionally supported and co-founded by the Swiss Development Cooperation, and the initial years focused on development in South-East and South Asia. As part of Transforming Agri-Food Systems in West and Central Africa (TAFS-WCA), an integrated regional initiative of the One CGIAR (WP-2), IRRI and sarmap aim to adapt, calibrate, and develop the RIICE technology for Bouake, Ivory Coast, in collaboration with AfricaRice and the Alliance Bioversity-CIAT. This report covers pilot activities conducted to generate rice areas, Start-of-Season, Leaf Area Index (LAI), and end-of-season yield maps for the wet season 2023, as well as training and coordination activities with national stakeholders.
2. Data and Methods
2.1. Study area
The study focuses on the Bouake region in Ivory Coast, as depicted in Figure 1, which is situated at the country's center and acts as the interface between the interior and coastal regions. Agroecologically, it is situated in the transitional zone between the humid forest and the savanna zones. Bouake receives an average annual rainfall of 1370 mm, characterized by two distinct rainy seasons from April to July and from September to October. Bouake region has a diverse agricultural landscape, mainly growing rice, maize, cassava, yams and vegetables. Rice is a staple food crop in the region and

2.2. Data
Satellite data
Time series C-band Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) imagery, specifically Sentinel-1A (S1A) at 20m resolution, was obtained freely from the Copernicus Open Access Hub (https://dataspace.copernicus.eu). Around 30 S1A images (ascending orbit 118) were acquired in both VV and VH polarizations with a consistent incident angle from June 2023 to Jan 2024, and are used to delineate rice areas, identify the start of season (SOS) dates, and model LAI maps. The acquisition dates cover the wet season, from agronomic flooding, sowing or planting up to harvest. In addition to S1 data, additional supporting data used include the GLO-30 Digital Elevation Model (from Copernicus DEM, TanDEM-X mission) as input in image pre-processing and classification. Optical imagery such as Sentinel-2 and Landsat 8-9 were also acquired over the monitoring period. The optical images were used and NDVI images derived in order to support the generation of rice and non-rice mask that will be used in the main rice classification.

(ii) Leaf Area Index temporal dynamics for selected fields for calibrating crop growth
Leaf Area Index measurements were taken starting 20 days after transplanting, every 12 days corresponding to the days of Sentinel-1 image acquisition, until flowering, for capturing and calibrating crop growth temporal dynamics. A total of 5/6 sets (dates) of LAI data were collected during the crop growing season between October 10 and November 3. The LAI measurements were done with the PocketLAI app, an android based application developed by Cassandra Lab at the University of Milan, Italy. PocketLAI estimates LAI based on the gap fraction which is the fraction of sky that can be seen from below the canopy. The protocol used to measure across a single field is shown in Figure 3. Across fields and during the season/period monitored, field recorded LAI values varied from 1.0 to 3.1 (Figure 4). Significant LAI variability is observed between fields, with some fields showing little LAI increase across crop stages and over time. 2. 3. Methods
A combination of Sentinel-1A and Landsat 8-9 imagery was used to detect, and map cultivated rice areas and the start of the season. The following methods and technologies were implemented to map the rice area using the MAPScape-Rice tool.
Satellite data acquisition and data processing
The processing of SAR and Optical data is done using MAPscape-RICE, an image processing software developed by sarmap specifically for rice information extraction. The downloaded SAR data (Sentinel-1 Ground range intensity data, VV and VH polarization) and optical data (Sentinel-2 and Landsat 8/9) are processed using dedicated and automated processing chains. The SAR processing chain performs, in a fully automated way, a series of steps to convert the multi-temporal SAR GRD data into terrain geocoded backscatter σ° values: (i) strip mosaicking, (ii) co-registration, (ii) time-series speckle filtering, (iv) terrain geocoding, radiometric calibration and normalization, (v) anisotropic nonlinear diffusion (ANLD) filtering, (vi) removal of atmospheric attenuation and (vii) temporal smoothing. Rice classification
Nelson et al. (2004) proposed the MAPscape-RICE knowledge-based rice detection algorithm, and is used in this study (Figure 5). Before the main rule-based rice classification can take place, we need to generate a rice and non-rice mask showing potential rice growing regions. This helps us focus on areas where rice is likely to be grown and exclude areas where there is very likely no rice. Much effort is made on generating a rice baseline map (rice and non-rice mask) and analyzing different temporal features from both SAR and optical time series data. The Bouake region has a challenging crop ecosystem where the land cover is heterogeneous, and the rice fields are small and scattered, mostly less than 1 hectare in size. Also, cloud cover is very common across the country most of the time, which makes it difficult to use optical data for rice classification. Additionally, the poor road network, especially during rainy days when roads become impracticable, and security concerns make it hard to access the fields for ground data collection. Ground data quality is crucial for accurate mapping of rice in a complex ecosystem like the Bouake region.

Using processed time series SAR and optical data, we generated an initial version of a rice baseline map (Figure 6). This was achieved by using multi-temporal features from SAR (e.g., min and span ratio) and NDVI features (e.g., min at season start, max at midseason, increment) from Landsat- 8/Sentinel-2. The selection of temporal descriptors was based on agronomic practices, local knowledge, and crop calendar (Nelson et al., 2014). These descriptors were combined with the Sentinel-2 based global LULC map (layer) provided by the European Space Agency (ESA) (Zanaga et al., 2022) and used to classify rice and non rice using unsupervised methods and expert rice mapping knowledge. A higher likelihood of the presence of rice (or weight, through the classification tolerance parameters) was given in the cropland class identified in the LULC ESA map than in the grassland and shrubland classes. Visual inspection did identify crops in the latter two classes. This allowed the exclusion of rice crops in classes such as forest, settlement, etc., but still allowed for the possibility of crops in the shrubland and grassland classes.
The resulting classified initial rice baseline map was then mapped and compared to the cropland, shrubland, and grassland classes identified in the LULC ESA map (Figure 6). The green- colored areas represent the primary rice-growing areas, as captured in the ESA LULC map under the

Though the primary rice and non-rice masks captured potential rice growing regions with the help of SAR and optical temporal features, visual inspection of the product and comparison with Google Earth data showed still there are commission and omission errors across the study region. Particularly, wetland vegetation near water bodies was classified as potential rice-growing areas due to its similar temporal signature patterns. In addition, agriculture fields which are probably growing rice but are small in size, and/or covered with shrubs and/or trees may be omitted from the rice baseline map. The moderate radiometric and spatial resolution of Sentinel-1 and Landsat data (20-30m) are not enough to capture those small and tree-covered rice growing fields in the rice baseline map. Therefore, there is a need to improve this map, as it is a critical input for the main rice classification. To achieve this, the geospatial intelligence team is intending to incorporate additional datasets like SAOCOM and PlanetScope. These datasets offer longer wavelength (L-band) and spatial (5m) resolution, respectively, enabling the team to generate features that can delineate rice and crop fields from other land covers more effectively. DEM information can also serve as discriminant variables for inland valleys and higher lands. This is still in progress and is expected to be completed in the following months of 2024. The updated rice baseline and rice ecosystem, followed by the final rice map, will be produced in 2024 and shared with stakeholders and the project team.
Yield estimation
In terms of yield processing, rice mapping and yield estimation are interconnected, as the products of the rice mapping process, particularly the SOS map and LAI, are used in generating the input for the crop yield model (CYM). The CYM inputs are a crucial component within the Rice-Yield Estimation System (Rice-YES), in generating the yield estimates. Rice-YES captures the spatial variability of rice yield based on the inference of rice crop growth indicator in the form of Leaf Area Index (LAI) derived from SAR temporal signature during the early expansion stage of rice crop. The algorithm correlating SAR signature to LAI is embedded in MAPscape-RICE software. Rice-YES software serves as an interface that integrates the SAR-derived spatial information (LAI and SOS date) and the ORYZA crop growth model. ORYZA is a weather-driven and process-based rice crop growth model that captures complex and dynamic interactions among weather, soil, varietals, and agronomic management practices affecting rice yield (see Setiyono et al., 2019).
Figure 7 illustrates the operational diagram of the yield estimation processing. The assimilation of SAR-derived LAI products begins after the rice crop reaches the early expansion stage (roughly 40 days after SoS for a 120-days cropping duration of rice). During this early part of the rice-growing cycle, leaf expansion parameters in ORYZA can be effectively calibrated against real ground conditions inferred from satellite observations. LAI values derived from SAR are used to recalibrate the early leaf growth parameters in ORYZA, in particular the relative leaf growth rate (RGRL) variable. The RGRL variable was an ideal target for calibration given the known sensitivity of biomass accumulation and yield output of ORYZA to changes in this coefficient (Tan et al. 2016).

Field experiment
Calibration of the dominant varieties for a particular geographical region is required for optimal performance of the crop growth model used for yield estimation, ORYZA. The variety/crop file used in ORYZA contains the phenological and growth characteristics of the variety being used for yield estimation in a given geographical area. These data were not available for the varieties generally planted in the Bouake region. Consequently, field experiments were established and implemented at the AfricaRice experimental station at Bouake to acquire such phenological data and analyze the rice yield performance of dominant rice varieties in the irrigated rice ecosystems.
The experiment also allowed us to check and validate the response of different fertilizer rates to the yield of two dominant rice varieties, WITA9 and JT11, under irrigated ecosystems. A randomized complete block design (RCBD) with fertilizer (four levels) as the main plot and variety (two rice varieties ; WITA9 (V1) and JT11 (V2)) as a subplot, with three replications, included four levels of fertilizer (F) treatments with different doses of N fertilizer with P and K fixed. The four fertilizer levels were as follows:
● F0 – No NPK (0-0-0)
● F1 – Low N (49.96 Kg N/ha)
● F2 – Medium NPK (99 Kg/ha)
● F3 – High NPK (149 Kg N/ha)

Title: Digital Twin Drought Monitoring Tool
Description: The drought monitoring tool for the Limpopo River Basin integrates Earth Observation (EO) datasets, meteorological indices, and hydrological modeling to track drought conditions in near real-time. Developed under the IWMI Digital Twin platform, it leverages climate data, precipitation records, and vegetation health indicators such as the Standardized Precipitation Index (SPI) and Vegetation Condition Index (VCI) to assess drought severity and trends. The system incorporates satellite-derived rainfall anomalies, evapotranspiration assessments, and water balance calculations, helping policymakers and researchers understand the impact of drought on water resources, agriculture, and food security. The tool identifies regions most affected by dry conditions, enabling proactive decision-making for drought mitigation and adaptation strategies. By visualizing changes in water availability and vegetation health, it supports long-term planning for irrigation, water allocation, and climate resilience efforts. This comprehensive approach enhances early warning capabilities, helping governments and stakeholders implement timely interventions to minimize the socio-economic impact of droughts.

INTRODUCTION
Climate extremes, including drought, floods, and cyclones, contribute to elevated risk in marginal rainfed agricultural areas and livestock production. These events worsen the agricultural system, which is the least diversified and where many populations depend directly or indirectly on it. A severe drought or a series of consecutive drought seasons aggravates social and economic problems and hinders overall livelihood. Each year, droughts result in significant socioeconomic losses and ecological damage across the globe. The countries of Africa are no exception in experiencing the severe impacts of climate change. Research from most regions in Africa shows increasing trends in annual mean temperature and declining precipitation (Ghebrezgabher et al. 2016).
Since the 1980s, Southern Africa has witnessed a significant rise in the frequency and intensity of droughts, with much of the region experiencing severe water shortages. Droughts are often linked to El Niño events, which have historically caused

Drought assessment employs a range of indices to capture various aspects of drought conditions. Indices like the VCI, Temperature Condition Index (TCI), Vegetation Health Index (VHI) and SPI focus on specific attributes of drought, such as agricultural, meteorological, or hydrological drought. The integrated indices that focus on precipitation (meteorological), streamflow (hydrological) and vegetation (agricultural) can provide a more comprehensive understanding of drought (Wei et al., 2021).
Drought management integrating EO data underscores the importance of reliable risk assessment, clarifying the relationship between drought hazards and societal impacts (Hedayat and Kaboli, 2024). One significant technological innovation in this space is the IWMI Digital Twin (Garcia et al., 2024), a simulation platform designed to model and predict various water-related phenomena (Gurusinghe, 2024; Botai et al., 2023). Using near real-time data inputs such as rainfall, river flows, and satellite imagery, the IWMI Digital Twin creates a virtual replica of real-world water systems. This helps policymakers and water managers make informed decisions about resource management and agricultural planning, enabling them to respond more effectively to water-related challenges like floods and droughts.
Ensuring sufficient food production to prevent such crises requires implementing advanced drought monitoring and early warning systems. Earth observation (EO) datasets play a crucial role in monitoring and forecasting drought situations with their large synoptic view and repeated observation. EO- based drought indices are tools for estimating and monitoring occurrence probability, duration and severity of drought in a specific region (Ding, 2011). EO data, along with advanced technologies like cloud computing platforms like Google Earth Engine (GEE), has become a valuable tool for drought monitoring, impact assessment, early warning, and risk identification in recent years due to its ability to monitor drought conditions on various scales. With the large data repository in the cloud environment and the capability of processing large quantities of EO data at varied scales, GEE provides an important platform for disaster monitoring (Gorelick et al., 2017). They provide significant information that helps understand the extent of the drought and its impact on the agricultural system.
Indices like the Standardized Precipitation Index (SPI), rainfall anomaly, Vegetation Condition Index (VCI) and many more provide insights into the tangible impacts of drought on agricultural sectors and water resources within affected areas. EO has appeared as a transformative technology, offering extensive analytics for environmental monitoring, particularly in regions where agricultural drought is a significant concern. The Limpopo River Basin

This basin is an essential water source for these countries, supporting agriculture, industry, and the economy. Disasters like droughts and floods increase vulnerability, necessitating interventions that prioritize equitable access to resources, education, healthcare, and sustainable agriculture. Water balance is fundamental to understanding water resource availability within a hydrological system. The water balance equation evaluates the relationship between the inflows and outflows of water within a hydrological system. It is typically represented in its most basic form as Equation 1. Inflows primarily consist of precipitation (P), including rainfall and snowfall. Outflows are mainly attributed to runoff (Q) and evapotranspiration (ET), where evapotranspiration encompasses water loss through evaporation from the surface and plant transpiration. Additionally, changes in groundwater and soil moisture levels are represented as ΔS in the equation.
P = Q + ET + ΔS
Therefore, Q+ΔS=P-ET
Hydrological processes within a basin are highly interconnected, meaning water usage or extraction in upstream areas directly impacts the water availability for downstream regions. Likewise, activities such as deforestation or the expansion of agriculture upstream can significantly alter the quality of water resources further downstream. As water is a common resource shared by all countries within the Limpopo basin, each nation has established its framework for water management. A quantitative understanding of this shared resource is essential for creating effective and sustainable management strategies across the basin.
The chart illustrates the water balance (P-ET) for the Limpopo basin's cropland area, comparing 2023 with the long-term average from 2001 to 2022 (Figure 11). In contrast, several months, such as January and April, show a deficit, with negative water balance values, suggesting potential drought conditions during these periods. The long- term trend line remains more stable, offering a benchmark against which the anomalies in 2023 can be assessed. These variations highlight the challenges of managing water resources in the region, particularly in the face of climate variability that affects precipitation and evapotranspiration patterns.

Climate extremes, including drought, floods, and cyclones, contribute to elevated risk in marginal rainfed agricultural areas and livestock production. These events worsen the agricultural system, which is the least diversified and where many populations depend directly or indirectly on it. A severe drought or a series of consecutive drought seasons aggravates social and economic problems and hinders overall livelihood. Each year, droughts result in significant socioeconomic losses and ecological damage across the globe. The countries of Africa are no exception in experiencing the severe impacts of climate change. Research from most regions in Africa shows increasing trends in annual mean temperature and declining precipitation (Ghebrezgabher et al. 2016).
Since the 1980s, Southern Africa has witnessed a significant rise in the frequency and intensity of droughts, with much of the region experiencing severe water shortages. Droughts are often linked to El Niño events, which have historically caused

This helps policymakers and water managers make informed decisions about resource management and agricultural planning, enabling them to respond more effectively to water-related challenges like floods and droughts.
Ensuring sufficient food production to prevent such crises requires implementing advanced drought monitoring and early warning systems. The Limpopo River Basin
The LRB is the fourth largest river basin shared by four Southern African Development Community (SADC) Member States: Botswana, Mozambique, South Africa, and Zimbabwe in the semi-arid climatic region. Its total catchment area is approximately 408,250 km² (Figure 1). Water balance is fundamental to understanding water resource availability within a hydrological system. The water balance equation evaluates the relationship between the inflows and outflows of water within a hydrological system. It is typically represented in its most basic form as Equation 1. Inflows primarily consist of precipitation (P), including rainfall and snowfall. Outflows are mainly attributed to runoff (Q) and evapotranspiration (ET), where evapotranspiration encompasses water loss through evaporation from the surface and plant transpiration. Additionally, changes in groundwater and soil moisture levels are represented as ΔS in the equation.
P = Q + ET + ΔS
Therefore, Q+ΔS=P-ET
Hydrological processes within a basin are highly interconnected, meaning water usage or extraction in upstream areas directly impacts the water availability for downstream regions. Likewise, activities such as deforestation or the expansion of agriculture upstream can significantly alter the quality of water resources further downstream. As water is a common resource shared by all countries within the Limpopo basin, each nation has established its framework for water management. A quantitative understanding of this shared resource is essential for creating effective and sustainable management strategies across the basin.

Third, what type of intervention is planned, such as irrigation expansion involving groundwater or surface water. For example, users can determine where irrigation should be expanded, and identify suitable water sources based on key indicators. The dashboard also supports the generation of scenarios for irrigation efficiency improvements and groundwater recharge management. At the same time, users can view changes in the consumption of key food groups across specific scenarios targeted towards the adoption of healthy diets, reduced water use, and increased crop yields. Users can visualize datasets, download data, and focus their analysis on the entire Ganges Basin or specific states. In the calculator, drivers like population growth, food demand, exports and imports, productivity, food waste, land availability, gross domestic product, and afforestation/reforestation can be modified through in-built scenarios that drive the model outputs. The FABLE Calculator is an established country-level calculator that supports the preparation of policies related to the food system and land-use change. For its dashboard project, NEXUS Gains developed a basin-level calculator using data collected from states in the Ganges Basin. This calculator was calibrated with historical data for 2005, 2010, and 2015. Starting in 2020, scenario assumptions were applied to modify the future trajectory of parameters. Outputs from the calculator include daily kilocalorie consumption of various food groups per capita across different scenarios until 2050. The scenarios implemented in the dashboard can therefore incorporate measures for sustainable transformation towards healthy diets among the population of the Ganges Basin. This shift in diets drives change in the calculator towards feasible land-use change for agricultural production. Inclusion of results from various other associated indicators, such as those for reducing greenhouse gas emissions, is currently under development. As India navigates its path toward sustainable development in the face of climate change, resource constraints, and population growth leveraging digital tools such as the NEXUS dashboard will be crucial for informed decision-making. This dashboard not only helps in identifying and quantifying trade-offs, but also fosters collaboration among various stakeholders by making WEFE interconnections more apparent. This ensures that policies are equitable and effective in promoting sustainable food security not just in India but across the Indo-Gangetic Basin. For more insights into this project, and access to interactive tools designed specifically for policymakers, please visit the NEXUS Gains dashboard. Outcome
The ILRI Genebank houses a vast forage genetic pool that can be leveraged to address feed shortages and enhance farmers' resilience to climate change. However, traditional methods of forage characterization and screening from large collections have been expensive and time-consuming, often requiring several years to identify the best-suited forages for various purposes and contexts.
To overcome this challenge, the Feed and Forage Development (FFD) forage diversity research team has developed and applied genomic tools to accelerate the selection of optimal forage accessions and expedite the deployment of genebank materials for broader use by farmers. By utilizing DNA markers, the research team identified core collections of forage species, including cowpea, lablab, Sesbania sesban, Rhodes grass, oats, Urochloa spp., buffel grass, and Napier grass. These core collections are smaller, more manageable subsets that represent the genetic diversity of the extensive genebank holdings. Consequently, candidate best-bet varieties were rigorously identified and prepared for national variety verification trials.
The Ethiopian Institute of Agricultural Research (EIAR) has shown strong interest in these outcomes and successfully led the implementation of national variety trials for the selected forages. Currently, EIAR is evaluating the performance of the promising subsets to submit applications for the registration of new forage varieties in Ethiopia. This milestone provides livestock keepers with new forage options, improving feed supply, livestock productivity, and livelihoods.
Partners
The Ethiopian Institute of Agricultural Research (EIAR) is a key partner in this work. Through collaborative research agreements signed between the International Livestock Research Institute (ILRI) and EIAR, the institute has successfully conducted national variety verification trials and is now leading the application process for new variety registrations. Universities such as Ambo, Debre Berhan, and Jimma, along with regional agricultural research centers, have also been important collaborators, providing land and resources for field evaluations of the selected forage varieties.
Why did we do this research?
The impacts of climate change, population pressure, and land degradation have placed significant strain on the feed resource base in Ethiopia and beyond, adversely affecting livestock production and productivity. Developing new forage varieties that perform well under various climatic stresses and soil fertility conditions is therefore essential for cultivating sufficient quantities of high-quality feed.
In particular, forage varieties that are drought-tolerant, exhibit higher water and nutrient use efficiency, are suitable for land reclamation, improve soil fertility, enhance carbon sequestration, and reduce enteric methane emissions are urgently needed. This research plays a critical role in making such varieties available to farmers, enabling the development of a more resilient livestock farming system. This, in turn, helps smallholder farmers increase livestock outputs, leading to improved income, nutrition, and livelihoods.
Furthermore, this research facilitates the efficient utilization of the ILRI forage genebank’s genetic resources, contributing to societal well-being and environmental protection
3
Evidence
The following are a summary of evidence for this outcome:
o Out of more than 205 buffel grass (Cenchrus ciliaris) accessions maintained in the ILRI forage genebank, a subset containing 41 accessions (20% of the population) that represented the genetic diversity of the whole collection were identified using genome wide SNP markers (Negawo et al., 2020). This allowed us to fast-track field evaluation and national variety trials. Some of these selected accessions have already been evaluated under field conditions across locations (Bishoftu, Ziway and Guder/Ambo) under national variety trials (NVT) (Figure 1). Few of the accessions are already showed good performance for biomass yield and are candidates for the next verification trial and variety release. This has accelerated the selection process (reduced at least by two to three years), reduced the cost of selection, and improved selection efficiency as compared to evaluating the entire more than 200 accessions.
o Similarly, the FFD team analysed the genetic diversity of Napier grass collections from the ILRI forage genebank and EMBRAPA (Brazilian Agricultural Research Corporation) using SSR markers and 54 unique genotypes that genetically distinct from the ILRI collection were selected and introduced to the ILRI genebank (Negawo et al., 2018). Two of these genotypes, together with additional genotypes from the ILRI collection, were selected as a core set using genome wide SNP markers (Muktar et al., 2019). Because of its high biomass yield and drought tolerance (Habte et al., 2022), two of these genotypes have now advanced to national variety trial (Figure 2).
o Moreover, the same approach has helped to evaluate a subset of the ILRI genebank collections for cowpea, lablab, and oat under field conditions in replicated field trials across years and locations, and identified best performing genotypes for forage biomass yield, grain yield, dual purpose type, and early maturing types out of each subset per species. We have also generated high-density genome wide markers nearly for the entire collection of each species, in order to select additional best performing genotypes out of the remaining genotypes that were not phenotyped under field conditions through genomic prediction approach (Muktar et al., 2023). The team, in collaboration with partners across the world, has led the development of reference genome for Lablab (Njaci et al., 2023).

Next steps
o Collaborate closely with EIAR to compile performance data for candidate varieties.
o Assist in preparing and submitting applications to the Agricultural Authority of Ethiopia for the approval and official registration of new forage varieties.
o Launch new national variety verification trials (NVT) for recently identified best-bet forage accessions that are ready to enter the pipeline.
o Extend the use of genomic prediction and marker-assisted selection to additional important forage species within the ILRI genebank to enhance the efficiency of variety selection.
o Establish forage demonstration plots to showcase the performance of newly released varieties.
o Organize capacity-building training programs for national partners to strengthen their skills in forage evaluation, genomic tools, and sustainable management practices.
o Establish and strengthen partnerships with public and private entities across other sub-Saharan countries to facilitate the regional registration and adoption of newly screened varieties.

These core collections are smaller, more manageable subsets that represent the genetic diversity of the extensive genebank holdings. Consequently, candidate best-bet varieties were rigorously identified and prepared for national variety verification trials.
The Ethiopian Institute of Agricultural Research (EIAR) has shown strong interest in these outcomes and successfully led the implementation of national variety trials for the selected forages. Currently, EIAR is evaluating the performance of the promising subsets to submit applications for the registration of new forage varieties in Ethiopia. This milestone provides livestock keepers with new forage options, improving feed supply, livestock productivity, and livelihoods.
Partners
The Ethiopian Institute of Agricultural Research (EIAR) is a key partner in this work. Through collaborative research agreements signed between the International Livestock Research Institute (ILRI) and EIAR, the institute has successfully conducted national variety verification trials and is now leading the application process for new variety registrations. Universities such as Ambo, Debre Berhan, and Jimma, along with regional agricultural research centers, have also been important collaborators, providing land and resources for field evaluations of the selected forage varieties.
Why did we do this research?
The impacts of climate change, population pressure, and land degradation have placed significant strain on the feed resource base in Ethiopia and beyond, adversely affecting livestock production and productivity. Developing new forage varieties that perform well under various climatic stresses and soil fertility conditions is therefore essential for cultivating sufficient quantities of high-quality feed.
In particular, forage varieties that are drought-tolerant, exhibit higher water and nutrient use efficiency, are suitable for land reclamation, improve soil fertility, enhance carbon sequestration, and reduce enteric methane emissions are urgently needed. This research plays a critical role in making such varieties available to farmers, enabling the development of a more resilient livestock farming system. This, in turn, helps smallholder farmers increase livestock outputs, leading to improved income, nutrition, and livelihoods.
Furthermore, this research facilitates the efficient utilization of the ILRI forage genebank’s genetic resources, contributing to societal well-being and environmental protection
3
Evidence
The following are a summary of evidence for this outcome:
o Out of more than 205 buffel grass (Cenchrus ciliaris) accessions maintained in the ILRI forage genebank, a subset containing 41 accessions (20% of the population) that represented the genetic diversity of the whole collection were identified using genome wide SNP markers (Negawo et al., 2020). This allowed us to fast-track field evaluation and national variety trials. Some of these selected accessions have already been evaluated under field conditions across locations (Bishoftu, Ziway and Guder/Ambo) under national variety trials (NVT) (Figure 1). Few of the accessions are already showed good performance for biomass yield and are candidates for the next verification trial and variety release. This has accelerated the selection process (reduced at least by two to three years), reduced the cost of selection, and improved selection efficiency as compared to evaluating the entire more than 200 accessions.
o Similarly, the FFD team analysed the genetic diversity of Napier grass collections from the ILRI forage genebank and EMBRAPA (Brazilian Agricultural Research Corporation) using SSR markers and 54 unique genotypes that genetically distinct from the ILRI collection were selected and introduced to the ILRI genebank (Negawo et al., 2018). Two of these genotypes, together with additional genotypes from the ILRI collection, were selected as a core set using genome wide SNP markers (Muktar et al., 2019). Because of its high biomass yield and drought tolerance (Habte et al., 2022), two of these genotypes have now advanced to national variety trial (Figure 2).
o Moreover, the same approach has helped to evaluate a subset of the ILRI genebank collections for cowpea, lablab, and oat under field conditions in replicated field trials across years and locations, and identified best performing genotypes for forage biomass yield, grain yield, dual purpose type, and early maturing types out of each subset per species. We have also generated high-density genome wide markers nearly for the entire collection of each species, in order to select additional best performing genotypes out of the remaining genotypes that were not phenotyped under field conditions through genomic prediction approach (Muktar et al., 2023). The team, in collaboration with partners across the world, has led the development of reference genome for Lablab (Njaci et al., 2023).

o Assist in preparing and submitting applications to the Agricultural Authority of Ethiopia for the approval and official registration of new forage varieties.

Dormancy-breaking treatments play a crucial role in enhancing seed germination and promoting seedling growth in Macroptilium and Clitoria species. In the case of Macroptilium species, it was observed that applying dry heat for a duration of 15 to 20 minutes significantly improved the germination percentage of seeds. Introduction
The International Livestock Research Institute (ILRI) genebank preserves a large collection of legumes, grasses and browses. The accessions are maintained and made available for use in agriculture and research to enhance food security. The collections conserved in the genebank need to be monitored to determine viability status and make the right decision before the viability falls below the threshold. However, most of the collections represent wild species and, unfortunately, there is limited information on their viability monitoring and dormancy status (Sartie et al. 2020). Monitoring the viability of such wild species is typically more challenging than other crop species, due to the higher prevalence of seed dormancy (FAO 2014).
Macroptilium and Clitoria are important perennial legume species that play a crucial role in sustainable agriculture. Both species serve as a valuable source of high protein feed for livestock. Their nutritional profile makes them an excellent feed option, contributing to improved animal growth and productivity. Additionally, these legumes can thrive in various environmental conditions, making them adaptable choices for farmers looking to enhance the quality of their pastures and provide superior nutrition to their livestock.
However, like many other forage species, they have a high seed coat dormancy problem (Rusdy 2016; Silva et al. 2020; Pincay-Ganchozo et al. 2021), challenging the growers and seed quality analysts. Both species exhibit physical dormancy, posing a major difficulty when assessing viability in genebank. The limited water absorption capacity of these species blocks the imbibition process, obstructing embryo growth and delaying germination, which results in poor field establishment. To enhance the percentage of normal seedlings a wide range of treatments and several experiments were done to break the physical dormancy in many forage species (Gresta et al. 2011; Baskin and Baskin 2014; Rusdy 2017; Olbana et al. 2023).
However, information on dormancy breaking methods for some forage species was scanty and there is a need to optimize the germination test protocol to monitor collections in the genebank. Also, most of the dormancy breaking methods were time consuming, labour intensive and difficult to work with when a large number of samples needed to be scarified. Therefore, the present study aimed to investigate the best scarification methods for dormancy breaking to enhance germination and to examine the possibility of release from dormancy during storage in Macroptillium and Clitoria species seeds stored under genebank conditions in medium-term storage (MTS).
Methodology
Experimental procedures
Ten accessions of Macroptillium and Clitoria were selected based on the quantity of seeds stored at medium-term storage from the genebank (Table 1). The experiment included four pretreatment methods. The pretreatment methods were 98% concentrated sulphuric acid treatment (15 and 20 minutes for Macroptilium, 5 and 10 minutes for Clitoria), hot water treatments at 80°C ±5 for 4 and 6 minutes, sandpaper scarification (Diamond GLASS Paper No. 11/2) and dry heat treatments at 80°C (15 and 20 minutes). For both species, untreated seeds were used as a ‘control’ to compare against treated seeds.
The concentrated sulphuric acid treatment was carried out by soaking the seeds in the prepared solution for the allocated time and then washing the seeds repeatedly under cold running water and redrying. For hot water treatment, the samples were immersed in a water bath (Gallenkamp BKS-350-010 220/240 V) heated at 80 ±5°C for the given minutes using a muslin cloth and cooling at room temperature. Sand scarification was done using glass paper by rubbing the seed surface to soften the seed coat to facilitate water imbibition. The dry heat treatment was done in the oven at a given temperature for a given minute.

Germination test and seedling evaluation
Germination test was conducted using four replicates of 20 seeds each. Seeds were arranged on Whatman Grade 4 filter paper (TISCH Scientific) moistened with distilled water held in 90 mm diameter Petri dishes. The Petri dishes with seeds were incubated at a constant temperature of 25°C with 12 hours light/12 hours dark. The first germination count was made five days after sowing and the final count was made on the fifteenth day. At the final seedling evaluation, the hard seeds were dissected using a scalpel blade and the embryo was visually observed to check whether it was alive or not. The evaluation of seedlings as normal, abnormal, dead, hard and fresh ungerminated was done following ISTA guidelines (ISTA 2019).

Dormancy breaking treatment had a significant effect on seed germination and seedling growth of Macroptilium species accessions. All pretreatments showed significant differences in all accessions tested. Dry heat treatment had a positive effect on the germination percentage of Macroptilium species compared to other treatments

Discussion
Dormancy breaking treatments are important in enhancing seed germination and seedling development in crops. Different methods have been used to overcome seed coat dormancy in forage species. In this study, different pretreatment methods were explored for breaking dormancy in Marcoptilium and Clitoria spp and the result showed significant variations in germination percentage and subsequent seedling growth among the pretreatments. Among the treatments, dry heat treatment for 15 to 20 minutes at 80°C emerged as the most effective approach for increasing the germination percentage in Macroptilium species.
For Clitoria spp, the use of sandpaper to abrade the seed coat, immersing the seeds in hot water for four minutes and concentrated sulfuric acid (H2SO4) treatment for five minutes have contributed positively to germination percentage. Various scarification methods have also been found to significantly enhance germination percentage for Clitoria species (Nagar and Meena 2015; Shobharani and Sundareswaran 2018; Pincay-Ganchozo et al. 2021).
In general, the seeds of Marcoptilium and Clitoria spp exhibited physical dormancy that can be alleviated by different pretreatments and the result from this study provides invaluable insight for improving seed quality management of collections stored in the genebank.

Introduction
The International Livestock Research Institute (ILRI) genebank preserves a large collection of legumes, grasses and browses. The accessions are maintained and made available for use in agriculture and research to enhance food security. The collections conserved in the genebank need to be monitored to determine viability status and make the right decision before the viability falls below the threshold. However, most of the collections represent wild species and, unfortunately, there is limited information on their viability monitoring and dormancy status (Sartie et al. 2020). Monitoring the viability of such wild species is typically more challenging than other crop species, due to the higher prevalence of seed dormancy (FAO 2014).
Macroptilium and Clitoria are important perennial legume species that play a crucial role in sustainable agriculture. Both species serve as a valuable source of high protein feed for livestock. Their nutritional profile makes them an excellent feed option, contributing to improved animal growth and productivity. Additionally, these legumes can thrive in various environmental conditions, making them adaptable choices for farmers looking to enhance the quality of their pastures and provide superior nutrition to their livestock.
However, like many other forage species, they have a high seed coat dormancy problem (Rusdy 2016; Silva et al. 2020; Pincay-Ganchozo et al. 2021), challenging the growers and seed quality analysts. Both species exhibit physical dormancy, posing a major difficulty when assessing viability in genebank. The limited water absorption capacity of these species blocks the imbibition process, obstructing embryo growth and delaying germination, which results in poor field establishment. To enhance the percentage of normal seedlings a wide range of treatments and several experiments were done to break the physical dormancy in many forage species (Gresta et al. 2011; Baskin and Baskin 2014; Rusdy 2017; Olbana et al. 2023).
However, information on dormancy breaking methods for some forage species was scanty and there is a need to optimize the germination test protocol to monitor collections in the genebank. Also, most of the dormancy breaking methods were time consuming, labour intensive and difficult to work with when a large number of samples needed to be scarified. Therefore, the present study aimed to investigate the best scarification methods for dormancy breaking to enhance germination and to examine the possibility of release from dormancy during storage in Macroptillium and Clitoria species seeds stored under genebank conditions in medium-term storage (MTS).
Methodology
Experimental procedures
Ten accessions of Macroptillium and Clitoria were selected based on the quantity of seeds stored at medium-term storage from the genebank (Table 1). The experiment included four pretreatment methods. The pretreatment methods were 98% concentrated sulphuric acid treatment (15 and 20 minutes for Macroptilium, 5 and 10 minutes for Clitoria), hot water treatments at 80°C ±5 for 4 and 6 minutes, sandpaper scarification (Diamond GLASS Paper No. 11/2) and dry heat treatments at 80°C (15 and 20 minutes). For both species, untreated seeds were used as a ‘control’ to compare against treated seeds.
The concentrated sulphuric acid treatment was carried out by soaking the seeds in the prepared solution for the allocated time and then washing the seeds repeatedly under cold running water and redrying. For hot water treatment, the samples were immersed in a water bath (Gallenkamp BKS-350-010 220/240 V) heated at 80 ±5°C for the given minutes using a muslin cloth and cooling at room temperature. Sand scarification was done using glass paper by rubbing the seed surface to soften the seed coat to facilitate water imbibition. The dry heat treatment was done in the oven at a given temperature for a given minute.

Germination test and seedling evaluation
Germination test was conducted using four replicates of 20 seeds each. Seeds were arranged on Whatman Grade 4 filter paper (TISCH Scientific) moistened with distilled water held in 90 mm diameter Petri dishes. The Petri dishes with seeds were incubated at a constant temperature of 25°C with 12 hours light/12 hours dark. The first germination count was made five days after sowing and the final count was made on the fifteenth day. At the final seedling evaluation, the hard seeds were dissected using a scalpel blade and the embryo was visually observed to check whether it was alive or not. The evaluation of seedlings as normal, abnormal, dead, hard and fresh ungerminated was done following ISTA guidelines (ISTA 2019).

Dormancy breaking treatment had a significant effect on seed germination and seedling growth of Macroptilium species accessions. All pretreatments showed significant differences in all accessions tested. Dry heat treatment had a positive effect on the germination percentage of Macroptilium species compared to other treatments

Similarly, for Clitoria species, the dormancy breaking treatments showed significant differences in the percentage of normal seedlings germinated compared to untreated seeds (Figure 2). The sandpaper, hot water (4 minutes) and H2SO4 (5 minutes) treatments showed good germination and these treatments considered as best scarification methods for this species. The control (untreated) seeds did not show good germination result and the seeds remained hard at the final evaluation in both species.

Discussion
Dormancy breaking treatments are important in enhancing seed germination and seedling development in crops. Different methods have been used to overcome seed coat dormancy in forage species. In this study, different pretreatment methods were explored for breaking dormancy in Marcoptilium and Clitoria spp and the result showed significant variations in germination percentage and subsequent seedling growth among the pretreatments. Among the treatments, dry heat treatment for 15 to 20 minutes at 80°C emerged as the most effective approach for increasing the germination percentage in Macroptilium species.
For Clitoria spp, the use of sandpaper to abrade the seed coat, immersing the seeds in hot water for four minutes and concentrated sulfuric acid (H2SO4) treatment for five minutes have contributed positively to germination percentage. Various scarification methods have also been found to significantly enhance germination percentage for Clitoria species (Nagar and Meena 2015; Shobharani and Sundareswaran 2018; Pincay-Ganchozo et al. 2021).
In general, the seeds of Marcoptilium and Clitoria spp exhibited physical dormancy that can be alleviated by different pretreatments and the result from this study provides invaluable insight for improving seed quality management of collections stored in the genebank.

1. Introduction
In Lao Peoples Democratic Republic (Lao PDR) most of the population is living in rural areas depending on agriculture for their livelihoods. Farmers have historically practiced subsistence-based integrated farming, which combines crops, livestock and trees in a complex landscape mosaic. Family farming remains the main agricultural system in Lao PDR and has occupied a central role in the sustainable development of the agricultural sector.
The intensification of conventional agriculture is leading to a simplification of agricultural landscapes, land degradation and biodiversity depletion, and an increase of health risks for farmers and consumers. Agricultural productivity and profitability in Lao PDR are becoming increasingly vulnerable to climate change, especially under rain-fed conditions. Sustainably managing soil fertility and soil health while maintaining productivity is a challenge. Agroecological practices have developed in response to these challenges. These practices help addressing critical issues such as soil fertility decrease, biodiversity loss, water scarcity or increasing the constraints on crop and livestock productions; and they have been identified as promising and efficient ways to achieve the Sustainable Development Goals (SDG) and to adapt and mitigate climate change.
The CGIAR initiative on Agroecology under which this activity took place is a transdisciplinary, participatory, and action-oriented approach aimed at enhancing food system resilience, equity, and sustainability. The Initiative aims to develop and scale agroecological innovations for small-scale farmers and other agricultural and food system actors across different socioecological contexts in seven low- and middle- income countries.
The Département of Agriculture and Land Management (DALaM) is responsible for the nationwide development and management of agricultural property. Its primary obligations include conducting research, coordinating with relevant stakeholders the conduction of surveys for effective management and land use planning information, and coordinating with relevant parties the conduction of soil research and other production factors for the purpose of enhancing soil health.
The aim of this activity was to support the agroecology transition at the local level, particularly for the producer in Attapeu province, Lao PDR. DALaM and the International Water Management Institute (IWMI), with the support of the French Agricultural Research Centre for International Development (CIRAD), have proposed to conduct the Soil Doctors Program (SDP) within the Agroecology project with the aim of improving soil health and productivity in Attapeu by collaborating with project partners, delivering land

This report covers the SDP carried out in Attapeu from November 18 to 22, 2024, which was supported by staff from DALaM and the Provincial Agriculture and Forestry Office (PAFO), with the aim that the Soil Doctors will be able to train farmers in their respective villages.
These activities continued the implementation of the Global Soil Doctors Program in Lao PDR, which started in September 2023 as a collaborative effort between DALaM, PAFO, the District Agriculture and Forestry Office (DAFO), FAO Laos, and FAO's Global Soil Partnership1.
Objectives
▪ To create a system of farmer-to-farmer training by enhancing farmers' ability to manage their soils in sustainable ways.
▪ To assist governmental organizations and agencies engaged in field-level agricultural extension.
▪ To support field research based on interactions between the Soil Doctors and partners, including access to demonstration and experimental fields; and
▪ To promote the concept of soil testing prior to recommendations on soil management and agroecological practices.
2. Implementation of the soil doctors program
DALaM facilitated the training based on the educational material developed by FAO which was adjusted by DALaM to fit the Lao context. The implementation of the program followed different steps:
Step 1: Selection of soil doctor candidates (September 2024):
▪ Describing the certification procedure and the Global Soil Doctors program.
▪ Describing the soil doctors' requirements:
Individuals that are 18 years of age or older (no gender limits)
- Those who labor hard and maintain good health in agricultural production
- To be a willing and suitable local soil doctor.
- To own a parcel of agricultural land (farm, garden, etc.) that is at least 0.5–1 hectare in size is required.
- They have consistently created agricultural products that are incredibly effective.
- To obtain approval from the partner (wife/husband) or other family members.
