1.3 Biodiversity
There is no record of any past biological study of the lake and its surroundings. Local people have recounted the many different plant and animal species, including fish and waterbirds, that once inhabited the area. However, this knowledge of biodiversity has not been documented, and most of these species are no longer present. Given the important ecological functions provided by the vegetation to sustain the wetland and lake environment, and the significance of fish for local livelihoods, it is crucial to conduct extensive studies of the local species of plants and animals and to reestablish relevant habitats. Understanding the local biodiversity, including the species and their habitats, is critical for effective management and conservation.
Direct observation reveals that there is almost no aquatic vegetation, or plants present in the lake itself. In the immediate surroundings of the lake, particularly in the paddy and cash crop landscape, there is no vegetation that could support regeneration. A few shrubs can be seen between 5 and 10 meters from the lake shore during the dry season, scattered haphazardly in the southwest and behind the villages to the east of the lake. Although the communities reported a dozen species of aquatic plants, most of these are not currently sighted.

1.4 Resource and land Use
The Sekong River valley, which flows through the middle of the province, is considered the “rice bowl” of Attapeu. It is one of the larger rice-growing areas in Lao PDR, although yields are low. Paddy rice and watermelon farming have been the major agricultural crops around the lake, while livestock grazing and the utilization of non-timber forest products from the mountains and wetlands have been the most common land use practices in the larger area. Recently, cassava planting has become a major cash crop on the newly cleared land on higher ground.
Many of the paddy fields and surrounding areas along the channel between NL and the Sekong are privately owned, mainly by residents. However, large plots of land used for teak and other plantations mostly belong to people from outside the communities. A field trial site belonging to the provincial Department of Agriculture and Forestry is located to the east of NR18A, between Hom and Thamaleuy villages.
Like the lands along the channel between NL and Sekong, much of the land immediately around the lake is privately owned by community members and has been used mostly for dry season rice and watermelon production. Hom village is situated very close to the southeast of the lake, and Thamaleuy is to the northeast, mostly on the other side of NR18A. A narrow strip of land close to the lakeshore in the south, west, and northeast of the lake is also used for planting watermelon, mainly after the rice is harvested. According to the village chiefs of Hom and Thamaleuy, 80% (about 24 ha) of farmland around Thamaleuy belongs to Hom, and only 20% to Thamaleuy.2

Current uses of NL include water for rice irrigation in the dry season, animal drinking and wallowing, and fishing all year round. The proximity of paddy fields to the lake makes it easy to access irrigation. A few households next to the lake also use the water for home gardening but not for domestic consumption due to its high turbidity from excessive fishing in the dry season.
The lake is subject to open access fishing by local villagers in the surrounding areas. Some fishers claim private access to small segments of the lake with established brush gardens to attract fish, and harvesting is done either with nets or by the pumping dry method. This traditional fishing practice has been inherited for generations but lacks legal recognition by any authority. The lake is heavily fished, with no areas reserved for protection or as dry season refuges, and the fishing methods include destructive practices such as pumping dry and electrocution.
PVC pipes are fitted to the bunds of paddy fields to facilitate water flow across the fields, and fish are reported to use these pipes to cross between fields. Where water channels leading to the paddy fields are present, fish traps, some fitted with fences (locally known as “lee”), are not uncommon. These traps appear to target fish on their way back to the main water body in the late wet season. However, fishing with traps and associated fences is banned in the main channel/creek.
A few fishponds are also present next to the creek, about 1,400 meters northeast of the lake, where the channel outlet from the north of the lake meets the creek. These ponds are privately owned and could be managed to provide dry season refuge ponds as well as for fish production. Given the frequent sighting of fish traps, it can be assumed that fishing is quite important, especially in the wet season, and fish migration across the landscape in the wet season is also significant. A few borrow pits can be seen right beside the southeast shore of NL, behind Hom village.

No information is currently available on their level of education. Rice cultivation has been the backbone of local livelihoods, typically occurring between June and December, with an average yield of 1.5 tons per hectare. Unlike their counterparts in selected villages from Sanamxay district, where organic rice production is practiced with support from Indochina Development Partner (IDP) – a private sector entity exporting rice to Europe – rice farming practices in this area follow traditional methods. However, some changes have been reported recently, with more farmers applying chemical inputs to their rice production, ranging from fertilizers to pesticides.
Since 2009, the government has raised awareness among farmers about reducing the use of chemical fertilizers and turning to composting, providing training on making compost. Despite this, adoption levels were low. In 2020, many villagers turned to multiple cropping for their cash crops, planting watermelon, sugar cane, and vegetables. While much of the land surrounding NL is dedicated to rice farming during the wet season, 5-6 hectares of land, particularly areas close to NL where water access is easy, are used by 17 households for watermelon farming. In 2024, watermelon farming covered an area of 5-6 hectares. Farmers grow watermelon on an alternating year basis on the same plot of land, allowing a year for the soil to rest and regenerate its fertility.

1.6 Governance of Nong Lom area
1.6.1 Existing legislations and institutions
Lao PDR has implemented various laws and regulations to govern its agricultural sector. Key agencies with relevant mandates include:
o The Ministry of Agriculture and Forestry: Oversees several departments, including:
o Department of Agriculture: Responsible for the development and promotion of sustainable agriculture practices, crop production, plant protection, and agricultural extension services.
o Department of Irrigation: Handles the planning, construction, and maintenance of irrigation systems to support agricultural production.
o Department of Agricultural Extension and Cooperatives: Provides advisory services, training, and technical support to farmers and promotes the development of agricultural cooperatives.
o Provincial and District Agriculture and Forestry Offices: Implement and monitor agricultural and forestry activities at the local level.
Article 4 of the Law on Agriculture (01-98/NA, 10 October 1998) protects the rights and interests of farmers with relevant policies and regulations to promote agricultural production. Article 5 protects agricultural land from inappropriate modification without prior approval from the ministry. Article 25 of the Land Law (No. 70/NA, 21 June 2019) states that land use conversion can only be made if necessary to maximize benefits and improve livelihoods, in line with the Land Allocation Master Plan, land use strategy, and sectoral and local land use plans. Article 6 ensures that thirty percent of the overall land nationally is set for use and development, with forest land covering not less than seventy percent.
The Government of Lao PDR recognizes wetlands as important natural resources providing ecosystem services such as water regulation, biodiversity conservation, and carbon sequestration. The Law on Environmental Protection and Management (No. 07/NA, 2019) and the Law on Water and Water Resources (No. 06/NA, 2019) provide the legal framework for the protection and management of wetlands in Lao PDR. These regulations are crucial for managing NL lake.
The Department of Livestock and Fisheries of the Ministry of Agriculture and Forestry, along with its sub-national offices under the Provincial Agriculture and Forests Office (PAFO) and District Agriculture and Forest Office (DAFO), is responsible for the management and development of the Lao fisheries sector. The first comprehensive national law governing fisheries in Laos was the Fisheries Law 2009 (No. 03/NA, 09 July 2009). There is no local-level law or regulation governing fisheries management; local practices must refer to national law provisions. The law regulates the management, conservation, and development of fisheries resources in Laos, including the protection of aquatic biodiversity, the prevention of illegal fishing practices, and the promotion of sustainable fishing practices.
Article 4 stipulates that fish and other aquatic fauna in the public domain are the property of the national community and shall be centrally governed by the State uniformly throughout the country. The State recognizes the use rights of individuals and organizations in accordance with laws and regulations. Sustainable water management: Community-managed solar groundwater
in Laos
Laos, a country with significant seasonal water fluctuations, experiences acute water scarcity during the dry months of March and April. This scarcity impacts not only the agriculture sector but also the daily lives of rural communities, especially those of women and young girls responsible for water collection.
The reliance on spring water for domestic needs and surface water for agriculture becomes problematic during the dry season. In the Attapeu Province, particularly in the districts of Sanamxay and Samakkixay, the lack of reliable water sources during these
critical months leads to hardships in water collection and poses a threat to agricultural sustainability (Figure 1).
In addition, a significant amount of surface water is abstracted from the NongLom wetland to irrigate cash crops during the dry season. It is important to minimize pressure on water abstraction and ensure effective management of water resources, particularly in cases where the current status of the wetland and groundwater interaction is not well understood.

Objectives
The research aims to investigate the potential of solar irrigation systems as a sustainable solution to mitigate water scarcity in the communities. It particularly focuses on enhancing climate resilience by utilizing solar-powered groundwater for household consumption and small-scale cash crop irrigation, as well as promoting sustainable, community-managed water resources. The study aims to address the following key questions:
(1) How can solar-powered groundwater improve quality of life for small-scale farmers?
(2) What measures can be taken to ensure proper abstraction, management, and monitoring of groundwater sources?
(3) What is the current state of hydrological connectivity between the wetland and surrounding groundwater systems?

The study employs a mixed methods approach. The majority of activities on the ground are as follows:
1. The construction of groundwater wells equipped with solar- powered pump systems and water tanks, developed through a collaborative process of vision-to-action involving community visioning consultations, co-design of infrastructure, and co-development.

The following text section comes from a specific evidence file named URL https://gender.cgiar.org/news/navigating-resilience-pathways-laos-integrating-gesi-agroecology-initiative: "menu close GENDER insights Navigating resilience pathways in Laos: integrating GESI in the Agroecology Initiative authored by Cathy Rozel Farnworth, Anne Rietveld on December 10, 2024 tagged with Institutions and norms Laos Social Inclusion Climate changes threaten to outpace people s adaptability and resilience. The CGIAR Initiative on Agroecology, working in Attapeu, Laos, explores how women and men are creating diverse pathways towards economic and ecological resilience, and is creating gender-transformative interventions for equitable benefits. Climate change is causing extreme weather events such as droughts and floods to occur more frequently in Laos. These shocks are profoundly impacting local livelihoods and ecosystems in harmful ways. Lakes, crucial for fishing, are drying up more and more often. Diets are less diverse because forests which were previously used to source wild foods are being cut down to make way for cassava plantations.* Subsistence livelihoods are no longer feasible. The need to adapt quickly is placing women and men under enormous pressure to plan their livelihoods and work together. Previously, women worked on the farm, and in household and care work. Men were considered the breadwinners and worked mostly as agricultural laborers, in construction, and other low-skill jobs in the nearby cities or further afield. Today, women and men farmers face challenges but also opportunities as they become integrated into the market economy. Women are setting up small, home-based shops selling essential everyday items, and both women and men seek work on private large-scale plantations. Nevertheless, the pace of change is so rapid that it is hard for people to keep up. The CGIAR Initiative on Agroecology in Laos, led by IWMI, is placing gender equality and social inclusion (GESI) at the center of its efforts to achieve resilience in the Attapeu province in southern Laos. The initiative is unpacking the ways in which women and men are creating diverse pathways towards achieving economic and ecological resilience, and using this knowledge to devise strategies that address gendered vulnerabilities to ensure equitable benefits from the interventions, particularly in relation to improving water management (see Box 1). Box 1. Examples of agroecological, climate-smart innovations that were co-designed and introduced in Attapeu new rice varieties (red rice) that are pest resistant and require low inputs solar-powered groundwater pumps for vegetables for more sustainable irrigation integrated wetland management through community-driven governance frameworks that address biodiversity loss and water scarcity soil improvement practices such as integrating legumes into cropping cycles, and assessing soil quality to reduce dependency on chemical inputs Capacity-building a first step towards integrating GESI in participatory research A starting point for integrating GESI effectively into the initiative was to strengthen the capacity of the team, most of whom have biophysical science backgrounds. The AE-I Laos team collaborated with two gender scientists from the global AE-I team to develop an interactive GESI training program of five days in the classroom and four days in the field. The classroom training created a safe space for the team to test a suite of three participatory tools and revise them to fit local conditions. Biophysicists on the team shared their technical knowledge on challenges facing local communities. The field days allowed the team to test their new skills in conducting gender-integrated participatory research, guided by the gender experts leading the training. Two months later, a national expert trained the team in the Gender Action Learning System (GALS) a gender-transformative methodology. This was followed by six days of training in four communities (including the two discussed here). IWMI Laos country lead Mark Dubois emphasized that the training and follow-up joint research has provided the team an opportunity to mainstream GESI across the entire IMWI Laos program, and make real progress towards achieving IMWI s strategic goal of facilitating effective and inclusive participation and addressing global inequalities. Guiding framework captures GESI dimensions of resilience Central to the AE-I Laos team s understanding of resilience is the Conceptual Framework on Economic Resilience Pathways. The framework highlights five key elements that shape women s and men s abilities to build resilience: Gender norms: Addressing restrictive gender norms to foster equitable decision-making and collaborative resilience-building both at household and community levels. Intersectionality: Supporting the development of inclusive approaches that address the specific needs of diverse community members. Life course stage: Individuals resilience pathways are shaped by their stage in life, with varying capacities and vulnerabilities across these stages. Personal traits: Characteristics such as adaptability, risk-behaviour, curiosity and willingness to innovate, influence how individuals respond to shocks and opportunities. Power and agency: The ability of people to act independently and to move towards desired outcomes in their lives. The framework identifies three primary pathways that individuals may take for resilience building: Absorptive pathways: These involve immediate coping mechanisms to withstand shocks. Adaptive pathways: Medium- to long-term adjustments that include diversifying livelihoods, adopting climate-smart agriculture, etc. Transformative pathways: Fundamental, systemic changes that address the root causes of vulnerability, such as redefining gender roles or improving the gender-responsiveness of governance. A critical recognition is that sometimes people fail to cope they are unable to adequately respond to shocks, leading to increased vulnerability. Two ethnic groups mapped gender norms and community changes The participatory research methodology was then designed using this framework as a basis, and consisted of four tools adapted to the local context. To conduct the research, two distinct communities living in two adjacent villages were brought together. The first village was mostly inhabited by the Oy ethnic group, and the second by the Lao Lum, the dominant ethnicity in Laos. We ensured the inclusion of marginalized groups, people living with disabilities (PLWD) and people from economically disadvantaged backgrounds who rarely participate in village events by using purposive sampling criteria. Overall, 24 people (12 women and 12 men) participated. The tools: Community River of Life: Participants mapped environmental, hydrological, economic and social changes over the past three decades at the community level, highlighting how these influenced gender roles and relations (mixed-gender groups). Individual Rivers of Life: Community members reflected on personal milestones, challenges, and moments of joy, providing gendered insights into resilience-building (single-gender groups). Gender Norms Analysis: Participants listed and ranked gender norms, and discussed their relevance and the ways in which they are changing (single-gender groups). Innovative Characteristics: Participants explored how gender norms influence the ability of women and men to innovate, and discussed the work of the AE-I (single-gender groups). These activities were complemented by key informant interviews (one per community) with representatives of the village committees (also represented in the Nong L m management committee), youth union representatives, and Lao Women s Union representatives. In addition, we met with the head of the shared health center, the head of the local bank, and heads of the primary and secondary school. These people represent cross-cutting institutions shared by the two villages. Further interviews were conducted with the provincial head of the Lao Women s Union and the Deputy of Department of Agriculture and Forestry (a woman). Gender roles, farming practices and income sources are changing Women and men in these two communities have distinct roles and responsibilities in agriculture (mostly paddy and vegetables, although people are increasingly growing cassava and, to some extent, sugar cane). Men typically undertake land preparation, while women manage most other tasks in the paddy fields and in their home gardens. However, these roles often intersect particularly during harvest, where collaborative efforts are common. Women and men both fish, although the nearby lake has dried up completely several times over the past 20 years. This has killed most aquatic vegetation, and reduced fish diversity and numbers. The water from these lakes is also used to irrigate paddy and vegetable plots. Previously, men hunted, but this livelihood has now died out due to deforestation. The evolving economic landscape is reshaping gender roles and responsibilities for both ethnic groups. While men are still viewed as primary breadwinners, women are increasingly expected to earn money through home-based enterprises. A few women (and in some cases children) temporarily leave their village to work on nearby plantations alongside their spouses. Women s participation in community meetings often exceeds that of men, partly due to the absence of many men who work outside the community. This is strengthening women s influence in local governance particularly in relation to health, where women dominate outreach. Institutions like the Lao Women s Union (LWU) and local banks have enacted national legislation on gender equality. For instance, joint spousal consent is required for loans, and inheritance laws ensure equitable asset distribution among children. This is particularly important among the Oy: a patrilineal community, where assets were previously preferentially passed to male children. The Lao Lum is traditionally matrilineal, where inheritance passes through the female line. These legal changes are helping to build women s asset base and to strengthen their voice in intrahousehold and community-level decision-making. These findings are informing interventions and collaborations through GALS in Attapeu. The team is also now cognisant of the more-sharply-differentiated gender relations in more remote communities than the two communities included here, and will refine interventions to address those. Transforming researcher mindsets is critical to scaling GESI integration Members from the AE-I Laos team expressed they learned a lot from their engagement in this study and are eager to take the efforts further. Ammala Chanthalath (IWMI) said, for instance, My involvement in this study was a very important experience that helped me learn how to conduct research in the future. It has taught me to consider the complex interplay of gender norms, power and agency, intersectionality, and life stages in understanding resilience. Somphasith Douangsavanh (IWMI) also testified to learning a lot from his involvement in the training and study. He particularly likes the tools from GALS, especially the Gender Balance Tree, which made him reflect on his personal life too. Before knowing this exercise, I had never written down how I spend time daily, and I did not fully understand what my wife does in detail. After completing the exercise, I realized who is doing most of the work at home. Somphasith s and Ammala s reflections show that working on gender equality and social inclusion is not only academic or professional, it also affects us, our ideas, our biases and truths. The AE-I Laos work on GESI has helped to build a consciousness among these biophysical scientists that gender is very important and must be considered in all projects. Background
Laos is a developing country that goes by the formal name of Lao People’s Democratic Republic. Laos’ economy is one of the fastest-growing in Southeast Asia, with a lower-middle income, a markedly rising urbanization and population density and falling rates of malnutrition (GHI 2019; World Bank 2022). Although agriculture is the main source of income, livelihood and nutritional security in Laos, rice has historically been the country’s most significant staple food grain grown (CIA 2023), and there have been significant increases in rice crop area and productivity (World Bank 2022). Since 2000, there has been a growing demand to become self-sufficient in low-cost animal protein, with aquatic species as the most potential food source (Chaparro et al. 2014). The production of these foods has also demonstrated year-over-year exponential growth (FAO 2022), indicating the importance of aquatic foods within the country. However, Laos’ aquatic food production is still relatively small, both in terms of local consumption and international trade volume (Vongvichith et al. 2018). To meet the demand, the Laotian government and a number of local, regional and international organizations have offered extension assistance. As a result, Laos generated 65 percent of its own aquatic foods in 2020 (FAO 2022).
Despite enormous potential, just 42,000 ha of the country’s land are set aside for freshwater aquaculture, while 1.236 million ha are used for capture fisheries (Hortle 2009; LAOPDR 2016). Current efforts have focused on creating sustainable and doable strategies for growing aquaculture within farming communities. Growing rice fields increases
the likelihood of rice field-based fisheries, which are a well- accepted indigenous method of obtaining aquatic food in Laos (Freed et al. 2020). However, rice–fish farming is still unpopular and has a low acceptance rate, even though it was introduced to Laos in 1937 and rice fields are one of the country’s most important fishing sites (LAOPDR 2016; FAO 2022; Thongsamouth 2021). Farmers are unable to make use of the advantages of rice–fish farming systems, which may be due to the lack of necessary information and assistance (Saikia and Das 2008) along with inadequate infrastructure (Li et al. 2023). However, because of ideal temperatures, sufficient water supply, and affordable labor and land, Laos offers great potential for developing rice–fish farming systems. In recent decades, several promotion and extension projects have been carried out by governmental, intergovernmental and nongovernmental organizations, including the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), WorldFish and the Japan International Research Center for Agricultural Sciences in recognition of the significance of developing rice–fish production systems in Laos.
The southern province of Attapeu is the focus of this report. However, the overall image of rice–fish production systems in the region is unknown because of the paucity of statistical data and pertinent literature, which makes it difficult for rice– fish production systems to contribute more in the future to a wide range of sustainable development goals. Therefore, attention has been given to grasp the potential and impact of three prototype experimental rice–fish farming systems in Attapeu’s Sanamxay District. It has led to the prediction of a possible agroecological transition route through integrated rice–fish farming in the region.

an integrated rice–fish farming system (IRFFS) (Figure 1), where culture-based and capture IRFFS coexisted. Although capture fisheries based on rice paddies previously existed in this region, FAO and the Department of Livestock and Fisheries (DLF) of Loas’ Ministry of Agriculture and Forestry have been the main promoters of IRFFS.

The surveyed region has two primary types of rice–fish farming operations: one for rearing fingerlings and the other for table fish production.
IRFFS for rearing fingerlings
This model is practiced in the villages of Oudamxuy and Donephay, where farmers usually stock fingerlings (5–7 cm) of silverbarb, tilapia and common carp within paddy fields. It involves only minor changes with the least amount of human labor. Farmers dig trenches as fish refuges along one or both of the adjacent sides of the paddy fields. When working with the native rice variety (Oryza sativa), the stocking density for fingerlings is typically maintained at three per square meter. The paddy fields are prepared with buffalo manure prior to transplanting. During the first 10 to 15 days after stocking, any synthetic chemical treatment is avoided. In the paddy fields, sufficient water availability is maintained for 4 or 5 months because of small irrigation systems, allowing fish to grow up to the advanced fingerling stage (20–25 cm size). IRFFS for producing table fish
In this type of IRFFS, advanced or regular fingerlings are stocked in small or medium-sized impounded waterbodies within paddy fields for the purpose of producing table fish (Plate 1). These waterbodies are approximately 4 feet deep and are connected to the paddy fields through various ditches. Similar to earlier techniques, fingerlings are reared in this
system by keeping the water at a minimum of 3 feet. Prior to paddy harvesting, water was contained in impoundments, and ditches served as a passageway for the fish to the refuge; here, fish are cultivated for 8 to 10 months before reaching table size. Alternatively, advanced fingerlings are sometimes raised exclusively in impoundments to grow into table fish. As previously mentioned, there are similarities in land preparation and a greater frequency of using commercial feed to raise fish.

Nutrition and livelihoods
The main crops in this area are steamed rice (mallie) and sticky rice (tandoum, taseno, pongum) with an annual productivity of 2 t/ha and 3 t/ha, respectively. Cassava, various vegetables, and livestock are their other agricultural resources. Households consume the majority of agricultural harvests, with any surplus
sold at the local market. There is heavy reliance on one’s own labor and readily available biodegradable resources, and costs are low for mechanical support and buying seeds. When it comes to IRFFS, fish are continuously and partially harvested from paddy fields for 1 or 2 months in order to be stored for domestic use. However, production trends for table fish are primarily concerned with grabbing the interest of the local market, even though the primary uses of capture fisheries are food security and household nutrition. The market price for rice fluctuates year-to-year, ranging from LAK 3500 to 6300/kg, although the price of fish is relatively stable throughout the year.

This study discovered that systems for producing rice and fish, such as IRFFS and rice field fisheries, continue to have prospects and challenges. Some of the most important characteristics that have the potential to support IRFFS in this area include the availability of enough family labor, the type

The Effect of Different Harvesting Frequencies on the Performance of Food-feed oat Varieties under Rainfed Conditions
Kindu Mekonnen, Melkamu Bezabih, Aberra Adie, Temesgen Alene, Fikadu Tessema, Million Gebreyes, Haimanot Seifu and Anthony Whitbread
Background
The demand for livestock feed and human food is increasing over time. Research on dual-purpose crops can be one of the options to address both feed and food shortages. Oats is a crop with significant potential to serve as a source of both feed and food. Forage oats, in particular, has a short growth cycle (less than 90 days), making it ideal for producing fodder while freeing the land for other crop cultivation in areas where arable land is limited. It can be used as green fodder or hay. Oats forage is rich in protein (10-13%) and energy (8-9 MJ ME/kg DM). Consequently, it is one of the technologies validated and widely promoted by the Africa Research in Sustainable Intensification for the Next Generation
(Africa RISING) Ethiopian Highlands Project.

Figure 1. Multi-cut oat trial plots in Lemo district (Photo credit: ILRI/Workneh Dubale)
The forage has the potential for regrowth and can be harvested multiple times under favorable conditions. When used for dual- purpose functions, the crop can be harvested at the vegetative stage and then left to regrow and mature for grain production. It was hypothesized that multi-harvest options could provide farmers with a flexible way to access green fodder over an extended period, thereby alleviating feed shortages during the crop planting seasons. Consequently, an investigation was conducted to evaluate the performance of forage and food oat varieties under different cutting treatments. The aim was to

CGIAR INITIATIVE OF MIXED FARMING SYSTEMS
recommend cutting frequency regimes that would optimize the use of this crop for both livestock feed and human food.
Approach
The trials were a continuation of the Africa RISING project work in the Ethiopian highlands and were conducted at two operational sites of the One CGIAR Mixed Farming Systems Initiative in Ethiopia. The research was carried out through participatory on-farm trials, involving three nationally registered oat varieties: a forage variety called Bate, and two food varieties named Sorataf and Hulegeb. These varieties were subjected to different cutting treatments after establishment during the main rainy season. For the trials, experimental plots were established with each oat variety planted in a 2×3 m² plot, replicated three times following a randomized block design. The cutting regimes applied were:1) Cutting at the vegetative stage and again at the hay stage; 2) Cutting at the vegetative stage and after grain maturity, 3) Cutting once, either at the hay stage or after grain maturity. Fodder biomass and grain yields were measured, and the nutritional composition of fodder samples
was analyzed in the laboratory.
Main findings
A trade-off was observed between fodder and grain yield components when the oat varieties were subjected to different cutting treatments (Table 1). Generally, both grain and fodder yields, along with overall economic benefits, were higher when the crops were cut only once, either at the hay stage or after grain maturity. For instance, there was a 78% reduction in forage yield when the Bate variety was subjected to cutting at both the vegetative and hay stages compared to a one-time cut at the hay stage (Table 1).
This suggests that oats regrowth during the main rainy season was not vigorous, which contrasts with earlier observations under irrigation. Under irrigation, forage oats showed vigorous regrowth after vegetative stage cutting, resulting in yield advantages over a single cut (Mekonnen et al., 2022; Bezabih et al., 2022). Optimal light intensity and soil moisture are critical factors for stimulating oats regrowth. However, during the main rainy season, low light intensity and excessive rainfall appear to inhibit regrowth
after the first cut.

Cutting frequency
As expected, high-quality forage per unit of dry matter was obtained when oats forage was harvested at the vegetative stage, followed by the hay stage (Table 2). However, in terms of yield per hectare, higher energy and nutrient levels were achieved under the one-time cutting regime (Figure 2). This suggests that the decline in forage quality was offset by the significantly higher biomass yield.
A key constraint observed with the twice- cutting management of food oats was delayed crop maturity, which occurred after other crops had been harvested and removed. This exposed the crops to bird attacks in most cases and browsing in some
areas. To address this issue, adjustments to planting times are necessary so that crop maturity aligns with other crops, maximizing the food-feed benefits in a twice-cutting regime.
Conclusion and recommendation
The performance of the oat varieties was significantly influenced by the cutting management. The results showed that during the rainy season, oats regrowth after the first cut was weak, suggesting that farmers might experience substantial yield reductions with a twice-cutting regime, even though they could obtain forage for their animals more quickly than with a single harvest at the hay
stage or full maturity.
CGIAR INITIATIVE OF MIXED FARMING SYSTEMS   
Therefore, a one-time cutting regime is recommended when growing oats under rainfed conditions during the main rainy season. However, under irrigation, multiple cutting regimes can provide better yield advantages, as vigorous regrowth after the first harvest has been observed during the dry period. When practicing a twice-cutting regime, it is essential to closely monitor vegetative growth and time the first cut to occur just before stem elongation for
optimal results.

It can be used as green fodder or hay. Oats forage is rich in protein (10-13%) and energy (8-9 MJ ME/kg DM). Consequently, it is one of the technologies validated and widely promoted by the Africa Research in Sustainable Intensification for the Next Generation
(Africa RISING) Ethiopian Highlands Project.

The forage has the potential for regrowth and can be harvested multiple times under favorable conditions. When used for dual- purpose functions, the crop can be harvested at the vegetative stage and then left to regrow and mature for grain production. It was hypothesized that multi-harvest options could provide farmers with a flexible way to access green fodder over an extended period, thereby alleviating feed shortages during the crop planting seasons. Consequently, an investigation was conducted to evaluate the performance of forage and food oat varieties under different cutting treatments. The aim was to

recommend cutting frequency regimes that would optimize the use of this crop for both livestock feed and human food.
Approach
The trials were a continuation of the Africa RISING project work in the Ethiopian highlands and were conducted at two operational sites of the One CGIAR Mixed Farming Systems Initiative in Ethiopia. The research was carried out through participatory on-farm trials, involving three nationally registered oat varieties: a forage variety called Bate, and two food varieties named Sorataf and Hulegeb. These varieties were subjected to different cutting treatments after establishment during the main rainy season. For the trials, experimental plots were established with each oat variety planted in a 2×3 m² plot, replicated three times following a randomized block design. The cutting regimes applied were:1) Cutting at the vegetative stage and again at the hay stage; 2) Cutting at the vegetative stage and after grain maturity, 3) Cutting once, either at the hay stage or after grain maturity. Fodder biomass and grain yields were measured, and the nutritional composition of fodder samples
was analyzed in the laboratory.
Main findings
A trade-off was observed between fodder and grain yield components when the oat varieties were subjected to different cutting treatments (Table 1). Generally, both grain and fodder yields, along with overall economic benefits, were higher when the crops were cut only once, either at the hay stage or after grain maturity. For instance, there was a 78% reduction in forage yield when the Bate variety was subjected to cutting at both the vegetative and hay stages compared to a one-time cut at the hay stage (Table 1).
This suggests that oats regrowth during the main rainy season was not vigorous, which contrasts with earlier observations under irrigation. Under irrigation, forage oats showed vigorous regrowth after vegetative stage cutting, resulting in yield advantages over a single cut (Mekonnen et al., 2022; Bezabih et al., 2022). Optimal light intensity and soil moisture are critical factors for stimulating oats regrowth. However, during the main rainy season, low light intensity and excessive rainfall appear to inhibit regrowth
after the first cut.

Cutting frequency
As expected, high-quality forage per unit of dry matter was obtained when oats forage was harvested at the vegetative stage, followed by the hay stage (Table 2). However, in terms of yield per hectare, higher energy and nutrient levels were achieved under the one-time cutting regime (Figure 2). This suggests that the decline in forage quality was offset by the significantly higher biomass yield.
A key constraint observed with the twice- cutting management of food oats was delayed crop maturity, which occurred after other crops had been harvested and removed. This exposed the crops to bird attacks in most cases and browsing in some
areas. To address this issue, adjustments to planting times are necessary so that crop maturity aligns with other crops, maximizing the food-feed benefits in a twice-cutting regime.
Conclusion and recommendation
The performance of the oat varieties was significantly influenced by the cutting management. The results showed that during the rainy season, oats regrowth after the first cut was weak, suggesting that farmers might experience substantial yield reductions with a twice-cutting regime, even though they could obtain forage for their animals more quickly than with a single harvest at the hay
stage or full maturity.

Therefore, a one-time cutting regime is recommended when growing oats under rainfed conditions during the main rainy season. However, under irrigation, multiple cutting regimes can provide better yield advantages, as vigorous regrowth after the first harvest has been observed during the dry period. When practicing a twice-cutting regime, it is essential to closely monitor vegetative growth and time the first cut to occur just before stem elongation for
optimal results.

1. About RTB EAGEL
The RTB East Africa Germplasm Exchange Laboratory (RTB EAGEL) in Kenya is aimed at supporting the exchange, conservation, and distribution of high-quality plant materials, or germplasm, for key root, tuber, and banana (RTB) crops. Located at Kenya Plant Health Inspectorate Service (KEPHIS), Plant Quarantine and Biosafety Station (PQBS) in Muguga, Kenya, this lab is set to play a crucial role in addressing agricultural challenges in East Africa, particularly for crops such as Cassava, Yam, Sweetpotatoes, Potato and Banana, which are essential for food security and livelihoods in the region. The lab will focus on ensuring the health and quality of plant germplasm, using advanced biotechnological methods such as disease indexing, pathogen detection, and cleaning to eliminate viral and bacterial infections from plant materials.
By offering clean, disease-free planting materials, the lab will help improve crop resilience, yields, and sustainability for smallholder farmers. Additionally, the RTB EAGEL will facilitate the exchange of germplasm between different regions and countries, contributing to biodiversity conservation and accelerating the development of improved crop varieties. The lab will also be instrumental in training and capacity building, equipping local scientists, researchers, and farmers with skills in germplasm management and crop improvement techniques. Overall, the RTB East Africa Germplasm Exchange Laboratory is poised to be a critical hub for crop improvement and sustainable agricultural development in the region, promoting food security and enhancing the livelihoods of millions of farmers in East Africa.

3. Operations 3.1 Workflows & Stages
The workflow at RTB EAGEL is designed to ensure the high quality and health of planting materials for root, tuber, and banana (RTB) crops, including Sweetpotato, Potato, Banana, Cassava, and Yam. It starts with the reception of samples, which are entered into a database for tracking. These samples are then placed in a quarantine glasshouse to prevent contamination. After initial quarantine, they are moved to a post-entry quarantine growth room for further observation and acclimatization. Once the plantlets have passed these preliminary stages, they undergo virus indexing using methods such as grafting and Elisa tests to identify and eliminate any viral infections. Upon receiving a health certificate confirming their disease-free status, the plantlets proceed to tissue culture processes. This includes surface sterilization, thermotherapy, and meristem tip culture to further ensure pathogen-free materials.
The plantlets are then hardened in glasshouses to adapt to external conditions and subsequently moved to growth rooms for multiplication and sub-culturing. This is followed by additional hardening in either glasshouses or screenhouses, depending on the crop's specific needs. Healthy plantlets are then distributed to stakeholders and conserved in vitro in growth rooms to maintain genetic diversity. Finally, some plantlets are conserved in vivo in
screenhouses to ensure long-term adaptation and preservation. This structured approach ensures that RTB EAGEL delivers high-quality, disease-free planting materials to support sustainable agriculture and food security in the region. The workflow and stages differ slightly from crop to crop and the same are reflected in the individual workflows (along with stages) attached in annexure.

The seed sector is critical to agricultural productivity, yet entrepreneurs in this space face significant challenges, including limited financial management skills, operational inefficiencies, financial constraints, and lack of market reach. These issues are compounded by the reliance on ad-hoc, manual processes for decision-making. To address these challenges, this report introduces the Business Investment Decision (BID) tool, a comprehensive digital platform designed to empower seed-sector entrepreneurs and businesses. The BID tool offers structured formats for financial planning, investment analysis, and business growth, enabling users to make informed decisions. Currently available in Excel and web-based formats, with plans for a desktop version, the tool includes modules for business background, business environment, financial management, budgeting, valuation, risk management, and more. Its target users include small and medium enterprises (SMEs) in the seed sector, as well as businesses in other industries at various stages of development. The tool has been validated through applications in diverse settings, including RTB EAGEL in Nairobi and Potato ARC Technology in India. Introduction
The seed sector plays a critical role in shaping the agricultural economy, influencing crop productivity and food security. However, despite its significance, entrepreneurs in this sector face numerous challenges that limit their potential for growth and efficiency. These challenges, deeply rooted in the operational and financial management practices of seed businesses, underscore the need for targeted interventions and innovative solutions (Manjunatha et al., 2013). One of the most pressing issues is the lack of financial management skills among seed entrepreneurs. Many are unable to maintain structured financial records or effectively manage cash flows, leading to inefficiencies and resource misallocation. This gap is compounded by the financial constraints these businesses often face, including limited access to credit and other financial resources, which further hinders scalability and innovation (Kumar & Ali, 2010). Another challenge is the existence of operational inefficiencies, as entrepreneurs often rely on outdated or manual processes that increase costs and reduce productivity. Limited market reach remains another critical challenge; seed businesses frequently struggle to expand their customer base due to inadequate marketing strategies and tools. Furthermore, the sector remains largely unorganized, with minimal use of structured decision- making frameworks or digital tools to streamline operations and finances (MacRobert, 2009).
Only a small fraction of seed-sector enterprises currently utilizes organized frameworks or tools, while the majority depend on manual, inconsistent, or ad-hoc approaches that lack scalability and adaptability. These challenges collectively inhibit the sector’s ability to align with modern agribusiness practices, resulting in missed opportunities for growth and competitiveness (ter Steeg & Louwaars, 2024). Addressing these issues requires the introduction of innovative tools that can empower entrepreneurs with data-driven insights, streamlined processes, and scalable frameworks. The Business Investment Decision (BID) tool emerges as a promising solution to bridge these gaps, offering a structured approach to decision-making that can revolutionize how seed-sector businesses operate and thrive.

The solution: BID tool
Introduction to the BID tool
The Business Investment Decision (BID) tool is a comprehensive digital platform designed to address the operational and financial challenges faced by entrepreneurs. By introducing structured decision-making frameworks, the BID tool provides businesses with a systematic approach to managing operations, analyzing investments, and planning for growth. Currently available in both macro-enabled Excel and web-based formats, the BID tool offers flexibility and accessibility to meet the diverse needs of users. Plans are underway to launch a standalone desktop application, ensuring broader reach and enhanced usability. This iterative development approach reflects the BID tool's commitment to evolving alongside the needs of its users, making it a versatile solution for the dynamic needs.
Objective of the BID tool
The primary objective of the BID tool is to empower seed-sector enterprises by equipping them with structured decision-making frameworks. The following frameworks are designed to enable:

Financial Planning: Helping businesses maintain organized financial records, project cash flows, and optimize resource allocation.

Investment Analysis: Offering insights to evaluate and prioritize investment opportunities, ensuring sustainable business growth.
• Business Growth: Supporting scalability through adaptable frameworks that align with modern business practices.
By addressing the critical challenges faced by entrepreneurs, the BID tool aims to transform the seed sector into an organized and data-driven ecosystem.
Modules of the BID tool
The BID tool is built around a modular architecture, with each module addressing a specific aspect of business management. Together, these modules offer a holistic framework to evaluate, plan, and execute business decisions effectively. Following are the modules of the BID tool -
• Business Background: This module captures the enterprise's foundational details, including its mission, vision, and core objectives. It helps businesses document their history, market presence, and strategic direction.
• Business Environment: Analyzing external factors such as market trends, competitive landscape, and regulatory frameworks, this module enables businesses to understand their operating environment and identify opportunities and threats. This mainly contains SWOT and PESTEL analyses.
• Business Model: This module evaluates the enterprise’s value proposition, revenue streams, and customer segments. It provides insights into the business's operational structure and areas for innovation. This mainly contains value proposition canvas and business model canvas (BMC).
• Operations: Focused on streamlining workflows, this module addresses production processes, supply chain management, and resource allocation. It aims to enhance operational efficiency and reduce costs.

Financial Management: This critical module includes functionalities for:

• Costing and Financial Statements: Allowing businesses to prepare, analyze, and manage their financial records.
• Ratio Analysis: Offering tools to assess liquidity, profitability, and solvency, providing a comprehensive view of financial health.
• Budgeting: This module enables businesses to forecast expenses, track performance and compare variances against financial goals.
• Valuation: Helping enterprises determine their valuation based on asset based, market based and profits- based metrics. This module supports investment decisions, mergers, and funding opportunities.
• Partnership: Designed to evaluate and manage collaborations, this module assesses the potential risks and rewards of partnerships and alliances.
• Risk Management: Identifying and mitigating potential business risks, this module equips businesses with strategies to navigate uncertainties and enhance resilience.
How the BID Tool Works
The Business Investment Decisions (BID) tool is an innovative solution designed to optimize decision-making processes in the seed sector. It integrates technology, analytics, and user-centric design to enhance operational efficiency and support strategic business planning. The tool operates through the following key features:
a) Interactive Dashboards - The BID tool includes visually engaging dashboards that present real-time data in an easily interpretable format. These dashboards allow users to track key metrics, monitor business performance, and visualize trends. Decision-makers can quickly identify areas that require attention and make informed decisions based on comprehensive insights.
b) User-Friendly Interface - A core strength of the BID tool is its intuitive design, ensuring accessibility for users with varying levels of technical expertise. The interface prioritizes simplicity, enabling users to navigate seamlessly, input data effortlessly, and retrieve actionable insights without extensive training.
c) Automated Analytics - The BID tool harnesses advanced algorithms to automate data analysis. It processes complex datasets to generate actionable insights, predict market trends, and assess the impact of various business scenarios. This automation reduces manual effort and ensures accurate, timely outputs, empowering users to focus on strategic decision-making.
d) Customizable Tool - Flexibility is a cornerstone of the BID tool. Users can tailor the tool to their specific needs by customizing parameters, dashboards, and outputs. This adaptability ensures relevance across different contexts and scales of operations, making it suitable for diverse business environments in the seed sector.
Objectives of the BID Tool
The BID tool aims to address critical challenges in the seed sector while fostering alignment with modern agribusiness practices. Its objectives include:
a) Streamlining Operations - By automating routine tasks and digitizing workflows, the BID tool enhances operational efficiency. It minimizes time-consuming manual processes and optimizes resource utilization, allowing organizations to focus on their core activities.

b) Data-Driven Decision-Making - With built-in analytics capabilities, the BID tool provides insights derived from data. Users can leverage these insights to make informed decisions, improve forecasting accuracy, and align strategies with market demands.
c) Scalability - The BID tool is designed to grow with the business. Its flexible frameworks and customizable features support scalability, enabling businesses to expand operations while maintaining efficiency and adaptability.
d) Bridging the Gap - The BID tool aligns traditional practices in the seed sector with contemporary agribusiness methodologies. By integrating modern tools and analytics, it fosters a culture of innovation and ensures the sector remains competitive in a rapidly evolving industry landscape.
Methodology
The development of the Business Investment Decisions (BID) tool followed a structured and collaborative methodology to ensure its relevance, usability, and effectiveness. The process emphasized innovation, inclusivity, and stakeholder engagement through the following steps:
Design Thinking Approach
The BID tool was conceptualized using the Design Thinking framework, focusing on understanding user needs, ideating creative solutions, and iterating prototypes. This approach enabled the creation of a tool that is both practical and user-centric, addressing real-world challenges faced by stakeholders in the seed sector.
Key stages included -
• Empathy Building: Understanding the pain points and needs of stakeholders.
• Defining Objectives: Clearly outline what the tool should achieve.
Ideation: Brainstorming solutions to address identified challenges.

Prototyping: Creating early models of the tool to test features.
Testing and Iteration: Refining the tool based on user feedback.

Consulted Experts Across Stakeholder Groups
To ensure the BID tool is robust and caters to the diverse needs of the seed sector, the development team engaged with a wide range of experts, including:
• Seed Sector Entrepreneurs: Provided insights on business challenges, market dynamics, and operational requirements.
• Germplasm Laboratory Staff: Contributed technical expertise on seed quality, research processes, and compliance standards.
• Agriculture Economists: Helped integrate economic modeling and cost-benefit analyses into the tool.
• Agribusiness Experts: Shared knowledge on supply chains, marketing strategies, and sectoral trends.

Conducted Interviews and Focus Group Discussions (FGDs)
Extensive interviews and FGDs were conducted with key stakeholders to gather qualitative data on their specific challenges, expectations, and requirements. This iterative engagement allowed the team to identify common pain points across the seed value chain, understand sectoral nuances and local market dynamics and most importantly validate the relevance of proposed features.
Conducted Workshops to Brainstorm Tool Features
Workshops were organized to bring together stakeholders, domain experts, and technical teams. These sessions served as platforms for collective brainstorming on the tool's features and functionality. The objective of these workshops was to refine the tool's design and ensure it addressed both strategic and operational needs. The outcome obtained was that we were able to generate actionable ideas that were incorporated into the tool, such as interactive dashboards, easy to use formats, automated analytics, and customization options.
Target Users and Validation
Target Users
The BID tool is designed to cater to a diverse range of users, ensuring that its applicability extends beyond the seed sector to other domains of agriculture and even non-agricultural businesses. Its modular structure and flexible functionalities make it a valuable resource for the following target groups:

Seed Sector Businesses and Entrepreneurs: The primary target audience includes businesses and entrepreneurs in the seed sector. While initially designed to address challenges in this specific industry, the BID tool's frameworks and modules can be easily adapted to other crop-related enterprises.

Small and Medium Businesses (SMEs): The tool is tailored to meet the needs of small and medium-sized enterprises, which often lack access to structured decision-making frameworks and digital financial tools.
• Entrepreneurs at Various Stages of Business Development: The BID tool is equally effective for entrepreneurs with early-stage ideas as well as those with mature businesses. It provides structured guidance for startups while offering advanced analytics and planning capabilities for established ventures.
• Universal Business Applicability: Although designed with the agricultural sector in mind, the BID tool is versatile enough to be applied across industries. Its modules address universal business concerns such as financial management, operational efficiency, and risk mitigation, making it relevant for businesses of any type or size.
Validation of the BID Tool
The BID tool has been validated in diverse real-world settings to ensure its effectiveness and adaptability:
• RTB EAGEL – Nairobi, Kenya: The tool was applied to Root, Tuber, and Banana-based agribusinesses in Nairobi. It demonstrated its capacity to structure decision-making and streamline financial planning in an environment with resource constraints. The diverse and complex nature of RTB EAGEL’s operations helped us develop multiple functionalities in the tool and bring out the diverse functionalities to the forefront.

Potato Apical rooted cuttings (ARC) Technology – CIP, India: In India, the BID tool was validated through its application to the Potato ARC technology, a project spearheaded by the International Potato Center (CIP). This

Potential Benefits and Impact
The BID tool offers several advantages that can significantly enhance the business outcomes of its users. Firstly, BID aids in instant business plan creation. The tool provides an easy-to-learn interface, enabling users to create a comprehensive business plan quickly. This feature is especially beneficial for entrepreneurs who may not have formal business training. It also aids in the ease of use for beginners and amateurs. It has been designed with accessibility in mind, the BID tool simplifies complex processes, making it ideal for users with little to no experience in financial management or strategic planning. The users can thereby focus on business development, by automating and streamlining accounting and financial management tasks, the BID tool allows users to concentrate on growing their business rather than being bogged down by technical details. BID tool also significantly improves fundraising potential. The structured financial projections and analysis provided by the BID tool can be used to secure both equity and debt financing. Its outputs are designed to meet the requirements of investors and financial institutions, enhancing the likelihood of successful fundraising. The entrepreneurs can easily develop business prospects analysis. The tool enables users to evaluate the viability of their business over a five-year horizon, incorporating various financial, operational, and market factors into its projections. Most importantly, the tool allows for parameter flexibility. Users can easily modify assumptions and parameters to explore different scenarios and outcomes. This feature makes the BID tool particularly useful for scenario planning and sensitivity analysis.
Future Research and Development
The future of the BID tool is centered on continuous improvement and expansion to meet the evolving needs of entrepreneurs across industries. The next stages of development will focus on enhancing the tool’s functionalities, expanding its scope, and leveraging emerging technologies to further strengthen its utility. The key areas of focus for future research and development include the following -
Finalization and Expansion of the Web Version
One of the primary objectives soon is to complete and finalize the web version of the BID tool. This version will offer users a more accessible platform that can be used across different devices and operating systems. The web- based format allows for seamless updates, real-time collaboration, and easier access to users in remote or underserved regions. Future research will focus on optimizing the web version for performance, user experience, and scalability, ensuring it can cater to many users without compromising functionality.
6.1 Development of a Desktop Version
In addition to the web version, the development of a desktop application will be prioritized. This version will offer enhanced security features, offline accessibility, and greater computational power for businesses requiring more intensive data processing. It will be designed for businesses that prefer a locally stored solution, as well as those in regions with limited internet connectivity. Future research will involve exploring compatibility with different operating systems, user preferences, and providing a more robust offline experience.

Addition of Inferences and Advisory Modules
The BID tool’s functionality will be extended with the addition of inference and advisory modules. These modules will offer personalized business insights based on the data entered into the system, providing actionable recommendations and forecasts. The advisory features will guide entrepreneurs through complex business decisions, offering real-time analysis of key metrics and strategic choices. Future research will explore algorithms and data analysis methods that can generate insightful recommendations tailored to individual business scenarios.
Integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI)
Artificial Intelligence (AI) will play a pivotal role in the next phase of BID tool development. AI integration will enable the following advancements:

Industry Comparisons: AI-powered algorithms will allow users to compare their business metrics with industry benchmarks, providing context and competitive insights that can inform strategic decisions.
• Elaboration of Business Strategy Responses: AI will help refine business strategies by analyzing historical data, market trends, and current conditions. This will allow the tool to suggest business strategies, optimize decision- making, and provide simulations of different scenarios based on real-time inputs.
Future research will focus on the development of machine learning models and AI systems capable of enhancing these features, ensuring that users receive the most relevant, up-to-date information to drive their decisions.
Real-Time, Live Data Integration
One of the most promising directions for future development is the integration of real-time, live data into the BID tool. This feature will allow users to access up-to-date information on market trends, commodity prices, financial data, and other key factors that influence business decisions. Real-time data feeds will enhance the tool’s ability to provide accurate forecasts, ensuring that entrepreneurs can make decisions based on the latest available information. Future research will involve partnering with data providers and building infrastructure to handle and process large datasets in real time.
Integration with Bookkeeping and Accounting Records
Another area of focus for future research is the integration of the BID tool with existing bookkeeping and accounting software. By connecting the tool to popular accounting platforms, such as QuickBooks or Xero, businesses can automate the flow of financial data directly into the BID tool, eliminating the need for manual data entry and improving accuracy. This integration will also enable the tool to provide deeper financial insights, such as cash flow projections, balance sheets, and income statements, based on live business data. Research will explore the technical requirements for seamless integration and the user interface necessary to make this feature intuitive and user-friendly.

Conclusion
The BID tool represents a significant advancement in addressing the operational and financial challenges faced by seed-sector entrepreneurs and small businesses, in general. By providing a structured, user-friendly platform, the tool empowers businesses to overcome inefficiencies, financial constraints, and limited market reach. Its modular design, encompassing critical aspects like financial management, operations, risk analysis, and valuation, equips users with comprehensive decision-making capabilities. The BID tool has proven its utility through real-world validation in projects like RTB EAGEL in Nairobi and Potato ARC Technology in India. These applications demonstrate its versatility across different contexts and its potential to transform business practices, not only in the seed sector but also in other industries. Key benefits include its ability to simplify business planning, ease of use for beginners, adaptability to changing parameters, and utility in fundraising and long-term strategy formulation.
Looking forward, the tool’s development roadmap is poised to enhance its impact further. The finalization of the web version, introduction of a desktop application, and the integration of AI and real-time data will expand its functionality, making it more robust and versatile. Features like live data feeding, industry comparisons, and seamless integration with accounting systems will provide entrepreneurs with powerful insights, fostering data- driven decision-making and long-term sustainability. The BID tool is therefore a critical innovation that bridges the gap between traditional, ad-hoc business management practices and the demands of modern, competitive markets. It serves as a catalyst for operational excellence and financial growth, ensuring that entrepreneurs in the seed sector and beyond are equipped to succeed in an increasingly complex business environment. By continuously evolving to meet user needs, the BID tool promises to play a pivotal role in driving the next generation of agribusiness and small enterprise success.

INTRODUCTION
Business Investment Decision (BID) Tools are designed to provide a comprehensive, modular digital platform for business enterprises in order to empower them with structured decision-making frameworks for financial planning, investment analysis, and business growth. These tools were developed through the Seed Equal Initiatives Project of the CGIAR.
The tool enables business enterprise operators to be able to develop an operational business plan inclusive of your business details, business environments (SWOT & PESTEL Analysis), Business Models (Value Proposition Canvas, Value Maps & Business Model Canvas), Operations (Product workflows), financial management (variable costs & fixed costs), sales projections, Partnership Development and Business Risk Management.
Business details fed into the system is used to generate the full business plan and financial reports as seen in the user guide.
The BID tools comes in two versions;
1. Web version; accessible through http://bidtool.cipotato.org or https://mt.co.ug/bid_tools_bplan
2. Excel Version which is downloadable through the same web links above
The BID Tool is divided into ten important modules;

MODULE 2: Business environment
The Business Environment module covers SWOT Analysis and PESTEL Analysis.
2.1. SWOT ANALYSIS
SWOT analysis is a framework to help you in identifying and analysing your business's strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats. S- Strengths Internal factors that gives the business a competitive advantage i.e. factors within your control W- Weaknesses Internal factors that places the business at a disadvantage i.e. which are within your control O- Opportunities External factors that the business could capitalize on i.e. which are not under your control T- Threats External factors that the business could capitalize on i.e. which are not under your control
2.2. PESTEL ANALYSIS
PESTEL analysis is a tool that will enable you to analyse and monitor the macro- environmental (external marketing environment) factors that have an impact on your factors in the external environment. P- Political What political factors affect the business? Consider government policies, regulations, trade tariffs, and political stability E- Economic What economic factors impact the business? Consider economic growth, exchange rates, inflation, and employment rates S- Social What social factors influence the business? Consider demographics, cultural trends, lifestyle changes, and consumer behaviours T- Technological What technological factors affect the business? Consider technological advancements, innovation, automation, and R&D activity E- Environmental What environmental factors impact the business? Consider climate change, environmental regulations, sustainability, and resource availability L- Legal What legal factors influence the business? 1. About RTB EAGEL
The RTB East Africa Germplasm Exchange Laboratory (RTB EAGEL) in Kenya is aimed at supporting the exchange, conservation, and distribution of high-quality plant materials, or germplasm, for key root, tuber, and banana (RTB) crops. Located at Kenya Plant Health Inspectorate Service (KEPHIS), Plant Quarantine and Biosafety Station (PQBS) in Muguga, Kenya, this lab is set to play a crucial role in addressing agricultural challenges in East Africa, particularly for crops such as Cassava, Yam, Sweetpotatoes, Potato and Banana, which are essential for food security and livelihoods in the region. The lab will focus on ensuring the health and quality of plant germplasm, using advanced biotechnological methods such as disease indexing, pathogen detection, and cleaning to eliminate viral and bacterial infections from plant materials.
By offering clean, disease-free planting materials, the lab will help improve crop resilience, yields, and sustainability for smallholder farmers. Additionally, the RTB EAGEL will facilitate the exchange of germplasm between different regions and countries, contributing to biodiversity conservation and accelerating the development of improved crop varieties. The lab will also be instrumental in training and capacity building, equipping local scientists, researchers, and farmers with skills in germplasm management and crop improvement techniques. Overall, the RTB East Africa Germplasm Exchange Laboratory is poised to be a critical hub for crop improvement and sustainable agricultural development in the region, promoting food security and enhancing the livelihoods of millions of farmers in East Africa.

2.3 SWOT analysis
The SWOT analysis for RTB EAGEL highlights several key internal strengths and weaknesses as well as external opportunities and threats that influence the organization's operational and strategic position. Notable strengths include a skilled workforce and specialized infrastructure like a tissue culture lab and diagnostic facilities, which support effective virus cleanup and pathogen indexing. The organization stands out as a one-stop service provider, offering both regulatory and scientific services, and benefits from established collaborations with stakeholders such as farmers, processors, research institutions, and funding bodies. RTB EAGEL’s credibility is bolstered by ISO certification and its role as the COMESA reference lab for plant health and SPS (Sanitary and Phytosanitary Standards), making it a unique entity in pathogen cleanup, particularly for crops like banana and yam.
On the other hand, some internal weaknesses pose challenges. The organization’s isolated location impacts accessibility and traceability, while unreliable power, poor water quality, and an inefficient financial management process hinder operational efficiency. Furthermore, the absence of a dedicated business management team and a slow procurement process could affect the organization's agility and responsiveness.
Externally, RTB EAGEL can capitalize on favorable opportunities such as an exclusive regulatory act for Vegetatively Propagated Crops (VPC) enacted in 2024 and rising consumer interest in indigenous crops like roots, tubers, and bananas. Its visibility is enhanced through affiliations with regional bodies, potentially strengthening its network. However, threats like insufficient initial funding, gaps between funding and project timelines, and the risk of funding cessation before achieving financial sustainability present serious obstacles. Addressing these financial uncertainties will be critical to ensuring RTB EAGEL’s long-term success and impact.

3. Operations 3.1 Workflows & Stages
The workflow at RTB EAGEL is designed to ensure the high quality and health of planting materials for root, tuber, and banana (RTB) crops, including Sweetpotato, Potato, Banana, Cassava, and Yam. It starts with the reception of samples, which are entered into a database for tracking. These samples are then placed in a quarantine glasshouse to prevent contamination. After initial quarantine, they are moved to a post-entry quarantine growth room for further observation and acclimatization. Once the plantlets have passed these preliminary stages, they undergo virus indexing using methods such as grafting and Elisa tests to identify and eliminate any viral infections. Upon receiving a health certificate confirming their disease-free status, the plantlets proceed to tissue culture processes. This includes surface sterilization, thermotherapy, and meristem tip culture to further ensure pathogen-free materials.
The plantlets are then hardened in glasshouses to adapt to external conditions and subsequently moved to growth rooms for multiplication and sub-culturing. This is followed by additional hardening in either glasshouses or screenhouses, depending on the crop's specific needs. Healthy plantlets are then distributed to stakeholders and conserved in vitro in growth rooms to maintain genetic diversity. Finally, some plantlets are conserved in vivo in
screenhouses to ensure long-term adaptation and preservation. This structured approach ensures that RTB EAGEL delivers high-quality, disease-free planting materials to support sustainable agriculture and food security in the region. The workflow and stages differ slightly from crop to crop and the same are reflected in the individual workflows (along with stages) attached in annexure.
4. Costing & Finance
RTB EAGLE derives its revenues from a diverse range of activities aligned with its mission of supporting agricultural research, genetic improvement, and capacity building. A significant portion of the revenue comes from the sale of in vivo and in vitro plant material, with in vivo cuttings and in vitro plantlets catering to both conservation needs and commercial requirements. These resources, cultivated in controlled environments to ensure quality and resilience, are essential for both the research community and agricultural industry stakeholders. Additional revenue channels include specialized services and training programs that leverage RTB EAGLE's research capabilities. Services like genotyping and diagnostics (certificates) offer crucial support to external projects and stakeholders, providing expert- level data and certification that are valuable for genetic research and agricultural compliance. Training and capacity-building programs, particularly in genomics and conservation techniques, extend RTB EAGLE's expertise to a broader audience, generating revenue through bench fees associated with research projects and grants. These diverse revenue streams enable RTB EAGLE to support its operational costs, advance research goals, and continually invest in innovative approaches to crop conservation and genetic enhancement.
Expenses encompass a broad range of costs. Variable costs form a significant portion of these expenses, covering necessary inputs like breeder material, consumables, soil, and growth media, all critical to the cultivation of high-quality plant material. Labor costs are also a substantial variable expense, as skilled staff and field workers are essential for daily operations and for managing plant propagation and conservation efforts. Additional variable expenses include transportation, which supports the movement of materials and personnel essential for research projects and outreach activities. Fixed costs, on the other hand, cover essential operational outlays such as power, fuel, and salaries for permanent staff. Capital investments represent longer-term expenditures aimed at enhancing the infrastructure needed for sustained research excellence. These investments include the construction and maintenance of buildings, acquisition of machinery, and regular upgrades to research equipment. Shared costs help streamline operations by covering administrative and support functions that benefit multiple projects within RTB EAGLE.
